subtopic: TRANSRADIO PRESS SERVICE-FINDING OF DIES COMMITTEE OF UNITED STATES CONGRESS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRANSRADIO PRESS SERVICE-FINDING OF DIES COMMITTEE OF UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
In view of the white paper issued by the Dies committee of the United States congress, which purports to establish that the Transocean news service is a combined German propaganda and espionage service, and that the Transradio press service is its transmitting and receiving agency, will the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), who has under his wing Canadian broadcasting, take the necessary steps to deal with the use of broadcasting facilities in Canada by the Transradio press service?

Interest Rates and Rents

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: TRANSRADIO PRESS SERVICE-FINDING OF DIES COMMITTEE OF UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
My hon. friend was kind enough to give me notice of this question. The governors of the broadcasting corporation are meeting in Ottawa next week, and will no doubt give consideration to the situation as developed by the Dies committee report.
I called the attention of the house as long ago as last June to the fact that we were not sure of the sources of certain information that was being broadcast. I think I went as far at that time as the situation warranted. Steps were taken to ban Transradio from the air. A storm of protest was aroused, and I think my hon. friend was one of those who protested in this house against the action we were taking.

subtopic: TRANSRADIO PRESS SERVICE-FINDING OF DIES COMMITTEE OF UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext: I do not recall it.

subtopic: TRANSRADIO PRESS SERVICE-FINDING OF DIES COMMITTEE OF UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
There was a storm of protest in the press; it was suggested that we were trying to muzzle news. The result was that it was felt that a comprehensive rearrangement of news over the air should be worked out. The broadcasting corporation has been working on that problem since then and has laid definite plans for a new type of news service beginning January 1 next.
In the meantime I may say that our censors have carefully watched the news put out by the forty or fifty broadcasting stations in Canada that have handled Transradio news, and they have found nothing whatever to complain about in the type of news put out.
I think the broadcasting stations that handle Transradio news will each have a problem of their own in the matter of deciding whether they wish to continue that news. I think they will have to decide a problem in public relations. Every one of those stations violently protested when the government suggested it was unwise for .them to carry that type of news, and I think perhaps we can leave them to work out their problem in their own way, until the broadcasting corporation decide what steps are to be taken in the matter.

subtopic: APARTMENT HOUSES IN TORONTO AND DISTRICT- SUGGESTED ACTION ON HIGH INTEREST CHARGES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: APARTMENT HOUSES IN TORONTO AND DISTRICT- SUGGESTED ACTION ON HIGH INTEREST CHARGES
speechtext:
I wish to ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) a question. During the discussion of his estimates on August 6 last I asked him if he would look into the question of rent control and high rates of interest. He said he would be glad to do so. Since that time he has given some measure of rent control. But I would call his attention to the high rents being charged by some apartment house owners in Toronto and district.
The second part of my question is this: Can something not be done about the exorbitant rates of interest charged by loan companies, loan sharks and others, dealt with last year by parliament? Will the minister look into this point and see whether the War Measures Act could not be broadened out as I suggested last August, to include not only the national moratorium referred to in that debate but some order in council dealing with high interest rates?

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: APARTMENT HOUSES IN TORONTO AND DISTRICT- SUGGESTED ACTION ON HIGH INTEREST CHARGES
speechtext:
The question of the hon. member
is somewhat of a double-barrelled one. In the first place, as he says, steps have been taken to have some regulation of rentals in areas where the war situation has created congestion bringing about an abnormal rise in rents. That of course comes under the regulations of the war-time prices and trade board, and a rentals administrator has been appointed. I shall be glad to call his attention to the matter of high rentals being charged in certain apartment houses in Toronto.
As to the second part of the hon. member's question, relating to interest rates being charged on mortgages, as I understood him to say, and possibly on other contracts, that is hardly a matter that comes within the purview of the Labour department. I suggest that the hon. member consider directing this part of the question to the Minister of Finance or to the minister whose department would be more directly concerned.

subtopic: APARTMENT HOUSES IN TORONTO AND DISTRICT- SUGGESTED ACTION ON HIGH INTEREST CHARGES
speechtext:
The War Measures Act,
I understand, takes precedence over existing legislation. There is no more difficulty about dealing with interest than with rents. It is the same point.

subtopic: QUESTION OF DISCLOSING UNIT PRICES OF MATERIALS SUPPLIED TO MILITARY DISTRICTS- GARBAGE CANS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: QUESTION OF DISCLOSING UNIT PRICES OF MATERIALS SUPPLIED TO MILITARY DISTRICTS- GARBAGE CANS
speechtext: In a return brought down on Wednesday last, sessional paper No. 121, moved for by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) with respect to the purchase of 26,000 garbage cans for use in military camps, the Department of National Defence refuses to answer the inquiry with respect to the price paid, taking the. attitude that it is not in the public interest to give unit prices on any commodity.

subtopic: QUESTION OF DISCLOSING UNIT PRICES OF MATERIALS SUPPLIED TO MILITARY DISTRICTS- GARBAGE CANS
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: QUESTION OF DISCLOSING UNIT PRICES OF MATERIALS SUPPLIED TO MILITARY DISTRICTS- GARBAGE CANS
speechtext:
I desire to call attention to this portion of the return and to ask if this is to be the considered policy of the government. Surely this house has the right to know the cost to the country of even such a prosaic item as garbage cans.
Furthermore, I desire to make this statement, that a portion of the return is incorrect, to my own knowledge and to the knowledge of the hon. member -for Victoria-Carleton.

subtopic: QUESTION OF DISCLOSING UNIT PRICES OF MATERIALS SUPPLIED TO MILITARY DISTRICTS- GARBAGE CANS
speechtext: Your knowledge might be incorrect.

subtopic: QUESTION OF DISCLOSING UNIT PRICES OF MATERIALS SUPPLIED TO MILITARY DISTRICTS- GARBAGE CANS
speechtext:
It states that all these garbage cans were put into immediate use. To my own knowledge and to the knowledge of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton those which were assigned to military district No. 7-929-were not put into immediate use but were stored in a warehouse in the city of Saint John under storage expense. They were delivered there in March last at a time when there were no military camps in existence in New Brunswick and when, so far as I know, none were even announced.
I call the attention of the government to this because some official has made a statement which is-I shall not say untruthful, but incorrect. The minister is away and he certainly is not responsible. But I do desire to know if we are to be given in returns or in answers to questions information with respect to commodities used for military purposes and with respect to storage. If there is no one here who can answer now I should like to have the question stand as a notice so that the matter can be looked into. It is a very small thing, but there is a matter of principle at stake.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: QUESTION OF DISCLOSING UNIT PRICES OF MATERIALS SUPPLIED TO MILITARY DISTRICTS- GARBAGE CANS
speechtext:
I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend both as to the importance of the matter involved and as to the principle.

I Shall' be very glad to ask the appropriate officers of the department to inquire thoroughly into all matters relating to the garbage cans.

subtopic: REPORTED DECISION TO ESTABLISH PROPOSED NEW NAVAL COLLEGE NEAR VICTORIA, B.C.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED DECISION TO ESTABLISH PROPOSED NEW NAVAL COLLEGE NEAR VICTORIA, B.C.
speechtext:
I desire to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald). In a Canadian Press dispatch from Halifax, appearing in newspapers over Canada under date of the twenty-first instant, it is stated that the city council of Halifax has asked the federal government to establish Canada's proposed new naval college at Halifax. In the dispatch it is stated that Mr. R. W. Mayhew, Liberal member of the House of Commons for Victoria-for whom I have every respect-had stated in Ottawa on the same day that he was authorized-"authorized," Mr. Speaker,-to state that the academy would be located near Victoria.
Will the minister state whether the hon. member for Victoria was authorized to make that statement; is it correct; if so, what reason does the minister give for not relocating the naval college at Halifax; and, why should not the minister himself, and not a private member, make such a statement?
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Apparently there has been some confusion in the mind of the newspaper man who gave to his paper a dispatch purporting to come from the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mayhew). There are really two things involved here: first, the question of the site of the naval college; second, the additional training for short periods, three or four months, which is necessary now under the stress of war to prepare officers for their commands.
In connection with the short training period it is true that we are seeking some additional quarters on the west coast; and on the east coast we have erected some buildings for the purpose which I have already mentioned, namely giving officers a short term course.

subtopic: REPORTED DECISION TO ESTABLISH PROPOSED NEW NAVAL COLLEGE NEAR VICTORIA, B.C.
speechtext: There will be only one naval college?

two?

It

mind when he spoke to the press men. They have construed that to mean that a site for a naval college has been selected. That is not the case; a site has not yet been selected for the college.

regret to say that I did not hear my hon. friend's question. If he will set it forth in writing I shall be glad to consider it and answer it the next day. I found it difficult to hear him at this distance.

I am rather sorry that in this far corner I was unable to hear distinctly what the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services said. I think that as a matter of privilege I should be entitled to repeat what actually happened.
While negotiations were going on for the property in question, I was familiar with certain circumstances and received permission, not from the minister but from other departments, to tell the people at home that that property had been bought for the purposes of the navy. The Canadian Press asked me yesterday to make a further statement, and I requested their representative to go to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services for the information. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, November 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Brooke Claxton for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Hanson (York-Sun-bury), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Blackmore.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to follow the lead of my colleagues and confine my remarks to the activities of my department which more intimately touch our war activities. Ordinarily there would be the war work of the national research council. My difficulty here is that, in spite of the magnificent work which is being done by that body, it is necessarily hedged around with the utmost secrecy. This interesting story will have to be told at another time. To-day I plan to confine my remarks to wheat.
May I just briefly express my appreciation of the remarks which have been made on this subject during the course of this debate by hon. members opposite. They have approached the subject in a fair, helpful and constructive manner. We all know that if we were faced with a very serious wheat problem when we were here last session, the gravity of the 1941 wheat outlook is many times more serious. Before touching on 1941 I propose to review the 1940 situation.
I desire to give to the house as detailed a statement as possible of the situation in regard to wheat since the house rose in August.
At the last session of the house I asked for certain amendments to the wheat board act as it then stood. These amendments were particularly important because they dealt with the appointment of an advisory committee to the wheat board, provision for regulation of deliveries, a new section dealing with the processing levy, and the inclusion of Vancouver with Fort William and Montreal as a delivery point on which the advance payment is made.
Before proceeding to deal with action which has been taken under the amendments to the act I desire to give to the house a statement of the position in which we found ourselves as the harvesting season approached and during that time.
With the close of the crop year at July 31 last, we had on hand 273,086,845 bushels of wheat in Canada and we had, in prospect, the harvesting of a wheat crop far in excess of the normal expectations of the agricultural industry. As the crop matured, it was seen
338	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. MacKinnon (Edmonton)
that provision would have to be made for a crop of at least 500 million bushels and the final result in the west now approximates 520 million bushels. Immediate consideration had to be given to the question how this crop was to be handled.
Because we realized that, unless storage facilities were available, a very difficult financial situation would arise for wheat producers, our aim was to provide for the handling of an amount of grain equal, at least, to that delivered by producers from a normal crop. The average wheat crop of western Canada over a period of the last ten years is 307,012,800 bushels out of which there was an average marketing of 262,390,535 bushels. But we went higher than this, and took as a basis for our plans an abnormal crop of 400 million bushels, about 100 million higher, and we reasoned that, if the government, through the wheat board, was able to take delivery of 335 million bushels, which would represent the deliverable part of a 400 million bushel crop, we would have placed the prairie farmer and western business interests in a position approximately coinciding with the normal expenditure of both these factors in the western economy.
Normally, of course, not more than 80 per cent of this 335 million bushels would be marketed in the first four months of the crop year to December first, and 20 per cent from December 1 to July 31 of the following year. Therefore, we set ourselves the task of arranging to take at least 268 million bushels by December 1.
To ensure that the farmers who threshed earliest, and that those who lived in close proximity to the elevators would not be able to deliver all their grain and thus shut out other farmers, the wheat board exercised the authority given to them at the last session and issued permit books. These books contained an affidavit to be signed by the farmer setting out the total seeded acreage that he had, the location of this acreage and the point at which he desired to deliver his grain. A statutory declaration covering these points was made in duplicate, one copy to be left in the permit book and the other returned to the wheat board at Winnipeg. As the farmer delivered his grain the exact amount was entered in the permit book.
In passing I may say that the wheat board have received nearly 300,000 of these statutory declarations, and they provide us with a fund of information in regard to seeded acreages which will be extremely valuable in connection with arrangements which may be made during the next crop year.

The purpose of the permit book was to provide an equitable sharing of the available elevator space. It was difficult, at the start, to know just what this share would be, but on the basis of preliminary calculations the wheat board first announced a quota of five bushels each of wheat, oats and barley per seeded acre. We immediately got hundreds of requests that the three quotas be made interchangeable, but it was originally calculated by the wheat board that, on this basis, not over three or three and one-half bushels of wheat could be taken. The wheat board knew from actual experience that the full' quota of five bushels each of oats and bailey would not be delivered by all the farmers as the greater quantity of these grains are held on the farms for feed purposes.
Because deliveries were inadequate to meet the demand for barley, the quota was increased from five bushels to ten bushels per acre on August 24, and on September 4 this quota was removed entirely. It was found that the bulk of barley was held for feed, deliveries would not exceed the demand, and would not interfere with storage. The action in removing the barley quota entirely has been fully justified by the result.
Because of a similar situation the quota on oats was removed entirely on September 9. Actually, the demand for oats has kept pace with the deliveries.
The first increase in the wheat quota came on September 9 and a large number of points were increased to 8, 10, 12 and 15 bushels per acre. With the gradual clarification of the situation, the general quota all over western Canada was increased on September 13 from five bushels per acre to eight.
The five bushel per acre quota would have provided for delivery of 139 million bushels. The eight bushel quota provided for delivery of 222 million bushels.
To clarify the situation, Mr. Speaker, with the consent of the house I would like to place on Hansard a statement showing the acreage in the three western provinces, the yield per acre, the production, the marketable surplus, the amount provided by the quotas and the quotas in percentage of marketable surplus, and also a statement showing the actual deliveries which have been made in the three provinces, and the percentage of deliveries to quota.

I am not going to take the time of the house to give these figures in detail now but I would summarize them by saying the total wheat area was 27,750,000 acres; the average yield per acre in the three provinces was 18.7 bushels, giving a total production of 520 million bushels, the figure mentioned a moment ago.
It will be noted that the actual yields were as follows: Saskatchewan, 16.7 bushels per acre, Manitoba, 19.9, and Alberta, 21.9. Allowing approximately 681 million bushels for feed, seed, etc., this left a marketable surplus estimated at approximately 451,500,000 bushels. The eight bushel quota provided for 222 million bushels. As at November 19, just the other day, additional quotas have been authorized at different points to an amount of 76,000,000 bushels, making total possible deliveries under the quotas 298,603,000 bushels or 66 per cent of the total marketable surplus. Actually as at November 15-just a week ago-223,819,660 bushels had been delivered, or a total of 74 per cent of the established quotas, as at the 19th. Please note that quotas have been provided for
298,603,000	bushels, although for one reason or another deliveries to the extent of 223,819,660 bushels only have actually been received.
At the present time 70 per cent of the shipping points in western Canada have a quota of over eight bushels, some of these running as high as twenty bushels where exceptional storage space is available or where very exceptional conditions have to be met, and I am now informed that the general quota will be raised from eight bushels to ten bushels next week. There will be further quotas established from time to time during the crop year as wheat is moved into export and consumption channels.
You will see from these figures, Mr. Speaker, that the board have been successful through the splendid cooperation of the elevator companies in providing storage, sufficient to look after the marketable surplus from a much greater than average crop, as mentioned by me a few minutes ago.
It is interesting also to compare the deliveries this year to date with the deliveries in previous years. The actual marketings from August 1 to November 15 have averaged during the last ten years 183,098,831 bushels. In the last three years, the average marketings have been 218,229,357 bushels, so that the actual marketings so far this year have exceeded both the three-year and the ten-year average and, as a matter of fact, have been exceeded only in four previous years- 1928, 1932, 1938 and 1939. The latter year, you will remember, Mr. Speaker, was not only 
a very heavy crop year, but a year in which the grain was marketed at an exceptionally rapid rate.
It is also interesting to note that the value of the crop marketed to November 15 is almost 810,000,000 over the average for the past ten years and is only $21,800,000 less than the average for the last three years up to that date. What is most important, however, is that the farmers will still have wheat undelivered to the value of over 120 million dollars, which is 70 to 80 million dollars more than the value of the grain in their hands at this date during any time in the last ten years. This is a large reserve of payment or purchasing power.
I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, something of the problem that the government has had to face in the last two years. We set a price of 70 cents per bushel for No. 1 wheat in store at Fort William and Vancouver, and for eastern Canada at Montreal, for both the 1939 and 1940 crops. The 1939 crop in the prairie provinces amounted to 493 million bushels. The 1940 crop, as I have said, is estimated at 520 million bushels. This means that in addition to the enormous expenditure on Canada's war effort, the dominion government has extended a guaranteed price on production totalling over one billion bushels of wheat, of which amount we expect approximately 900 million bushels will be delivered by the farmers.
We did this in the full knowledge of the effect that the war was having upon markets for wheat. The war itself and particularly Hitler's aggressions have greatly restricted the range of our markets. For example, in July, 1939, Canada shipped wheat to eleven countries in Europe, and in August, 1940, Canada shipped wheat to three countries only in Europe, the United Kingdom, Eire and Portugal, approximately 600,000 bushels in all to the latter two countries. Through its maintenance of a guaranteed price, and through the activities of the Canadian wheat board, the government prevented the effects of this narrowing of markets from falling upon the Canadian wheat producers, particularly of the prairie provinces and upon the western economy as a whole.
With the approach of the harvest season there was general fear throughout the west that with only a five bushel quota there would be widespread financial difficulties because of the inability of the farmers to obtain enough money from the grain they were allowed to market to provide for their necessary expenses. Quite frankly I also shared that view and so stated in this house at the close of the last session. The situation, however, improved much more rapidly than we had anticipated and the general quota increase from five-

The Address-Mr. MacKinnon (Edmonton)
bushels to eight bushels, together with the further increases in the quotas at so many points, materially changed the picture.
There are those who say that still more should-have been done. In addition to guaranteeing a price we should, they claim, either directly or through the chartered banks, undertake to advance up to 75 per cent of the value of all wheat remaining on farms, which would actually mean that we would have to extend our immediate obligations in respect to wheat by at least 75 million dollars.
Advances on this scale would have meant adequate arrangements not only for provision of weather-proof and theft-proof storage facilities but also for the setting up of local organizations throughout the west to look after the inspection, measurement and sealing of the wheat. No one, I think, could rightly ask the federal government to launch a loan programme of this sort without having the wheat properly stored, and subject to proper inspection. Our first object then was to increase to the greatest possible extent the elevator storage facilities so that the farmers could secure the full price for more of their grain.
We had in all a rated storage capacity of Slightly more than 442 million bushels including annexes. After allowing for working space this gave us an estimated 420 million bushels of actual storage capacity. As at July 31, there were 243 million bushels already in storage, leaving the available space at approximately 177 million bushels. I am dealing here, of course, only with Canadian storage. Steps were taken to encourage the construction of additional storage facilities throughout the prairies, and an agreement was made with elevator companies that the cost of temporary storage could be written off by them over a period of two years in reporting for income tax purposes. As a result of this action additional storage capacity to the extent of 60 million bushels has been built by elevator companies throughout the west.
With regard to loans against farm-stored wheat, the government approached the banks and elevator companies to act as principals in a loan programme. Because of the lack of adequate safe storage on the farms no private agency would assume the risk in making loans. These agencies, the banks and elevator companies, were in a better position to discriminate between good and bad risks than was the government, had the latter attempted to direct a lending programme. The very fact that private agencies would not interest themselves in this business suggested that a loan programme under the conditions of open storage on farms might be subject to wide abuses if undertaken by the government. The government had no alternative except to make as extensive provision as possible for deliveries from the farms and, as I have pointed out, this has to my mind been successfully accomplished.
We realize, of course, that even if we were able to accept normal deliveries, there would still be a large amount of grain which would have to be carried over on the farms for some months at least, and we adopted the principle of paying farmers the same rate of storage for grain held on the farm as was being paid to elevator companies, namely, two-thirds of a cent per bushel per month. This provision induced many farmers to provide extra storage for themselves, they preferring to store their own wheat and get the enhanced prices available thereby.
With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on Hansard the schedule of payments which will be made for farm storage.

It may be recalled that in my statement to the house at the last session I referred to the very considerable drop which had occurred in the price of wheat just at seeding time, due to the developments in Europe. The result of these developments was that instead of the farmers having a market of at least 90 cents a bushel, the actual price at Fort William was 71 and a fraction cents. It was felt that some arrangements should be made to assist the farmers, if at all possible, and the arrangement of the processing levy was decided upon. The amount of this levy was to be fixed by order in council but was not to exceed 15 cents per bushel according to the amendment. By order in council dated the 24th of July a levy of 15 cents per bushel was provided for, and it was realized that 15 cents a bushel would be the equivalent of 70 cents per barrel of flour.
When I announced the processing levy in the house, I stated that it was to be remembered that this levy should not result in an increase in the price of bread. Immediately the levy was announced, however, considerable agitation in regard to possible increases in bread prices commenced, and at Vancouver the price of bread was actually increased.
The war-time prices and trade board immediately took action, and on the 6th of August issued an order limiting the amount which could be passed on to consumers by the flour millers to one-half the levy.
A full investigation was held by the wartime prices and trade board of the representations made by the milling companies that they could not absorb one-half the levy in accordance with the board's order. The

The Address-Mr. MacKinnon (Edmonton)
position of the millers in this matter was substantiated after investigation by independent auditors, and the board on September 6 rescinded their previous order of the 6th of August and since that date the full levy has been passed on by the processors.
I have been represented in this debate as having stated that this processing levy would not be passed on to the consumer, but my only statement in this regard was the one to which I referred a few minutes ago when I said that it was not anticipated that the processing levy need result in an increase in the price of bread. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, there have been no increases in the price of bread, certain adjustments having been made by the bakers so as to absorb the processing levy.
Some farmers gristing their own wheat objected strenuously to paying this levy, but it has been our opinion to date that as the processing levy was intended for the benefit of the farmer he should not object to paying the comparatively small share which he was called upon to pay on wheat gristed for his own consumption.
Representations have been made of hardship in connection with this levy in certain parts of the maritime provinces and this is a matter that is giving us concern at the present time.
In the maritime provinces-Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick at least-a number of mills have been established to serve local communities. These mills have been started, I believe, by the provincial government, and I am told that they are just barely able to keep going and that this processing tax is bearing heavily upon them. It is not really a heavy tax, but in their present position they find it difficult to handle the levy. This is, as I have said, under consideration.

I would like to express my apreciation of the very great interest which has been shown by every member of this committee. Three meetings have been held, the first on August 26 and 27, the second on September 30 and October 1, and the third on Monday and Tuesday of this week. Another meeting will be held in about two weeks' time.
At the meeting this week the committee considered, with the wheat board, possible plans for 1941 and ensuing years. A subcommittee consisting of Messrs. Farnalls, Reece, Reid, Wesson and Campbell is now working on the whole problem and this subcommittee will report to a meeting of the whole advisory committee early in December. All members of the committee have shown a real desire to be of every possible assistance to the wheat board in working out the problems which have confronted them. Full reports have been made to me as directed by the act.
There have been many representations made this year to both the board of grain commissioners and to myself personally, and I am sure to my colleagues and to members of the house generally, in connection with grading of this year's crop. I suppose there is never a year when there are not complaints from some quarters in regard to the grades, but I would point out that under the board of grain commissioners we have built up an inspection and grading service which is recognized as second to none in the world. The result has been that a certificate issued by the grain board is accepted at face value in any part of the world to-day. It is important to our whole wheat export business that there be no lowering of the standard of our grades.
The most insistent complaint in connection with grading this year came as the result of the prevalence of cracked wheat in the deliveries. This, we are advised, was largely due to the fulness of the kernels, the dryness of the wheat and the fact that farmers were not properly adjusting their combines and their threshing machines. Ordinarily a certain

amount of cracked wheat can be permitted, but the situation became so widely prevalent that action had to be taken. The board of grain commissioners issued a statement, and followed that up with a broadcast by Mr. J. Ansel Anderson of the grain research laboratory. Once the matter was called to the attention of the farmers and remedies suggested, the prevalence of the occurrence of this cracked wheat immediately became less pronounced and comparatively few complaints were made in the last few weeks of the threshing season.
Another matter, Mr. Speaker, that has given us considerable concern was the situation that arose in Alberta due to a very large quantity of tough and damp wheat, the consequence of bad weather which occurred during harvest time in a portion of Alberta which ordinarily enjoys a dry harvesting season. It was at first estimated that a total of not more than 25 million bushels was in this category. Recent surveys would indicate that the figure will be very considerably less. Because there was no certainty at first that the elevator companies would be able to ship this wheat out before it began to deteriorate in their elevators, deliveries for a while were impossible. The wheat board took prompt action. Chief Commissioner Mr. George Mclvor and some of his staff made a special trip to Alberta to check personally on the situation. As a result immediate arrangements were made for additional cars to be placed at the particular stations affected, and this car movement is now working satisfactorily so that deliveries from farmers of tough and damp grain will be moved to terminal elevators for drying purposes. This will relieve what otherwise might have developed into a serious situation, with producers suffering loss on account of deterioration of their wheat.

Before going on to deal with the situation in the coming crop year, I would like to touch briefly on one matter which is frequently brought to our attention. This is the possibility of finding new uses for wheat.

Every probable avenue has been tentatively, if not exhaustively, explored by our national research council for years. The most popular idea is the development of power alcohol from wheat, but our experiments to date show that this is not economically practical. To make it so, according to our experiments, wheat would have to be purchased for about thirty cents a bushel. Experiments and investigations are continuing.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, those of us particularly charged with the responsibility for wheat are endeavouring to arrange for the construction of additional wheat storage. This we believe is needed to enable us to carry out our intention to accept from the producers all of the 1940 wheat crop in this crop year.
None of us is unmindful of the situation which we shall have to face, in dealing with the 1941 crop. We here, and those vitally interested in wheat production and in wheat handling, are and have been giving intense study to this problem. There can be great changes in the situation in a few months' time, but we all fully recognize that a wheat policy covering the 1941-42 crop year must be announced some time in February, well in advance of the seeding season. From the standpoint of the wheat board and my Department of Trade and Commerce, unless there are radical and unexpected developments overseas, the 1941 wheat policy will have to be decided upon with a knowledge that apart from domestic consumption only between possibly 140 and 175 million bushels can be exported in the crop year ending July 31, 1942.
I would remind the house that as Minister of Trade and Commerce, it is the marketing facilities through the board of grain commissioners and the wheat board which are under my jurisdiction. In other words, my department's responsibility begins with the delivery of the wheat to us. Any matters relating to operations on the farm lie within the jurisdiction of my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and with the provincial departments of agriculture.
I have endeavoured, Mr. Speaker, to cover all the points which have been brought to my attention since the house rose in August and to give to the house as much information as possible. I would like to say to the hon. members of this house that we stand ready at all times to give as complete and full information to them, respecting the wheat situation, as can properly be given. It is obviously impossible, however, for me to disclose the situation of the wheat board in regard to actual sales or actual prices at which sales have been made. I say also quite sincerely that we will welcome constructive criticism.

The Address-Mr. Bruce
I would like to express my sincere appreciation 'to the members of this house representing constituencies other than those in western Canada for the sympathetic consideration which we have received from them in dealing with the problems of the prairie wheat producer. The majority of the members realize the difficulties which the western farmers are facing, and it has been a matter of considerable gratification to me to know that we have the generous support of these members in connection with the actions which have been taken dealing with the wheat problem.
The problems which have been faced by the wheat board in the last few months have been tremendously difficult. I believe that the members of the board are to be congratulated on having so capably handled the problem. They have had to evolve and put into practice new methods and new ideas. That has been done successfully and with the minimum of friction. I wish to assure every member of this house, and particularly those representing agriculture, that this government stands squarely behind a policy of giving the utmost protection to the farmer. That, I think, has been proven by the burden which we have already assumed. We all understand that our primary purpose at this time must be so to organize our whole economic life in Canada that our success in the war will not be jeopardized in any degree. I believe the great majority of farmers are reasonably satisfied with what has been done and will be done by this government.
I hope that what I have said this afternoon will not be construed as an argument that all the wheat growers are in a happy position to-day and that little need be done for them. They are n6t unmindful of the responsibilities that Canada is assuming, and although the 70 cent per bushel advance payment may not give many farmers even a meagre profit over cost of production they are accepting this as part of their contribution to the war effort. We are undertaking to see that they do not bear an unfair share of the burden.

The United States have recently decided to build 300,000 pre-fabricated houses to take care of the situation which they expect to develop there during the coming year, and I think Canada, because of our great timber resources, is in a particularly fortunate position to undertake the building of pre-fabricated houses. Another matter which I had thought of discussing at this time but which perhaps will also be better deferred until after the Christmas recess is the question of national health insurance. When the national Unemployment Insurance Act was put on the statute books last session, nothing was done with regard to the problem of health. When the British House of Commons passed their national Unemployment Insurance Act in 1911, the first part, and I think the most important part of that act, dealt with health insurance, comprising not only insurance against ill health which necessitates the loss of employment but also the prevention and
The Address-Mr. Bruce

cure of sickness. I was in England when that act was introduced in the British House of Commons and I remember very well the many protests from the medical profession. As members of this house and members of the government, most of whom are professional men, know, there is always a degree of suspicion and fear lest some new enactment may interfere with the prerogatives of members of a profession. Although that fear was expressed loudly throughout England at the time, I am happy to be able to say that in the course of ten or fifteen years the men who were loudest in their protests against the enactment of health insurance in England admitted that it was a good thing not only for the British people but also for the medical practitioners as well; and to-day I think the profession in the mother country will be found to be unanimous in their support of the national health act. Hon. members may know that Germany introduced a similar act fifty years ago, and I believe it has operated successfully in that country.
I mention this now because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has told us that in January he is calling the premiers of the provinces together to consider the Rowell-Sirois report, and I hope that at that time this question will be brought to the fore, and that perhaps, if the provinces will give their consent, an amendment to the national Unemployment Insurance Act will be undertaken during the next session to include this important matter of health.

Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to join with the many other members who have addressed this house at this particular session, in expressing my pleasure at the high character of the addresses of the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I sometimes think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and others long experienced in this House of Commons must feel a certain degree of pleasure in seeing the influx of young men into our parliamentary life, and I am inclined to suppose, from talking to some of these older members, that this particular parliament is distinguished in that regard. It seemed to me a happy circumstance that

The Address-Mr. Graham
both the mover and the seconder were comparatively young men. and that they have elevated, by making such fine presentations to this house on that occasion, the high esteem which the country as a whole has for our young people.
As is quite proper, almost every hon. member who has addressed this house has dealt first with Canada's war effort. That undoubtedly is as it should be, because of course we are a unit in placing the war effort first in our minds and our hearts. There is no problem confronting this country that is not closely associated with the successful carrying on of that effort which we as a nation must make our foremost aim-as speedy a victory as possible in the war in which we are engaged. I for one desire to express to the Prime Minister and the members of his government my high appreciation of the leadership that he and his cabinet ire giving to the country and to parliament. I have listened to a number of criticisms directed at the government, but I admit that I am not so much concerned whether a particular unit is short a few shirts or a few boots if I am satisfied that the ministers in charge of our war effort are men of high integrity and lofty character, animated by the purpose with which we wish them to be animated, that is to say to give Canada the most efficient, effective and worth-while effort in the present war. Having listened to these accounts of stewardship given by the different ministers, may I say that to me, and I am sure to Canadians in general, the character, the working capacity and the high purpose of our ministers are a matter of great pride.
I have just finished reading a new life of the elder Pitt, Earl of Chatham, and when we think back to the political conditions which existed in those days we are inclined to wonder how there comes to be still an England. So again I wish to express my pride that, in the record which has been laid before this parliament and in the discussions that have followed, never by innuendo, by insinuation or by direct statement, having in mind the hundreds of millions of dollars which are being expended by this country in its war effort, has there been the slightest suggestion that the conduct of the government is not honest, that the men who are in charge of the war effort are not above possible reproach. It is no small thing that we as a country have men of such high character and integrity.
In connection with our war effort there are one or two matters of which I would like particularly to speak. One must again compliment the government upon having taken, at the outbreak of war, such speedy
rMr. Graham.]
action in attempting to control what might easily have been a course as disastrous as the one followed in the last war. I have in mind the matter of price control in respect of certain necessary commodities. That action must not have been taken without deliberation beforehand, and I believe the ministry is to be complimented upon having gained something from the lessons which were learned in such a costly manner during the last war, and upon applying the experience gained at that time to see that so far as humanly possible the same results may not flow again.
Yesterday I listened with keen interest indeed to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). With all essentials in that presentation I find myself in agreement. I suggest to him that in carrying out the financial policies of Canada the government must be careful to see to it that that equality of sacrifice based on ability to pay, as he described it, is fairly distributed among the different economic classes which make up our population. I know he has in mind that high purpose, but I would suggest to him that, despite all the efforts of the government there are certain results which spring, not from inflation but from the rapid expansion of the business life of the country. Naturally, labour becomes in greater demand.
I noticed a short time ago a request from the government that the practice of one industry of attempting to induce workmen to leave another industry, 'through the inducement of higher rates of pay, ought to be discouraged as something not in the interests of the whole. I believe the government realizes, however, that, despite the ability of the members on the price control board, it is an impossible task completely to eliminate a gradual rise in the cost of living during the great struggle in which we are engaged1. It seems to me, therefore, that the government must be extremely careful to see to it that the primary producers in Canada are not unfairly dealt with as a result of the expansionist movement which must come.
One or two of the speeches of hon. members in the official opposition have suggested to me a point which I believe ought to be discussed. I am a veteran of the last war, and I do not believe any veteran of that war would disagree with me when I say that on that occasion we had a definite path to follow. We had a certain number of months' training in Canada, and at that time our object was to reach England. After we arrived in England we received a few months more training, after which we were sent to France. The purpose we had set out to accomplish was then before our eyes, and we had a path we knew we were about to follow.

The Address*-Mr. Graham
It seems to me that in the present war the commissioned and non-commissioned officers and men who enlist in our army, air force or navy have a particularly high duty to perform in the service of their country. Human beings have not changed in some respects. When we are young we like to go places; when we are young we are full of energy and like -to do things. It seems to me that one of the tasks we must perform in connection with this type of warfare is so to train the officers and non-commissioned officers in their leadership that there will grow up in the ranks of our services a high respect for his majesty's uniform, and a high sense of the duty which devolves upon them. They are being confronted with a severe trial of patience, one -of the hardest trials to bear. Because of their inability to reach the front line and meet the enemy, they have a sense of frustration, and it seems to me that those who are their leaders must in some way inspire them to that high degree of character and patience which will help them to perform the task allotted to them in a manner of which not only will we be proud but which will reward them when they leave army life.
I like to think that hon. members, and particularly those who are veterans of the last war, have the duty of attempting to instil in the minds of the officer class with whom we come in contact the necessity for such direction. I believe the syllabus, the lectures on discipline, and a certain amount of the educational material being distributed among the men in the services should be designed with the idea of inspiring them, no matter what their ranks, with the duty that is cast upon them. They must be kept aware of the nature of their task, and of our hopes that they will discharge their duty with that high degree of credit attained by the men who served in the last war.
While listening to the debate I noticed the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) repeated what had been said at the last session by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), namely, that private members on this side of the house have a duty to perform in their relationship to the government, in much the same way as have private members in the opposition groups. I believe no one will disagree with that observation. I suggest, however, that that duty can be performed in many ways, and I would assure both those hon. gentlemen that members on this side of the house are performing their duty in many ways.
Sometimes I believe that the government must be confused with regard to the attitude taken by members of opposition groups. As
they point out, while it is their duty to oppose, to offer constructive criticism and to make suggestions, yet of necessity there must be a reasonable degree of consistency in those presentations. I could not help noting the paradox of the oft-repeated demand upon the government that they give more and more information, and greater detail as to what is being done, and the suggestion made yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver South that the government was spending too much time in that particular task. He suggested it should be engaged in giving attention to the education of the people in Canada, so that their efforts might be harnessed to our tremendous war effort.
