I do know, however, that
the hon. members to whom I have referred have in mind exactly the same idea as other hon. members have, namely, that the government of the day must conduct the war effort with the greatest degree of efficiency, and attempt to do all that is required. I suggest to the house that that is exactly what the government is doing-always bearing in mind the type of country in which we live, the people who live in it and the difficulties which must present themselves to any government of any political stripe which may have assumed the duty of conducting our war effort.
While it is true that as private members on this side of the house it is our duty to offer constructive criticism, I sometimes wonder whether we have not a somewhat heavier duty cast upon us than is placed upon the shoulders of members of opposition groups. Sometimes we envy the freedom with which the member in an opposition group may express himself. We on this side of the house are on a team, if I may so describe it, and we are charged with the duty of assisting the government in performing a task. On the other hand, members of the opposition may spray this side of the house with a machine-gun barrage of criticism, and they may direct their fire in any direction they see fit. Let me assure hon. members opposite that if -they will conduct themselves in the traditional manner of a good opposition we, in turn, on this side of the house, will perform our duty in the manner we deem fit and proper.
There are only two domestic matters upon which I should like to touch. One has been dealt with at considerable length to-day by
The Address-Mr. Graham

the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). I refer, of course, to what is known as the wheat problem. In discussing this particular problem I should like to take it out of that category of problems wi.th which western Canada only is concerned. If ever there were a national problem, in both size and the effect it has upon the country, it is surely this wheat problem. Of course, it is part and parcel of the problem of agriculture, and I want to say to hon. members from Ontario and the other eastern provinces that we from the west recognize it as such. When any problem affecting agriculture in the eastern provinces arises, they will find us ready and willing to assist them in securing measures of relief. In turn, we hope that they will help us when this huge problem confronts us.
I need not remind the house that many hon. members from western Canada were born in Ontario and the other eastern provinces. Many of us grew up in the east. We are, therefore, in a dual position and are able to appreciate, to some extent at least, the attitude of mind of the Ontario people, for example, and the attitude of mind of the people of western Canada. It is only by a joint and common effort in tackling all these problems that we can hope to find a solution.
I listened with more than usual interest to the address of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when he dealt quite fully with this problem. It will be recalled that he suggested that last year in western Canada-I think he had Saskatchewan particularly in mind-there had occurred what he described as a racket in connection with the grading and handling of wheat by the elevator system. I know the hon. member is the owner of an elevator. He is a member of this house and obviously he has taken a great interest in this particular question. He is also the operator of a large farm. I am sure he made that statement, having fully in mind his responsibility as a member of parliament.
I agree with him that if any such condition exists, it should be remedied immediately, but I must confess that I am a little surprised that such a charge could be made against the elevators in the particular province from which I come. We have a great cooperative elevator system known as the Saskatchewan wheat pool, and I can hardly credit that that organization, which dominates the elevator situation in that province, would lend itself to what might easily be described as a racket. I sincerely hope that this will be the final conclusion that we reach after all the information has been received. I feel sure that the wheat pool, by its example and fairness in handling the farmers' wheat, will have shown that there is no opportunity in my
fMr. Graham.]
province for the carrying on of any such racket as that described by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
The matter is one that seemingly could easily be checked. As I understand it, all wheat goes through the wheat board and there is a record, not only of the number of bushels but of the different grades of wheat which have passed through the country elevators. We know the amounts that were in the elevators prior to the marketing of this year's wheat, and it seems to me that it would be easy to determine whether the elevator systems had profited to any extent, great or small, at the expense of the producers.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle seemed to have little but criticism of the policy adopted by the government last year in connection with wheat. My experience has been somewhat different. Leaving aside for the moment the initial price paid to the farmer, I would say that the quota system adopted by the government has given the farmer an opportunity to market his crop in instalments. I suggest to the hon. member that that is not an unmixed evil. A great many benefits have been derived as a result of the farmer being given that opportunity. It will be remembered that the hon. member compared the amount of wheat delivered on a certain day in 1939 with the amount delivered on the same date in 1940, and estimated that some $50,000,000 less was in circulation in 1940 as compared with 1939. But any one who has lived in Saskatchewan will know that had that $50,000,000 been paid out, it would not have reached the hands of the producing farmers. In all likelihood it would have gone into the hands of the so-called creditor class. While we may have a certain measure of sympathy .for some of the creditor class, our first concern in this wheat crisis is for the farmer.
So we find that the farmer who was blessed with a crop, despite the fact that he could market only his quota, has a certain sense of security from looking at his well filled granaries. They are filled with a commodity which we all believe has an actual worth and will continue to be an actual asset to him for the coming year until deliveries are completed. Of course, all this is conditioned upon the agencies of the government being able to give an opportunity to the individual farmer actually to deliver his quota. In addition, it is based upon the assumption, as clearly indicated by the government policy, that before the end of the present crop year the farmer will be enabled to market practically all his crop.
Those of us who have lived long in the west know that there is a certain amount of value in the fact that throughout the year

The Address-Mr. Graham
the income of the farmer will be spread out, so that on no occasion will he be presented with an emergency or crisis in his family household. But I say to the government, and particularly to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that if an individual farmer in a certain district has not been able to deliver his quota of grain, the government should take notice of that and realize that it will be impossible for such a man to get along without some method of converting into cash the only commodity he has, that is, wheat.
All things considered, I find myself viewing with considerable satisfaction the application and the working out of the quota system as applied by the government last year under its wheat policy. Like other hon. members,
I realize that it would have been of greater value to the farmer had it been announced at an earlier date, but I realize also that there is considerable justification for the government not announcing its policy before it did.
We must remember also that at that time weather conditions made uncertain the type of crop yield in the west, and remember again the position of our usual markets. We all know that France unfortunately was in the midst of a break-down and that that market was disappearing. In addition, we did not know and we do not yet know the attitude of Russia. The same applies to Japan. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we never do expect the superhuman from the government, and when we remember the uncertainty as to the amount of crop we would have to deal with, and the uncertainty as to available markets, it is not, to me at least, a matter of wonderment that the government waited as long as time would permit for these important factors to become as clear as they could.
But, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has properly pointed out, in this crop year 1941 a wholly different situation presents itself. We now know fairly well the markets available to us. It is true we do not know the amount of the 1941 crop, but we do know the extent of the nationally-owned storage space available in the crop year 1941, and so I was highly pleased to hear the minister state to the house to-day that it was the intention of the government to pursue its study of this problem and in February, when the house reconvenes, to make an announcement of its policy for 1941.
What are some of the problems? I propose briefly to outline them without at the moment suggesting a solution.
Obviously the Storage problem is one which will have to be solved. We now know that we shall likely enter the next crop year with
all the present storage capacity filled. If that is the situation, it seems to me that the government must do one of two things, or both. One is to adopt a policy of increasing the present storage owned by the elevator systems or by the government. That, it will be noted, would permit the continuation of the quota system, if sufficient space were available, without having to advance money on the wheat in the farmer's hands. On the other hand the government might encourage the farmer more than it did last year to build granaries or storage facilities on his own farm sufficient to handle a larger portion of his crop. It seems to me a necessary corollary of the adoption of that policy or of both policies-the extension of our national storage facilities and encouraging the farmer to increase his own storage facilities on the farm-that the government must in this crop year consider the necessity of having to finance in some way the farmer who is holding his wheat on the farm.
There are in western Canada areas in which the mixed farming type of agriculture could, of course, be greatly increased, but there are other districts, my own among them, in which that would be found impossible, not because the farmers there do not desire to do so, but because climate, type of soil and other fixed conditions make it absolutely essential for them to continue the growing of wheat as the only possible method of staying in the farming business. For many of these fanners there is no possibility of changing from wheat to a mixed type of farming unless, I suggest, the government carries out a vigorous policy of broadening and making a greater use of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
In my particular district I had, during the recess, the pleasure of visiting the Maple Creek project, and it seemed to me that I could have done the prairie farm rehabilitation scheme and the eastern members of this house a great service if I could have taken them on that trip with me. The hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Evans) was kind enough to take me over that sixteen-mile project and nothing, I think, could be more astounding than to see how an otherwise barren district had been converted by the use of conservation of water into an oasis flowing, metaphorically speaking, with milk and honey. That project is a wise and worth-while idea. It will enable feed and fodder to be available to districts south and west of the project which have suffered from a visitation of grasshoppers. So if, perchance, the government intends to pursue a policy which will encourage the farmer to change his methods of farming and to go
The Address-Mr. Graham

into a more mixed type of farming, I should like to see joined with that a generous appropriation for Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act purposes, so that those districts which could be served by the provisions of that act would be given that opportunity.
Having dealt with the question of storage, I should like to discuss the question of price, which must be considered again this year. I know that representations were made by almost all the western members with regard to the price for last year's crop. The decision of the government was announced. But it seems to me that even if the government adopt the same line of reasoning this year as last year, they may have to recognize the rising cost of living and the necessity of putting the farmer in a position of equality with that of the year 1939. That is a subject which, I am aware, will require a great deal of consideration. The quota system itself has worked out fairly well; but if it is our desire not to encourage the growing of any greater quantity of wheat than is necessary this crop year, we must remember that there is in that quota system itself a certain encouragement to increased wheat acreage, and as the United Grain Growers' Grain Company of Winnipeg has pointed out, the government might well consider, in this whole problem of voluntary reduction of wheat acreage, changing the basis from that of acreage to that of bushels. I think that point deserves consideration.
The question of storage charges which was raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle raises the question whether, in the light of the experience that we have had during the past year, it might not be wise to take over all of the elevator storage capacity in Canada. We all recall that last year the elevator companies were quite pleased to offer to the government the taking over of their plant, provided that the government would compensate them with a return of some 6 per cent on the capital invested. I know that this is not something which would be done in normal times, but because of the nature of the problem, and because particularly of this constant and reiterated demand that storage and other service charges be reduced, it may be the policy of wisdom for the government to take over the elevator system and the storage facilities of this country.
I have already referred to the question of crop acreage. I think it is the consensus of opinion of those who live in western Canada that the only way in which we can wisely and effectively accomplish any crop reduction would be, not by any compulsory method but by encouraging a reduction in the wheat
[Mr. Graham.3
acreage and by the improvement of farming methods. I know that in my own district this year peculiar weather conditions resulted in a fairly good crop on summer-fallow and practically none on stubble. That in itself will be an encouragement to the average farmer who is not already doing so, to summer-fallow more of his land and to discontinue the sowing of grain on stubble.
The use of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, together with encouragement to the farmers to take up some other method of marketing coarse grain and wheat, or any other product they may go into, is the only means whereby we can reasonably hope to achieve success in the endeavour to reduce crop acreage.
Then there is the relationship between Britain and Canada in the marketing of wheat. The other night I listened with a good deal of pleasure to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I have followed closely everything he has said on this subject, not only in this house but elsewhere, and I was interested to hear him recount his experience and the knowledge gained in England. One of the points that emerged from his discussion is the fact that there is a certain barrier to the purchase by Britain of more of our agricultural produce, owing to the exchange relationship between the English pound and the Canadian dollar, and I for one would heartily welcome a declaration on the part of this government that, if for no other reason than to assist the motherland in her moment of trial, we are prepared to give her free access to the markets of this country and, moreover, are ready to absorb any differential that might result from exchange, so far as commodities with which we can furnish her are concerned. This would not only emphasize the relationship that exists between the mother country and ourselves, but assist in the marketing of products other than wheat in the old land, and it would allow our farmers to go in for diversified farming, discontinuing the production to so large an extent of commodities of which at present we produce so much and which we find it difficult to market.
My purpose in bringing up this question and in outlining some of the problems that will face the government and the people of Canada is not to offer any immediate solution or any definite, planned solution. My opinion is that it would be difficult indeed, without some technical information which one would necessarily require, to determine exactly how all these problems that I have suggested could best be solved. I have, however, a good deal of commendation for the suggestion of the United Grain Growers Company Limited of

The Address-Mr. Graham
Winnipeg, that the whole question of marketing wheat be turned over during the recess to a committee for study and report. I care not what sort of committee it may be, so long as the personnel are properly equipped for the task. It might be a committee of this house.
The minister has indicated that he is himself giving this matter great attention. That is obvious. The wheat board, the advisory council and the wheat committee of the cabinet, I have no doubt, are all bending their efforts towards a solution of the problem. It is not insuperable. The statement made by the Minister of Agriculture the other night, whether it was optimistic or pessimistic, in its evaluation of the factors relating to this great commodity, shows clearly that the problem can be solved. If it is properly studied, I have no doubt that the government can find a solution for it.
The various agencies which the government itself has set up will no doubt have a great deal of information on the subject; but I rather think it would be wise, during the recess, to give an opportunity, to representatives of different groups who are vitally interested in finding a solution of the problem, to appear before a committee and submit such information as they may have. That committee could call to its assistance any or all of the agencies of government which have been busy collecting information. Perhaps the advisory council to the wheat board might be sufficiently representative to perform that task on behalf of the country. In addition to the information which it would give to those charged with the study of the problem, it would be a splendid service to the farmers, who are suffering from a sense of misunderstanding. Nothing would make me happier than if the federal government could see fit to have the subject investigated in this way, so that we in the west and the farmers in the east would feel that ample opportunity had been given for the presentation of views. It would show that the matter was being sympathetically considered. The farmers and all others concerned would gain an appreciation of the problem, and when the solution came there would be a sense of partnership in the conclusions reached, which would greatly benefit the country.
At the present time agriculture is restless because it senses it is not keeping its proper place in the economic life of Canada, that it is not being treated as are other sections of the nation's activities. Every hon. member, no matter whether he represents a rural riding or comes from a city, realizes what it would
mean to this dominion if those engaged in this great basic industry were allowed to remain permanently in a state of depression.
This problem calls for the best in each of us. I am sure that there is no fundamental difference of opinion among the members of this house as to its being desirable that the government should find a proper solution.
I had intended to touch upon one other matter, the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission on dominion-provincial relations. May I say simply this, and I think it will sum up my views on the question:	I wish to
emphasize the position taken by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) the other night, and I suggest to those representing Ontario and Quebec particularly, the two great central pillars of confederation, that they come (to the conference as Canadians rather than as residents of a particular province. As we look back over Canadian history, so well outlined in the first volume of the report, is it not well for us to ask ourselves this question: What would Macdonald and Blake, what would our own beloved Laurier and, let me add, Sir Robert Borden do if they could attend such a conference? These wise leaders of the people, regardless of political affiliations, gave leadership at the time of confederation and afterwards in an effort to bring harmony into the dominion.
I will not recite, as I had intended to do, certain excerpts from the report in relation to Saskatchewan. There is a standing challenge there to have something done to meet the situation that exists to-day. We remember the words of Lincoln, that a nation cannot exist half slave and half free, and that is true to-day of Canada. The worst thing possible that could befall Ontario and Quebec- and we have a right to expect the highest leadership from those provinces-would be to leave any part of this dominion in the unfortunate position in which Saskatchewan finds itself to-day. And the finding with regard to Saskatchewan is made by a commission on which there was no representative from that province. The personnel was drawn from the two central provinces, the maritimes, Manitoba and British Columbia, and no one from Saskatchewan need be afraid of anything that might be said is suggestive of bias in favour of Saskatchewan.
Here we have the completed report of a detached and independent royal commission charged with the duty of examining that very question. So I leave that by again appealing to the private members of this house who come from the central provinces- yes, and other provinces-and to the provincial leaders of the provinces, that when

The Address-Mr. Graham

they come to that conference, while in some respects the recommendations may be questioned, while all the recommendations are not necessarily to be accepted, and while the figures in the report are to a large extent only estimates, they come firm in the purpose to find a solution of a problem for which a solution must be found.
In conclusion, I think the contribution which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has made to the public life of this country is such that his cup must be filled to the brim with pride even on the record he now has, but what a happy conclusion to a life so filled with accomplishment would it be if he could do two things: one, to lead this country to victory in this terrible war and preserve for us the measure of democracy upon which we can again build our way of fife, and, second, to set our own house in order through the report made by that royal commission.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This debate has been marked by sincere and honest expressions of opinion. I hope the house will credit me with a like sincerity. It has been said that Canada is fighting to preserve itself, and that its first line of defence is in Great Britain. That may be so, but the Canadian people realize that the people of England to-day are fighting for their lives and for the preservation of their homes. I cannot forget my native land; although it is forty years since I left I still have many relatives and many friends there, and I feel that they would wish me to express on their behalf their profound gratitude for the efforts and sacrifices which the Canadian people are making in their war effort.
I should like to associate myself with those who have asked that the government grant free transportation to soldiers on leave. I am sure that would be the wish of the vast majority of the Canadian people.
I should like also to say a word on behalf of a great many widows of soldiers who fought in the last war, whose lives were prematurely cut short on account of their war experiences. I am told that many thousands of these widows are destitute. Again I say that if the government would look after these widows and at least grant them the necessities of life, it would meet the wishes of the vast majority of the Canadian people.
I should now like to remind the house, in case my remarks may be misunderstood, as ours in this group often are by the press, that the basic philosophy of social credit is individual freedom, and that we detest dictatorship in any shape or form. It is said that democracy is government according to the

will of the people. If that is so, and we have had a democratic government-or so it is said-why is it that in the last twenty-five years we have had two major wars and, in between, a series of depressions, unemployment, poverty and destitution? Surely those conditions have not existed as a result of the will of the people. Since they have been prevalent, I can only conclude that we have had government according to the will, not of the people but of other interested parties.
There are two political philosophies: one, centralization or totalitarianism, and the other, decentralization or democracy. Social crediters stand for decentralization, and therefore democracy.
Twenty-two years ago the world was, we were told, made safe for democracy. For a time there was a period of great prosperity. But soon after the peace was concluded we ran into a time of great depression, which continued more or less up to the start of this war. In fact it is not too much to say that the cause of this war was the depression, which had lasted more or less for fifteen years. It is easy to blame Hitler, but there was a gap of fifteen years between the end of the last war and the rise of Hitler, and had the people of Europe and of the world not been subject to the conditions to which they were subjected, I am sure that Hitler never would have been heard of.
I have said it is obvious that we must have had government according to the will of parties opposed to the interests of the people. I do not think there is any doubt that these interests were financial. As the biggest banker in the British empire said:
Bankers control the policies of governments and hold in their hands the destinies of the people.
The world has been money mad. Only the bankers, the money lenders, have been listened to, and anybody who dared to criticize what the bankers said was either laughed at and discredited or treated to a conspiracy of silence. I remember that in September of last year, when the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) brought down the first war budget, he said, as he said yesterday, that the real cost of war must come out of current production; and I remember saying at that time in reply that that was true, that the real costs of war were blood and sweat and tears, and that therefore any debt which was left after the war was over was not real. Yet we have been paying the debts of the last war right up to the present one, without reducing the amount in the least; in fact it is bigger now than it was. When we add the debt of this war to that of the last, I cannot imagine what conditions will be like.

The Address-Mr. Jaques
I believe the bankers already have an idea of those conditions; they have said that we shall have hard times for generations. Moreover, this time is not like that of the last war. Then, the people accepted those conditions as being inevitable, but this time there are very many who do not believe that it is necessary to suffer privation as a reward for winning a war. Hence it is that we hear proposals such as federal union and "union now." The proposals are that each country shall surrender its sovereignty over finance, armaments, fiscal policy and the judicature. I should like to ask what would be left. The authority of parliament would be reduced to less than that of a provincial government, and the provincial legislatures would be reduced to the status of parish councils. Further, if we are to have no sovereignty, how can we have a sovereign? If we surrender our sovereignty we surrender our sovereign. Yet these proposals are publicized in the press; and just before I left Alberta, a Mr. Streit rvas given the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on a nation-wide hook-up to put those proposals before the Canadian people. If that is not treason, I should like to know what it can be called.
As a proof, just one proof, that governments have not the control of finance, I would refer to the description, in Viscount Snowden's " Memoirs " of an incident in 1931 where England had a financial crisis. He relates that he telephoned certain financiers in Wall street, New York, and asked them whether, if the British government were to reduce the standard of living of the unemployed and the scale of social services in general, that would be acceptable to these financiers. Think of it,-the British government going hat-inhand to international financiers and asking them if they would agree to furnish a little money provided the government reduced the standards of living of its own people! And what was the consequence? The navy mutinied.
To my mind the object of those international financiers was to make it impossible for Great Britain and the empire adequately to finance rearmament in order to face the German threat. How else can one account for the fact that, in the face of certain aggression by Germany, the allied countries refused to prepare themselves to meet it? I heard a Minister of National Defence say in this house that the Canadian flying corps had ceased to fly. Could he say that there was no room in the air? Could he say that there was no gasoline when Alberta has so much that pipelines are needed to get it out of the country? Could he say that there were 14873-23-$
no young men willing and anxious for the job? No. There was only one reason: we had no money; and we had no money because neither this government nor the government of any other democratic country is sovereign to-day. One and all are, and have been, controlled by international finance.
As I said before, we in this corner and our followers throughout the British empire detest dictatorship in any shape or form. Certainly we were never confused as to the difference between Germany, Italy and Russia. I remember that when, on many platforms, I have lumped those three countries together, people have objected; they said, "There is all the difference in the world between Russia and Germany." Then I would say, "Well, there are three eggs on this table. Here we have a hard-boiled egg-you can call that Germany. Here is a scrambled egg-you can call that Russia. And here is a poached egg-you can call that Italy. They look a little different. Some people like them fried, some like^ them poached, but they are all eggs, and nothing but eggs."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Germany is a bad egg.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I was coming to that. But there is another kind of egg-a rotten egg; and that is dictatorship by finance. Last summer I asked perhaps the greatest financial authority in Canada why it was that the French left off building the Maginot line precisely where the Germans broke through in 1914. We were told that France had the finest army in Europe. We were told that its Maginot line was impregnable, and that it had the finest flying corps in Europe. But the Maginot line was not even finished. It was like a bridge which went three parts of the way across the stream.
I asked that man if he could tell me why it was that the Maginot line had not been built past that certain point, and he said to me, " Well, they had a financial crisis, and they had to economize." Will anyone say that that crisis was accidental? I say it was deliberately brought about, and the result of their economy has been the loss of France-a real economy, indeed!
I remember trying for some hours in the committee on banking and commerce to persuade its members that saving money caused a Shortage of purchasing power. Of course I was reminded of the proverbial rainy day. Then, a report of a royal commission in Australia was put into the evidence to rebut the ideas I had advanced. That royal commission was appointed by the government of Australia, and its findings were that saving money did not cause a shortage of purchasing power.
The Address-Mr. Jaques

We were, however, told yesterday by the Minister of Finance, and we now are told repeatedly by the orthodox professors that the very object of selling war bonds is not to raise money to finance the war, but rather to cause a shortage of purchasing power. And so the orthodox have had to eat their own words. As I have said before, the canons of sound finance are silenced in war time by the cannons of the enemy.
If I may I should like to read a short quotation from the September issue of The Banker, a magazine published in London, England. In part it is as follows:
Are we to suppose that if these Spitfire funds had not been raised, the production of Spitfires would have been any the less? Clearly not. The factories would have been producing to the limit of their capacity in any case. Money to buy Spitfires has no more connection with the production of Spitfires than have the spring flowers.
And it goes on to say:
When the savings appeals argue that "every pound that flows in from the sale of defence bonds increases the flow of molten steel from the crucibles and blast furnaces" this is a plain misstatement of fact.
That is not the statement of a member of the social credit party. It is the statement of a banker, as it appears in The Banker of London. If it does not correspond exactly with the statement of the president of the Canadian Bankers Association in Canada, then I would say the difference may be explained by the fact that in England no one is sure whether he will be on this earth from one day to the next. In face of that fact, perhaps the man who wrote that article thought that confession would be good for his soul.
Then, in connection with any suggestion hon. members in this corner of the house make, we hear remarks about "funny money." Mr. Jaffray, president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, was quite eloquent on that subject last week, and left the suggestion that money created by any government and not by bankers must be "funny money." So far as it is possible to deny anything, it has been denied that there is such a thing as the creation of money. Yet it is obvious that it nvould be impossible to finance our war effort without money creation. Otherwise, what would have been the point of saying, as has always been said in this chamber, and in any other parliament, that it would be impossible to do this or that because it was not known where the money would come from.
Of course, money to finance a war is created. Let there be no mistake about that. I am not criticizing this government in par-
ticular. I am, however, criticizing the principle it upholds, one which has been upheld by every democratic government in the world. That is the reason why democracy is in the danger in which it finds itself to-day. Everywhere and in all countries parliaments have surrendered their sovereign rights over the issue and creation of money, and have delegated that power to private corporations responsible to nobody other than themselves. Those corporations are not even national. It is an international arrangement. And so they have played one country off against another.
After the last war a policy of deflation was forced on Great Britain. Mr. Jaffray may talk about "funny money," if he wishes; but speaking in the House of Commons in England in 1922, the Bight Hon. Bonar Law, some time Prime Minister of England, said this, as reported in Hansard for the month of May in that year:
We borrowed 8,000 million pounds. As a result of deflation we shall be required to repay 16,000 million.
"As a result of deflation"-no wonder the bankers always warn us about the dangers of inflation. But they never mention deflation. That debt was doubled-and if Mr. Jaffray says that our ideas about money are funny,
I will say to him that that money was hot, and very hot. It was stolen-deliberately and absolutely stolen.
I well remember that away out on the prairies of Alberta I had kept cattle through what was the longest winter in the history of western Canada, a winter which had lasted seven months. I thought I would be rewarded for my efforts, but when I came to sell those cattle I got only one cent a pound, as a result of that deflation. My debts were doubled and trebled; yet that is called sound money. It is the biggest racket the world has ever known. It is the cause of the terrible conditions that we have at the present time. There will never be peace, there will never be prosperity, there will never be true democracy until parliaments assume their responsibilities and control the creation and issue of money.

speechtext:
That is
what they were going to do, but they forgot about it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Many people advocate
federal union or the surrender of our sovereign powers as the only way to peace. They say that we must disarm and hand over our sovereignty to an international police force. The only way to ensure peace is to remove the causes of war. To disarm would be just the same as tying behind his back the hands

The Address-Mr. Jaques
of a victim of the seven years' itch. It would not remove the cause. To say that you are going to cure national problems by making them international is the same as saying that you are going to cure the inmates of a hospital by tearing down the partitions.
The Minister of Finance had this to say:
That in real terms, that is to say in terms of the loss to the nation of the production required for war purposes, the war is paid for substantially while it is in progress.
That is true. In other words, the real costs come out of current production. Therefore, when the war is over, the real costs will have been paid. Why, then, should there be a debt at the end of the war? If the real costs have been paid, then the debt cannot be real. I cannot see any flaw in that argument. As a matter of fact, there is no need for debt at the end of war. The minister continued:
That the task of finance is not only to provide the funds which are used to pay for the war services but more fundamentally is, by taxing and borrowing, to restrict the civilian demand .for economic resources in order that they will be available to the defence or supply departments when required.
That is reasonable; but if the war is financed, as it certainly is, by the costless creation of money, why should anyone expect to be rewarded for lending his money? Why should a man who has more money than he needs hold the country in his debt forever simply because he lends it to the nation? If it is not necessary, why borrow it? All the necessary money can be obtained by costless creation of credit. A London banker says that this is undoubtedly what is happening. Why should those people who do something which is quite unnecessary be rewarded by having the rest of the people in their debt for all time?
I can remember when the Minister of Finance was putting over the first war loan. He said he wanted the bonds distributed as widely and as evenly as possible. If we had taken him at his word and had done just that, what would have been the value of the bonds? Every one would have had the same number of bonds and we might just as well tear them up because every one would be paying his neighbour's interest. But as the minister went on to say, some of the people-I would say the vast majority

are too poor to buy bonds. The soldiers are too poor to buy bonds, and it is these people who are too poor to buy bonds who will be taxed to pay the interest on the bonds belonging to those who happened to have enough money to buy them. These bonds were offered as a safe and profitable investment, but it is
our soldiers who make them safe and profitable. If we are beaten, these bonds will not be worth the paper they are printed upon. When our soldiers come back from war they will be taxed to pay the interest on the bonds belonging to people who have taken no risks. That is not equality of sacrifice.
May I say a word about the farmer. Just before I left home to come to Ottawa I was asked to address a meeting of the executive of the united farmers of Alberta. I told them that I had not attended the meeting to make a speech, that I had come to listen and to learn their wishes, which I would lay before parliament. I told them that we had done our best at the last session, but I did not hold out much hope. I told them that if the Alberta farmers and other farmers in western Canada were in a depressed condition, that must be agreeable to this government because it was part of their fundamental policy; if a class of people have no money to spare, that is all to the good because the government will be spared the trouble of extracting it from them. A Liberal who was present rose and said he was sorry that I had introduced politics into the discussion. I said that I had not introduced anything of the kind, that I was not criticizing the government; that I was merely stating facts.
How many of these war bonds will be held by the farmers of western Canada? Next to none. Yet when the war is over, they will be taxed to pay the interest on bonds which they never had an opportunity of acquiring. I know of what I speak. I have farmed all my life and I know these people. If they are able to exist, that is as much as they can do. They cannot buy bonds; yet after the war they will have to pay. If the war lasts for years and years, as we have been told it may, what will be the state of debt in this country? As I said before, those people who have not been able to buy bonds will have to pay interest to those who have been able to buy them.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said at the end of his speech:
Never again must we allow any man or any group of men to subjugate by fear and to crush by the power of might the spirit and the lives of honest and humble men.
There is only one way to make that possible. The government must assert its sovereign right over the creation and issue of money. So long as governments-I am not blaming this one more than any other-allow money lenders, because that is all that bankers are, good servants but impossible masters, the worst kind that you could get, to dictate the policy of governments, how is democracy pos-
The Address-Mr. Stirling

sible? We believe that a strong, free and prosperous British empire is the best guarantee for the peace and sanity of the world; and instead of surrendering the sovereignty of the empire or of any part of it to any international force, which of course would be international finance, those sovereign powers should be strengthened by restoring to the crown in trust for the people absolute control of the issue of currency and credit.
On motion of Mr. Stirling the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 5.55 p.m.
Monday, November 25, 1940.
The .house met at three o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 1940 session was prorogued and

the 1941 session opened two days later because of a demand by public opinion for information. The demand was somewhat insistent, particularly from that portion of public opinion which has been looking on with admiration, at the effort which Britain has been putting forward, on our behalf as well as her own, and there was some apprehension-that portion of public opinion which is aware that the first division of the Canadian corps received its equipment for its training in Great Britain; which has some doubt in its mind yet, whether the second division has yet received all its equipment in Great Britain for its training, and knows that the third division and the fourth division in this country have not yet been fully equipped; that portion of public opinion which has heard of the shortage which exists in equipment for the reserve units of the Canadian army, shortage of motor cycles for motor cycle units, tanks for tank units, anti-tank guns, anti-aircraft guns, instruments for the signallers, the requirements of training for all those specialized units which to-day form a part of a modern corps, without which equipment they cannot train; and without training they are not only useless but a positive menace to those corps to which they are attached.
The house has now had read to it rather voluminous statements by the various ministers whom we know as the war ministers, with an historical preface by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). It has received a mass of information; it has been led through the ramifications of the boards and committees which are directing this work, and the process of digestion is going on.
Certain things, however, emerge. The plans outlined of course have not yet reached their full measure of production.
But the battle is now. Oh, the pity of it, that the government did not realize the intensity of the need months ago! The low countries had to be invaded before it was realized that Canada's utmost effort would not be too great. Had that been realized, as I maintain it should have been realized, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) would not have had to tell us the other day that the peak of production was yet eight months distant.
Hon. members may be inclined to say that this is being wise after the event, but is it? So far as the general public is concerned, probably it is. So far as the ordinary member of this house is concerned, probably it is. But I maintain that so far as the government

The Address-Mr. Stirling
is concerned, it is not. The government is the director of this effort. The government has been looking on at Great Britain directing the effort, the magnificent effort, of the people of the United Kingdom. Cables have been passing all the time; and you cannot make me believe that the government of the United Kingdom failed to keep this government aware in minute detail of what they foresaw, of the information with regard to the enemy that they had received, of what they were doing and were proposing to do, and as to those measures of cooperation in which the partners in this effort must share. It is not the custom of a government to impart the contents of secret cables. It would be hardly proper for them to do so; but these cables are passing all the time, and it is on the contents of these secret cables that governmental policy is laid.
Last session the Prime Minister, replying to me with regard to a certain matter, said that Canada bad not refused any request made by Great Britain. Of course she had not. But Great Britain does not make requests of the dominions until the ground has been thoroughly sounded and it has been made pretty certain that the request, if made, will be granted. But the cables are passing week in and week out, day in and day out. Envoys are discussing; ministers are visiting; communications are being exchanged, yet eight months had to elapse before this government really got into its stride and started Canada pushing. The inevitable result was perfectly evident, that if Britain could not hold its defence Canada was doomed. The measure of Canada's effort last winter was the measure of the government's policy at that time. Now we are told that Canada is making everything. If Canada under direction to-day can make everything, Mr. Speaker, under similar direction she could have made everything last winter, or begun to do so. Canadian industry has not been backward. Canadian industry has been only too anxious to get really busy. Aeroplane manufacturers were clamorous for work. The Department of National Defence had combed Canadian industry to such an extent that they had a card index containing a couple of thousand names of firms listing what they were capable of doing and perhaps what they were anxious to begin doing. Canadian labour is not backward. We have the word of their spokesmen, and we have the evidence of our eyes. We need only look at what labour has accomplished in the erection of the buildings for the commonwealth air training plan, and on top of that the provision of the establishments required for the training of the Royal Air Force.
No, Canadian labour has not been backward, but only recently has the tempo of
Canadian effort been quickened. The only thing that is changed is the government's policy on which that tempo was based and the realization, I say once more, that Canada's utmost effort will not be too great.
I am not going to attempt to deal in detail with the statements which have been made by the ministers; the process of digestion is still going on. They paint broad pictures; they withhold certain figures. With that I do not make complaint. The ministers must have the decision as to what is wise to give out in the way of figures, and what is not. But there can be only one reason for official reticence, and that is the danger that information may reach the enemy. Official reticence must not be used for any other purpose. Sometimes it appears to me that official reticence is being carried rather far. Let me give an example.
During the last session of this house we were most anxious to obtain a progress report on Bren gun production. We could not get it. The minister dealt in generalities; he told us the situation was satisfactory and that production was ahead of schedule. Again in the statement he made in this house ten days ago he used the same soothing language, and again we were not given the figures. Then three days later he handed them to the Canadian Press. I look upon that, Mr. Speaker, as somewhat of an affront to this house. The minister, giving what appeared to be a full description of Canada's effort in this matter, in which he knew the public was interested, did not give the figures on that occasion, but he handed them to the press three days later. There is no doubt whatever in my mind that a certain number of people, I do not know how many, have known those figures for some time past. Indeed last session I was told that certain members of this house had been informed as to those figures. I was not. But if there are enemy agents in our midst, as I have little doubt there are, it is pretty evident that Herr Hitler knew the figures of our Bren gun production before we members of the house knew them, and I do not think that is a satisfactory way to keep the ordinary member of this 'house informed when, individually and through the various parties, he has informed the government not once but many times that his desire to get on with and help in this effort was as great as that of the government. W'hy give the public the opportunity to wonder? Is it not better to give out information such as that, which surely cannot do any harm and -which tends to keep up the interest of those who are endeavouring to examine such matters?
The Address-Mr. Stirling

About a month ago I had the opportunity to take a parade at Vernon, British Columbia, through the courtesy of the officer commanding the camp there, on the fourteenth day of that period of training. I was greatly impressed with what I saw. I was greatly impressed with the fact that some 1,200 young men, as fine a bunch of youngsters as you could possibly wish to see, were before me revealing what they had learned in the short period of approximately eighty hours of training. It is due to the excellence of the work done by Colonel Sutton, D.S.O., and the officers and non-commissioned officers associated with him that that high degree of training in such a short time has been attained. They were a remarkable set of men, those teachers. They had been connected with many famous units-the Royal Marines, the Indian Army, t(he British Army and the Canadian Army; and so well had they made contact with those recruits, and so well had they imparted knowledge to them, that the atmosphere was good, the bearing of the men was good, and the way they had learned the rudiments of drill and of marching was excellent. I formed a very high opinion of that effort.
I am not going to enter into a discussion as to whether the thirty-day training plan is a good one, or could be bettered. Certainly I do not consider that any sensible man could possibly imagine that soldiers could be trained in thirty days. But there are one or two factors to which I am persuaded considerable weight must have been given, when the thirty-day training period was decided upon. One of those factors is the desirability of drawing together at thirty or forty places across the country young men of a certain age and from every province in Canada so that they may be looked at, so that they may rub shoulders one with the other, so that they may receive the rudiments oif training and discipline and thereby place themselves in a somewhat better position to receive that training which would be necessary if the day should come when far larger numbers of land troops are required.
The second thought which occurs to me in connection with the making of that decision is that because the equipment for the reserve units of the Canadian Army was known to be short, it was impossible to believe that there would be equipment available for the new recruits which would make it possible for them to receive the advanced stages of training at the present time.
What further results have there been from the national registration? The idea of a national registration was put before the house by hon. members from this side of the house. It was suggested on more than one occasion

before the government adopted it as a desirable procedure. Certainly it was not put forward with the idea of its being only a channel for military training. The purpose of the registration, this numbering of the people, was that of giving a great deal of information. It was to enable the segregation of potential labour, male and female, young and old, trained and untrained. It was to afford opportunities for the provision of training schemes for those who were not trained. We have not heard of any result arising from national registration other than that which has already arisen in connection with the training camps. I am sure the people of Canada would like to know what if any progress has been made in other directions.
When Great Britain was arming and Canada was not, a great many of our trained mechanics, both young and middle-aged, were sliding off to Great Britain to work which attracted them. Have we done anything deliberately to make up that shortage? I ask the question, because the correction of that shortage is seriously required to-day, and the need will increase as the months go by.
Not long ago a suggestion was made to me that a scheme which would make use of the machine shops and larger garages to be found in every city or town of Canada might well be developed. It was pointed out that, in those machine shops and garages, training could be given to those youngsters, of which there are so many, who have a mechanical bent. It was pointed out, further, that as training developed it might be possible in those shops to undertake sub-contract work, as parts of a greater whole. The man who made the suggestion to me was one well trained in mechanics, one who had served as a combatant in the Canadian Army but whose age and condition of life precluded his serving again. He is only one of that large number of men who have the necessary knowledge, premises at their disposal and the intense desire to use their talents, who could be used in Canada's war effort. If this suggestion has not yet received consideration, I put it to the government as one which in my opinion merits their attention.
We are told that Hitler's smaller submarines are being made bit by bit in just such shops scattered throughout Germany. After the work has been done in those shops the parts are assembled near water, and when the assembling has taken place they are sent out to do their deadly work. If Hitler's shops can be utilized in his war effort, then Canadian shops can most certainly be used by Canadian youths for our effort.
The voluntary service registration bureau was set up by the government to operate as a

The Address-Mr. Stirling
clearing house to which the thousands of applicants, desiring to take some part in our war effort, might send their names. I do not know what happened to them. I do not know how many thousands so applied. I do not know whether the government, when requiring labour of a certain kind, approached the bureau and succeeded in obtaining the necessary supply of help. I do not know whether the civil service commission made use of the bureau when vacancies occurred in the service. I believe however that the public of Canada would like to have a report on the efficacy of the registration bureau, because many persons I have met look upon it as merely a cemetery of hopes.
I should like, too, to draw the government's attention to the voluntary work which has been going on under the direction of the British Columbia Women's Service Club. I believe it was last June that Mrs. Kennedy, the controller, and Mrs. McGusty, the commandant of the Vernon Branch, came to Ottawa. After obtaining the support of hon. members from British Columbia they interviewed the late Hon. Norman Rogers who listened to the objects of their work and their desires, and appeared to be most interested in what they were endeavouring to do. I am not aware that any kind words worthy of note have been spoken to them. I am not aware that any of the services which they have been so assiduously training themselves to perform have been in any sense made use of. But it is quite evident that from week to week we approach more closely the time when industry and other activities will have to avail themselves of women's labour. I should think it would be most desirable that the government reconsider the recognition of units such as the one to which I have just referred, because at the back of each of these organizations is the intense desire to help.
In the neighbourhood of Princeton, an important mining section of British Columbia, the population of which is drawn from many countries of Europe, some of which are now under the nazi boot heel, a Spitfire fund was set up. Contributions both large and small have been flowing into it. No sooner had they commenced to collect than a discouraging reference to Spitfire funds appeared in the press. Is the government wise to discourage efforts of that sort? It is this sort of effort which provides a safety valve for the enthusiasm of certain Canadians. I am not in the least surprised to hear that the minister would much rather have the money go into the war loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext: I did not say that, nor have I discouraged these funds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
The minister says that he has not discouraged them, but my information is that the discouragement came from somewhere. I remember reading a paragraph or two in the press-I have not the article before me so I shall not elaborate-which gave me the impression that the government was inclined to discourage the collection of Spitfire funds. If the minister says that he has not, then I am mistaken and the people of Princeton have been mistaken. When they started collecting for this fund from that rather scattered and cosmopolitan population they were met with the announcement that the government was discouraging such funds. If the government have not been discouraging these funds, or even if they have, would they be good enough to explain their views further to the Canadian people?
I come now to the response by the public to the second war loan. Shortly after the loan campaign opened I received a letter from a man of standing in his community who told me that he and a number of his acquaintances had been deterred from investing in the war loan because of the waste and political partisanship in connection with the building of the camp at Yernon. I passed that letter on to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), who, in thanking me, said that he was going to take it up with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), and that he would also speak to him about it. Some three weeks later I received another letter from another man written in the same strain. I know this gentleman quite well and I have considerable confidence in his judgment. I replied immediately asking that he give me some details, whereupon I would lay them before the proper *minister. He furnished me with the details and I am passing them on to the minister who is carrying on the work of the Minister of National Defence in his absence, in the hope that the matter will be run to earth.
I know how easy it is to make charges of this description, and I know how hard it is to obtain the facts to substantiate them. People do not want to talk; people are afraid of losing their jobs. But it would appear that these things are prevalent. I regret to say that my own experience has been that they are quite prevalent. It is the duty of the government, by investigation or by any other means in their power, not only to set such charges at rest but to disprove them. The government, from the Prime Minister down, have assured this house that it is not their personal desire that partisanship should enter into this effort. I must accept their statements, and of course I do. But theirs is the brain that is directing this effort. To what extent has that brain taken active

The Address-Mr. Stirling

control of the hands and fingers that direct and control the details? That is the question. It is very easy for a minister to say, "I will not have anything to do with partisanship," but as soon as he has said that he attaches to himself the second duty of seeing that those who are responsible to him are honourably carrying out that undertaking.
As I have indicated already, the national registration was instituted, not only for the purposes of military training but to provide one of the instruments with which the National Resources Mobilization Act could be put into operation. That act gave the government very wide powers, and they have been using them. One of the things the government have done has been to set up an exchange control board. When a Canadian desires to go to the United States he must satisfy the exchange control board that his visit is reasonably necessary before he can obtain the exchange with which to carry out his trip. As I pointed out last session, there has been a steady stream of Canadian money going to the United States to pay for fruits, vegetables and many other things which, in my opinion, not only are not necessary at this time but constitute a positive waste of money which we need so badly for the purchase of things that are really required. Our exchange situation is becoming no easier. I read with great interest in the paper this morning a statement to the effect that the Minister of Finance had decided to publish a list of fruits and vegetables and was going to request licensed importers to refrain from importing them until further notice.

speechtext:
On a question of privilege, and for the purpose of setting my hon. friend right, I should like to say that that news story is entirely incorrect if it is taken as meaning that I authorized the circularizing of the wholesalers by the wholesalers' association. The news story itself does not say that, but I am afraid it may have led other persons to the same conclusion as that reached by the hon. gentleman. The representatives of the wholesalers came to see me some days ago, but there was no suggestion, either on my part or on theirs, that there should be any request made by their organization or otherwise to wholesalers in Canada not to import certain fruits and vegetables. I was considerably surprised to see the notice in the press to which the hon. gentleman has just referred. At this interview the wholesalers suggested that if steps were in contemplation by the government for the restriction of the importation

of fruits and vegetables, care should be taken to avoid undue hardship. They suggested also that they should be consulted before any steps were taken. I suggested that they should put their views in writing, which they have not done as yet. Apart from that there were no suggestions or requests or arrangement made at that interview.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
I am grateful to the minister for his explanation, and with that I shall have no further remarks to make with regard to this news item which I read in the manner he indicated. Evidently it does not correctly explain the situation at the present time. But I can continue with this thought. We have only a certain amount of money to use for necessities and it is utterly wrong for us to use it for things which can be dispensed with. In one week of June of last year $50,000 worth of tomatoes entered the Montreal market and $40,000 worth the Toronto market. I do not say that importations to that extent are still going on. But what I say is that if the Canadian consumer is using his money in that way-the Canadian consumer may be the thoughtless consumer- he should have impressed upon him the necessity that there is one better way of using that money, and that is to exercise the spirit of self-sacrifice so that we can attain an equality of sacrifice. That is the only way in which every Canadian dollar can be put to proper use.
And how the situation has been aggravated by an incident that occurred a few weeks ago in the west! Trade in the United States found itself short of certain varieties of apples of certain sizes. Finding that Canada could supply them it ordered them, and two or three hundred carloads of these apples were shipped from British Columbia to the United States at their request. Such a shout went up amongst United States producers that the reverberations reached Washington, and I am given to understand that further shipments have been somewhat discouraged. Now, what does this mean? For years United States produce has been streaming into this country, in earlier days without let or hindrance but with some preventive methods in later days, and when such a condition as I have described arises, with trade in the United States requiring something that Canada has, and asking for it, this roar goes up. Such a noise was made about it that an official of the Department of Agriculture in Washington, D.C., went out to the west, and this is what he is reported to have said, as quoted from the Wenatchee World of November 1:
As British Columbia growers possess popular sizes, American buyers have taken them. All supplies have been sold firm, and there has been no speculation and no consignment shipments. None have been dumped on our market.

The Address-Mr. Maybank
In that transaction hon. members will realize that instead of Canadians wasting their money in buying something they did not need they have just been endeavouring, by this little piece of trade, to build up Canadian exchange so that money would be available for our war effort.
It is a most unsatisfactory thing that our money should not be put to its proper use, and if that treatment to which I have already referred is not the treatment which the government has decided to make use of I suggest to the government that the time has come when, if the Canadian people are not using in the best possible way one of Canada's resources, the money Canadians have to spend, the government should make use of other legitimate devices to impress upon the Canadian people that there is only one way to use their spending money, and that is the best way. I do not know why the government has been so long in taking action with regard to this matter, drawn to its attention as it has been for six months. I cannot imagine that it fears the Canada-United States agreement because in that agreement the two signatories put their names to a war clause which would enable action to be taken by either country in case either or both were involved in war.
But the fruit and vegetable end of this great question is but one portion of it, and I am hopeful that the government will tackle the question from the point of view of impressing on the Canadian people that anything in the nature of luxuries which can be done without must be done without at this time in a spirit of equality of sacrifice. I believe that- there is still in this country far too large a number of people who do not realize the necessity for self-sacrifice. We must have drummed into our ears at all times equality of sacrifice so that a public opinion may be created which will frown on anything which is opposed to it, and that equality of sacrifice must not be alone among the people in this Canada of ours but must extend outside into the ranks of all who fight with us the battle of Britain.
Canada as long as she has been Canada has relied on the Royal Navy for her protection, and the Canadian people, many of them, have hung their heads because of it. True, in later years we provided ourselves with a most efficient little navy in no sense commensurate with our wealth, or with our trade, or with our necessities for protection. There was no equality of sacrifice there because it was the taxpayer of the United Kingdom who maintained the Royal Navy. We did not contribute but we greatly benefited by the existence of that formidable police force.
14873-24^
I was pleased indeed to listen to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs the other day when he recognized that disparity and spoke with hope of a considerable expansion of our Royal Canadian Navy. But let the government leave no stone unturned in impressing on the Canadian people the necessity of sacrifice, that the results of the national registration be used to the full, and above all let the very words National Resources Mobilization Act become an actuality. Let the services of the thousands of men and women who want to help be utilized. Let every effort be made to speed up and increase the tempo of Canada's war effort so that another occasion may not arise when Canadian heads have to hang because when the battle of liberty was on, the contribution which Canada made was too late.
Liberty is not a word,
But is a substantial thing,
A precious jewel, purchased At the dear rate of life itself,
And so to be defended.
Those words were written three hundred years ago by two English dramatists, and they bear the stamp of eternal truth.
