Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow in general or in any detail the remarks of the gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Stirling). I should like however to say this, that no person could cavil or complain in any way of the speech which the hon. gentleman has just made. I feel that I am in a privileged position to be able immediately to congratulate him upon a temperate, kindly and thoroughly gentlemanly speech such as. of course, one would expect and has a right to expect from the front benches of the opposition party.
There is perhaps a particular reason for not taking up in detail the remarks of the hon. gentleman. The reason is that his remarks were by no means a severe criticism of the government. Indeed it seems to me that the fact that so prominent a member of the Conservative party spoke in the manner in which he did just now, indicates that this government has been doing a mighty fine job of work in leading this country in its war effort. Such criticisms as the hon. gentleman offered were on comparatively minor points, and there cannot be much wrong when one of his calibre can find practically nothing to criticize. The government, in other words, is somewhat in the position of the chap who gave the name of the chief of police as a character reference. The chief of police when asked about the man, said that he did not even know him. Referring to the chief's

The Address-Mr. Maybank
comment, the man retorted, "Having lived thirty' years in the city, and the chief of police not even knowing me, I must be all right."
There is, however, one remark made by the hon. gentleman to which I should like to draw attention. He said, as I recall it, that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) made certain statements in the house with reference to Bren gun production, and that these statements were of a very general nature; but that a few days later, speaking to the press, he elaborated upon them and gave to the press information which he held back from this house. With all respect, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman is in error. If you will turn to page 149 of Hansard you will note what the minister said at that time with reference to Bren guns. I think the hon. gentleman will find upon inquiry that what was later reported in the _ newspapers was merely a different rendering of the same information which the minister gave the house, and that the minister did not withhold information from us and then, going outside and meeting the gentlemen of the press, give them more details. What was said on page 149 runs this way:
Regarding Bren guns; I have given my hon. friend the number up to the end of September. I am not giving the number delivered each week, but it is a figure which I must say is most satisfactory having regard to what was planned on when production started at the plant. These weekly deliveries are increasing steadily and by the end of the first year of production we expect to have three times as many guns delivered as were called for by the contract.
From there on, you see, it is a matter of arithmetic. The note I have indicates that the contract called for about 1,000 from April first this year to March 31 of the next year. It will be seen, therefore, that the minister, in giving his statement to the house in the fashion that he did, simply left it to the press to apply arithmetic to the problem and then the reporters could give a very definite statement to the country. It may well appear that the minister was more definite with the press than he was with the house, but that, I think was not the case, and I suggest that the hon. member was mistaken in his criticism in this regard.
So far as the general effort of this government is concerned, I have read somewhere that it might be described as a series of brilliant improvisations, and that incredible results have been achieved. I do not know whether that is an accurate statement, having regard to the use of the word "improvisations"; perhaps it is not properly used. We were not prepared at the time of the break through in the low countries and the collapse of France,

and I do not see very well how any country, in all the circumstances of democratic life, could have been prepared. The speeding of plans was necessary, and in that sense we can, I think, appropriately say that there has been a series of brilliant improvisations. So far as I am concerned, and chiefly because I am not a person who is very easily satisfied,
I wish to offer my meed of praise for the work of the government in leading this country, particularly during this last six or seven months since the debacle to which I have just referred. I do not intend simply to chant a paean of praise, yet since I am not, as I have said, a person easily satisfied, I do not wish to let the opportunity pass of expressing praise of the government, because I believe it is justified. I do this in the same straightforward manner that, as this house knows very well, I would quickly express criticism if I thought that it was what the government, or any other organization, deserved.
To-day I wish to speak mainly about problems and points of interest concerned with labour matters in the country generally, but before doing so there are some non-labour matters which I should like to mention.
In the first place I desire to add my voice to the voices of others who have spoken in favour of free transportation for the troops at Christmas time. It does not seem to me that half fare or fare one way for the man on furlough is sufficient. When something is offered which does not accomplish the result aimed at, it is just the same as offering nothing at all. Men who are distant from their homes cannot, because of lack of funds, go home and back during the Christmas furlough. There is no use offering them half fares. I suppose they could go home and then be brought back as deserters, but none of them wants to do that. It seems to me that there has been already enough expression of opinion along this line; practically ninety per cent of the house must be in favour of free transportation for soldiers, and I urge the government to see that justice is done and joy is given at Christmas time.
There is one other non-labour matter which I wish to draw to the attention of the house and, more particularly, to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald). The minister was here a few minutes ago, but had to leave to attend to some departmental duties; I know that what I am saying will have his attention later. It is, it seems to me, an odd situation of which I wish to speak. It appears that the rules with reference to a wife's allowance are quite different in the navy from what they are either in the air force or in the army. When a man in either of the last two

The Address-Mr. Maybank
mentioned services gets married, automatically his wife receives S35 per month allowance. Not so, apparently, in the navy. It seems there is a rule that the allowance will not be paid to any officer or rating married on or after November 1, 1928, unless and until he has attained the age of twenty-two years. An informant writes me:
Is it not an irony to ask the boys of Canada to fight for freedom and justice when we refuse them that at home? What difference does the age make? If a man of nineteen is old enough to fight for Canada, should his wife be left to starve while he is doing it?
I must say I heartily agree with my correspondent's point of view. My informant also tells me of a man under twenty-two years of age who received permission of his superior officer to marry; he believed that the allowance would go to his wife, but her allowance has not been paid and will not be paid.
The rule, as I have explained, is that if a man gets married when he is under twenty-two years of age the wife gets no allowance. The rule was passed in 1928, and it occurs to me that perhaps the navy is endeavouring to carry on the old tradition that a sailor boy should have a girl in every port. That might be interfered with if Jack were encouraged to marry. I do not know whether that is the reason for the rule but I can think of no other. The rule that the wife of a young man under twenty-two who marries with permission is to get no allowance ought to be changed at once. The wives of men in one force should get the same treatment as wives of men in the other forces. If it is not desired to have naval officers and ratings marry under twenty-two that could be the subject of a regulation, but if they are to be permitted to marry then this government should take the responsibility that it ordinarily takes for the wife of the enlisted man.
I now wish to touch upon some labour problems that have come to my attention. Frankly I am presenting one or two cases that are in the nature of grievances. I make no apology for doing so; nor do I present the grievances in any spirit of captious criticism or complaint.' But if the friends of a government will not tell it of the things that are wrong there is little chance of the government correcting them, and abuses will continue, to the detriment finally of the whole country.
Some of the instances I desire to mention relate to the government as an employer. I recall the oft-used expression that the government should be a model employer and so be an example to other employers. We like consistency. We passed an act popularly known as the Lemieux act and put into effect a
labour charter which is set forth in an order in council of last June. The principles of this type of labour legislation should be the guiding star of the government itself as an employer. But we have people working in the government service at salaries that are certainly less than fair. We have some, indeed, working for niggardly salaries and starvation wages. I do not say that the percentage is large, but in government employment, where the total number employed is so great, a large number are working for what is not by any means a fair wage. One man I know of, a married man with a family of three or four, has been regularly employed at a man's job

not a boy's job-for the last four or five years, and his net wage is $56 a month. His is not just an isolated case but is one of a class, and that is the wage that is being paid. This sort of thing is not fair. When we are at war there is all the more reason for seeing that injustices of this kind ire not allowed to continue.
Again we have persons employed by the government on what is termed the seven-day week basis rather than the six-day week. For years we have seen nearly all the world on a six-day week basis, but we have, and have had for years, at Fort Osborne barracks, firemen and other men working in high-pressure plants on a seven-day week basis and getting less money for seven days than the ordinary wage paid elsewhere for six days. I tried to get the matter straightened out some time ago. I had at that time the support of the late Hon. Mr. Rogers, who as Minister of Labour realized it to be a concern of his. I had the support, I believe, of the then Minister of National Defence, the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). Everything seemed to be going along all right until our attempts bogged down or were broken down in the treasury board. Now it seems to me that that sort of thing is, as Mr. Rogers recognized, a proper matter of concern for the Department of Labour. It seems to me to be the business of the Department of Labour to inquire into labour abuses; and they should look at labour conditions that are close at home as well as those far afield.
We still have our unemployment problem. I have spoken about the war effort of Canada, and I had in mind the Department of Munitions and Supply; I might just say a word with reference to that department. I have been in entire agreement with the policy followed so far by the Minister of Munitions. I realize that in the placing of contracts he had to consider practically just one thing- speed of performance. The need was urgent;
The Address-Mr. Maybank

the pressing need was to get deliveries, even though it resulted in centralization of industrial work in these central provinces, chiefly Ontario. Even though the policy resulted in very little war work going out to the prairies and other parts of Canada I am in entire agreement with what has been done, and I think that the minister of that department and all concerned with it are to be congratulated. But the situation has now reached the point where certain other principles can be taken into consideration.
The social aspect of these contract placements should be recognized. In my own district we have all manner of industries that could be put to use in war work. Some of them are being used, but they could be used a great deal more. It is not economic to be paying out money for unemployment relief and at the same time placing contracts without reference to the social needs of the country. This is the time to attack what has been called the "hard core" of unemployment. Nobody knows just what the hard core of unemployment is; someone coined that bright phrase, it seemed clever and many people took it up and used it as though they were saying something. Then people began to define the hard core of unemployment, and it turned out that whenever unemployment had been reduced to a point that the particular individual considered satisfactory, the hard core of unemployment had been reached and there was nothing further to be done. But we can dissolve the hard core of unemployment if we turn our attention to it, if we face up to the problem and devote to it the necessary time and money and energy, and, above all, imagination. There is no reason for any unemployment in this country to-day. I know there are many persons on relief whom it is difficult to absorb into industry, but something can be done for all. I have known workmen's compensation boards to spend money upon people who appeared to be totally incapacitated through injuries, and who were therefore unemployed. This, these boards did for financial reasons, to avoid further drain on their funds. They endeavoured to rehabilitate these apparent unemployables and restore to them their ability to earn a living. And most important of all, though perhaps this was incidental as far as the boards were concerned, they restored to these people the dignity which is possible only in conjunction with an earned living, which cannot exist when there is involuntary idleness coupled with a subsistence allowance.
I wish to speak now of another very critical labour problem of a different sort. The hon. member who preceded me touched upon this problem but did not enlarge upon it to any

great extent. From what little he said, however, I am inclined to think that we are in entire agreement on the matter. I am definitely worried, Mr. Speaker, over the possibility of a labour crisis in this country in spite of the fact that we have an unemployment problem at this moment. Indeed it would be possible to have a labour crisis, by way of a shortage, and at the same time have an unemployment problem. It seems paradoxical, but theoretically it is possible. At any rate I do not think any person can observe what is going on in the midlands of England without becoming fearful in regard to the labour situation in Canada. Just after the bombing of Coventry, for example, I noticed in the New York Times that certain United States industries were expecting special calls to be made upon them in reference to either Rolls-Royce engines, which apparently they were manufacturing, or perhaps similar aeroplane engines which might be substituted for the Rolls-Royce engines. The inference is clear. Evidently that engine plant in Coventry had been damaged.
For the last year or so the Winnipeg Free Press has had an excellent reporter in England. This reporter, Mr. Francis Stevens, recently returned to Canada. Within the last few days I read one of his stories, from which I culled this paragraph:
After what happened to Coventry and the horror heaped upon a midlands city last night by the nazi air force, we know without being told that Britain must turn to Canada as never before for sustaining strength in her lonely struggle to save civilization.
Of course what Mr. Stevens means is that in all probability Britain will have to turn to Canada to a greater extent than ever before for her supplies of munitions of war. In the past we have sometimes spoken of ourselves as the empire's bread basket. I fancy we are becoming, and shortly will become even more fully, the arsenal of the empire. I know, as I think we all know, that Great Britain has been facing difficulties in regard to labour shortages, and it is inevitable that we shall have the same difficulties unless we make the necessary preparations.
For example, if we inquire into the employment trend in this country it becomes clear that there must be a labour crisis. When we see the employment trend we are forced to realize that we are marching straight into the jaws of such a crisis. In the Financial Post of three or four weeks ago the development was shown. It was set forth that as of last September there were 2,717,000 persons gainfully employed in Canada. That was the peak employment up to that time. The figure for the previous September was about 26 per cent

The Address-Mr. Maybank
less. The monthly average for 1939 was
2,344,000,	very much less; and for the previous year the monthly average was 2,297,000. If you were to indicate that labour trend by means of a graph you would draw a line not merely upward but sharply upward, with no variations, no dips or jumps or anything of the sort; it would be very nearly a straight upward line.
I know that recently the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke as though there were no difficulties, though a short time previously it had been indicated in the house that the government was taking steps in regard to the matter. Some persons jumped to the conclusion that there was a difference of opinion. Some people feel that this is a time for sharp retorts to the Minister of Agriculture, in the hope of being able to register a blow in verbal combat. Well, there is no need for anything of that sort. It is very silly to behave in that fashion. The fact of the matter is that we can be facing this crisis and at the same time have difficulties presented by employers of labour such as the minister mentioned. Everyone knows the tendency of the employer to object to any interference with his personnel, and no doubt many employers cry before they are hurt and make all kinds of trouble. I do not mean to say that is the general rule, but there are persons like that in every walk of life. There is no need to get over-argumentative about a thing of this sort.
A few moments ago I mentioned certain figures suggesting the trend. If you look at the enlistment figures you come to the same conclusion. We might say that just before the war our forces numbered perhaps 4,500. I have not the exact figures showing the number of men in our forces at the end of the first year of war, as I was able to give them in dealing with the number of persons gainfully employed, but I take it that at the present time there are about 170,000 men in the army, 30,000 in the air force-these figures may not be exact, but I think they are approximate, and after all I am only indicating a trend-and a few days ago it was said that in the navy there were something like 15.000 men. To these figures must be added about 30,000 trainees. This last is a changing personnel, but that is about the number. This gives a total of about 245,000 persons who have been taken out of the possible employment pool. So you might say that since the war started, in the neighbourhood of half a million people either have been put to work or have been taken away from the pool of men from which workers come. Of course if that sort of thing goes
on and we do nothing about it we shall have to refrain from setting up industries that otherwise we might desire to set up.
It is not only the matter of a general labour shortage that we must consider; it is the shortage of particular kinds of labour. Perhaps we have not been as wise as we might have been since September, 1939. We should have paid more attention to what General McNaughton said the day after war broke out. He declared then that the war would be one of machines, and that it was vitally important not to deprive industry of certain skilled types of man-power on whom the rapid expansion of production depended. He wanted to set up a list of essential industries, and also a list of reserve occupations. Anyone can understand not a great deal being done in this respect during the hectic days we have gone through, but it would be folly of the worst imaginable kind if we were to continue in error.
As the house probably knows, Great Britain has been having considerable trouble of this sort. The Right Hon. Ernest Bevin some time ago warned employers against living in a fool's paradise. He said he was reluctant to make training obligatory, but that it might be necessary. Under his direction, as long ago as last February, organizations were set up for the training of men. There were 15,000 being trained at that time. The Economist reported that a longer time was needed to train a munitions worker than to train a soldier, and claimed that the government would turn out about 40,000 in the year. Just at that time, however, it appeared that the Germans were carrying on a similar training, and that they had already trained a half million workers for war industry. Mr. Churchill declared there was need for about a million women to go into industry. Great Britain now realizes she made a late and inadequate start. We are still later, and we must give the problem our most serious attention.
As I see it, we should begin at once with comprehensive and intensive training of people for industry. The best way to do this is to have people employed while they are learning. In that way we will get better learners and better results. National registration cards offer an excellent basis for this effort. Then, there are many people employed at the present time in non-essential industries who could be employed elsewhere. They could be employed in more essential walks of life. For example there are some who are driving trucks. I am not suggesting that the driving of trucks is not essential, but many who are
The Address-Mr. Mayhank

so employed could do work which is more essential. There are many thousands who could fill their places.
It is my recollection that at the time of the last war a great deal of the automobile driving was done by women.
It seems to me, too, that there are industries now operating which need not continue to operate, and whose workers might be better employed, from the national viewpoint, in a war industry. The easiest way to effect that transfer is to carry out the sound Liberal policy which many of us have advocated for years, namely, to let in goods from Great Britain. Now is the time when the advocate of low tariffs has all the force of the war on his side-the first time it has ever happened. I suggest that those who are making in Canada goods which could be obtained from Great Britain could be released for other more essential work.
Furthermore-although this is somewhat aside from the point I am making-the great need in Great Britain to-day is that of obtaining foreign exchange. She must sell her goods, and she could sell large quantities of them in Canada if we would only let them in more easily. If we freely admit British goods, Great Britain will then be able to pay for many things obtainable in Canada, and it seems to me possible that she would thus create a credit which could be used in the United States. That she needs this financial aid is clear. The press of yesterday reports that Lord Lothian has returned to the United States stating that in 1941 Great Britain is going to face a severe financial crisis. He is asserting to the people of the United States that Great Britain needs financial help. The very best thing we can do for Great Britain is to permit her to send her goods to Canada, and in that way while helping her we will help ourselves to solve our labour problem.
I do not wish to leave the suggestion that nothing is being done about this problem, because I know very well that a good committee has been set up by the government to look into the matter. My only reason for emphasizing the point is to urge upon the government that it, through that committee, and in every other way prosecute its inquiry to a point where it may with all speed and all energy take the necessary steps.
The government is to be commended for what it has done, and I just hope that there may be no slackening-I do not expect any- in its effort.
It is perfectly true to say that we have not been ready for several things which have happened, and we were in good company in that state of unreadiness. Probably it was impossible for any democracy to be ready.

But the situation now is different. We can see our problem looming up in front of us. Here is something for which we can be ready; here is something we can do. When the time comes for us to answer the call of Great Britain for more industrial assistance, we can be ready to give it.
It will be remembered that during the last war Lloyd George went about the country organizing industry. I can well remember his stating that he feared Britain might have to write over the doors of factories the words "Too late; too late." We must not be found in that position.
For about twenty years I worked on railroads in one capacity or another. During that time I performed a variety of jobs. Sometimes I have tried to decide just what it was that was most desired in a railroader, and I have come to the conclusion that a good railroader is one who is in the right place at the right time,. "In the right place at the right time"-that might very well be our motto in connection with the problem I have been dealing with. Let us hope that, representing the people of Canada, the government will be in the right place at the right time in connection with our industrial help to Great Britain, and if this is so, we shall never be too late:.

I am sure every hon. member realizes that this is a grave time through which we are passing. We in Canada should be as well aware of that fact as any other people in the world.
I believe some of the criticisms and suggestions offered by the two hon. members who have immediately preceded me in the debate are worthy of consideration by the government, but I was struck by the implication of the statement of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) that the people of Canada are only too anxious to do what they can in connection with the war effort. Then I recall what the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) said a few days ago-that there was a feeling of dissatisfaction and uncertainty throughout Canada. Perhaps " uncertainty " would be the most correct word to use. I am quite in accord with that opinion. As I said last year, you cannot force people into patriotism. I think we are beginning to realize that. The sooner we get down to basic facts, the sooner we ask ourselves why there is such a lack of patriotism, the better it will be for all. Let us not pat ourselves on the back. We must face this thing sooner or later.
The answer is that the people do not know what to do. They do not know what the government wants them to do. There is no

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
leadership. I do not mean that in any offensive way; I would not offend hon. members for the world. But I ask them to listen to reason. I can remember the laugh that went up from the other side of the house when I suggested two or three years ago that we should have one of the best equipped air forces in the world. But I defy those hon. members to stand up in their places to-day and laugh at that-or say it is a joke.
The people do not know what the government want them to do. The other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) told us that we should save. Everyone is advocating a 'belt-tightening process, just like the hon. member for Yale. What does he mean by belt-tightening? There is no policy laid down. The people are given no guidance. If you say to the people, "We do not want you to buy cars," I venture to say that there will not be a new car sold. But if you do not want them to buy cars the proper thing to do is to say to the manufacturers, " Do not make any more cars; we want your machine shops to produce war materials." Why attempt to advocate these things by a process of undue taxation and then have new cars in the show windows advertised at reduced prices or with the slogan, " Buy a car before Christmas to satisfy your wife."

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
I hope
my wife does not read that. But the thing is so ridiculous. On the one hand we have the manufacturers trying to encourage people to buy; the people are told to "buy before Christmas, fifty cents down and a dollar when we catch you." Anything to get them to buy before Christmas. On the other hand, we have the government stealing in with their taxation and taking the money away from the people. Will such a course lead to unity and satisfaction? Certainly not. If you do not want our women to buy new fur coats, the thing to do is to stop the manufacture of fur coats. If these manufacturing facilities are needed for war purposes, why not be man enough to say so? If you want more aeroplanes, be man enough to say so. Come out and face the facts; do not try to hide behind political seclusion.
See what happened to France. It was the financial policy that ruined France. France was sold out not by those whom we generally refer to as fifth columnists in the rank and file of the people, but by those in higher places. We must guard against this, or we shall have trouble in Canada. I am sure the people are only too anxious to do what they can, if they only knew what was needed.
The government must give guidance to the people. If that is done, I am sure they will respond.
I do not intend to dwell at any great length this afternoon on our war effort; I shall deal with it at a later time. I desire to speak more particularly about our farmers. The hon. member for New Westminster said that he did not know what was causing dissatisfaction among our people, but if he looks in our agricultural field he will find plenty of cause for dissatisfaction. There are no more patriotic people in the world than our agriculturists. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said the other day-he is gone again; he is not in his seat; he is the busiest man I ever saw; he flutters around and does not do a thing; our farmers have been contributing a great deal to the war effort. Yet there is no industry in Canada which has been treated so unfairly. Is it expected that that will be a basis for unity? You cannot get unity with that type of treatment.
Our farmers are at a loss to know what to do. Again the government is lacking in providing the necessary guidance. About a year ago the Minister of Agriculture advocated the increased production of bacon, and immediately the farmers gave it to him because he had asked for something definite. They said: If it is bacon the British empire wants, we will give it to them. Then what happened? There was an influx of bacon from the United States; the price dropped and the farmers got stung. The country wanted wheat and the farmers went ahead and produced wheat. What has happened? They are starving to death on the farms. Again there has been a lack of guidance.
Either the government do not know what they want, or they are deceiving the people. In either case they have no right to be leading this country during war time unless they have something better than that to offer. If the government will decide what they want. I am convinced that the farming people of this country will be only too ready to share the burden. It seems to me that every time the Minister of Agriculture gets in a jam, if he cannot pass it on to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) he looks ahead to the future. He seems to be most optimistic about the future. He can look ahead and say that in five years we will be short 50,000,000 bushels of wheat.

speechtext: He is counting on a couple of years of drought.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
He is waiting for Santa Claus. If we are going to be short 50,000,000 bushels of wheat in five years, which is not very long, then we should not be

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
greatly concerned over our wheat problem. The only thing lacking is the money. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that whatever was physically possible would be made financially possible. I do not know whether he meant that; the government have said so many things they did not mean. It is hard to tell just what they want. I do not think there is any danger to us in our present large supply of wheat. In fact, I think it is one of the most beneficial things we could have at the present time. We have no assurance that we are not going to have a drought in the west next year, or the year after. If that were to happen, then what would be the position of the British empire? It might prove to be one the greatest calamities for this country or the empire.
I should like to refer briefly to a pamphlet entitled "Wheat and War," and containing an address by George S. Mathieson, president of the Winnipeg grain exchange. Here is what this experienced grain man has to say in regard to our supplies of wheat:
The maintenance of this substantial reserve of wheat can well be one of Canada's contributions to the empire war requirements.
There is definite guidance for the farmer. He is being encouraged by an experienced grain man to raise wheat. Mr. Mathieson continues:
The price ultimately to be paid for it is a matter to be determined by world conditions when the demand comes. The picture, which envisages Canada with so much wheat that she does not know what to do with it, ignores the necessity of abundant reserves against contingencies. The wheat board, fully aware of this situation, need not be expected to offer for sale any more wheat than is actually wanted.
That is good advice. I think we are unduly concerned about the vast amount of wheat that we have on hand. We should be tickled to death with it. But the fact that we happen to have am abundance of wheat is no reason why we should force our farmers to starve to death. There is one thing which neither this nor any other government can control, and that is the future climatic conditions. The big cry goes up from the government, where shall we find the money? But there has never been any question about money when it comes to the war industries. The war industries get what profit they want. I recall that we passed legislation limiting profits to five per cent, but that legislation was rescinded and you do not know what profit is allowed now. They are getting what they want. The farmer, however, is definitely making no profit, and when you come to the point where you are making no profit but are going behind on every bushel of wheat you raise, it is time to take stock of things. I think a little consideration should be given to this subject.

As I said a moment ago, the Minister of Agriculture can always find some nice excuse out, and sometimes a fine speech is about all he has to offer. I have a clipping here from the Albertan of September 10, 1940. The Minister of Agriculture was speaking at Toronto, and these were his words of encouragement to the farmers:
Giving his address at the live stock day luncheon at the Canadian National Exhibition, Mr. Gardiner addressed his preliminary remarks to farmers and said he had "unpopular" statements to make.
The first was that "this is not the time for the farmer to increase his expenditures and hence not the time for business to be booming in agricultural areas."
If he was seeking to imply that business was booming in agricultural areas he does not know his agriculture, although he may have had a farm given to him by the Saskatchewan government and may go out there for his vacations. If business is booming for the farmer the minister certainly does not know agriculture, because business has never been booming for the farmer. But the minister went on to say this, which appears under the heading " Sees tough winter ahead " -and here again he is a prophet:
Experience had shown that farmers never enjoyed prosperity in the first two years of a war and "this "winter and possibly the next will be the toughest the farmers are likely to experience during this war period."
That is not a pleasant prospect. Farmers all over the west found it pretty hard this year to make ends meet, let alone pay their debts, and the only consolation the Minister of Agriculture has to give them is that next winter is going to be still worse. More of the belt-tightening process, and he expects by that to develop unity across Canada!
But the minister had a little more advice to give to the farmers. I have here a clipping from the Albertan of September 14, 1940, in which the minister is reported as follows:
World wheat marketing conditions may change between now and November 1. Agriculture Minister J. G. Gardiner to-day told a press conference-
November is come and gone and conditions are still the same, but the minister hoped they would be better before November 1. The report goes on:
-and it is possible the government may delay until the end of October-
So he put it off again!
[DOT]-its decision on how to help the wheat farmer who cannot turn his crop into cash because of lack of elevator space.
He finds himself in a difficulty and so he tries to wriggle out of it by putting the onus on the provinces, thereby satisfying his own

The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
conscience. So lie brings up this obstacle, and I thought this was rather good. Under the heading "Law's a barrier", the report goes
on:
Provincial law's, Mr. Gardiner explained to-day, regulate the deductions wdien loans are made on w'heat on farms. The threshing bill, the year's taxes, the accounts for repairs and for necessities of life must all be taken care of.
In this article the Minister of Agriculture complains that because of these obstacles the government cannot make loans to the farmers on wheat stored on the farms. I looked at the article again and I thought, what more would he want in there? There is provision in the provincial laws with respect to the threshing bill, the year's taxes, the accounts to be paid for repairs, and the necessities of life. The only things missings are the machine companies and the banks. The only objection the minister can have is that the banks and the mortgage companies were not protected by provincial legislation, and so provincial legislation should be changed. Well, Mr. Speaker, when we take the attitude that the farmer is not entitled to a decent standard of living I think the Minister of Agriculture who implies such a thing should be taken from agriculture and put into another office. He goes on and says:
I w'as told the law was so and so, and I replied that some laws could be changed by calling legislatures.
Why w'ould you want to call the legislatures together to change such a law? Legislatures w'ould not be worthy of the name if they assembled in the different provinces and took away from the farmers that measure of protection which is so necessary.
But the Minister of Agriculture has a rather soft spot in his heart, I was pleased to see. I was reading Hansard the other day and what he said was so touching that, knowing him as I do, I think I should read it to the house. He said, as reported at page 95 of Hansard:
I shall continue to fight the battles of the farmers of Canada. No adding to or taking away from duties or prestige will remove my life-long association with and love for farmers and farming.
That love for the farmers was so very touching, Mr. Speaker, that I thought then we should advise the Prime Minister to relieve the Minister of Agriculture of his many portfolios and give him another one entitling him to be called the minister of romance, because he has such a loving heart.

speechtext:
The government will have to come to the social credit policy before very long. Make no mistake about that.
Then we have another beautiful picture with reference to the storage problem. I bring this question up, not for the purpose of saying something which has already been said, but because I believe we are going to have a more acute storage problem on our hands next year than we have now. I can see quite clearly from the government's handling of the storage problem this year that we are heading into a very dangerous situation.
This problem of storage came up in the house last session. The whole question was thoroughly threshed over, but the government had no policy to offer, no solution to propose. They went blindly on until they came up against the situation we now face. The farmers were promised storage. Assurance was given that some sort of storage would be given to the farmers. The farmer himself was asked, probably indirectly, to provide some storage for his grain and the farmers in my own community deserve a great deal of credit for the way in which they attempted to provide as best they could their own storage facilities. Some of them even used parts of their homes as granaries. Others went out and constructed a rude type of granary with wire and sheaves, and others just had to pile it on the ground, it was left there and the rains came and a great deal of it was spoiled. But they did their share, anyway.
To add to the difficulties of the farmers in regard to storage of the 1939 crop, the price of lumber-most unfairly, I think-went up considerably. I admit that there was a scarcity of lumber because the government needed it for their war effort, but there was no need or justification for the increase in the price. If an article is scarce, the obvious thing to do is set the price; but that was not done, and the farmer was put to a greater expense in order to meet the requirements of the government, because it was the government that asked the farmers to provide storage.
372	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
Another unfair aspect of the thing was that, while the elevator companies were given their storage right away, the farmers did not receive their storage until three weeks afterwards. One would almost be tempted to think that this government was working for the interests of the elevator companies and the big concerns and disregarding the farmers. I read not so long ago an article in which it was stated that the elevators were guaranteed storage for eighteen months. The farmer never has been guaranteed his storage on the 1939 crop; in fact he is not going to be allowed to get very much storage, because no advance payment is to be made on the wheat. So that if he wants cash-and he is very badly in need of cash-he has to take his grain to the elevator. By this process the elevator companies will keep their elevators filled to the roof, and they are guaranteed the storage for the length of time mentioned. We all know that last year they made something like $15,000,000 from storage. Some of that $15,000,000 would have been a fine contribution to the farmers if it could have come to them this year.
Remember, too, that though the farmer was not given storage, the elevator companies are guaranteed storage, so they are going to keep their elevators filled and they will make as much money out of storage this year as they did last year.
I was looking the other day at the issue of Monetary Times for October 26, 1940, and I ran across this:
On the other hand, there is a large grain crop and carryover which the banks have been financing. From August to November, 1939, current loans were up $147,000,000 mainly on this account.
I want you to notice the next statement:
As long as the elevators remain full, this branch of the banks' business will not suffer.
So that there are two reasons why the elevators will be kept filled: first, that the banks shall make a profit; second that the elevator companies shall get again this year profits of $15,000,000. That is no way to treat the farming community, and it is no way to assure unity in this country. You play directly into the hands of the big concerns and let the little fellow go.
What will be the situation so far as next year's crop is concerned? I can quite well see that when the elevators are filled next year and there is another crop coming on, this government will appeal to the farmers to build granaries, though they will have lost the storage for 1939 and a share of the 1940 crop. Is that fair dealing? The elevators will have been filled by that time; they will remain full right through the period of the

war, and the obligation will again be thrown upon the farmer to provide the storage, although he will have no guarantee that he is going to make anything out of it. If that is conducive to unity and patriotism, I cannot see it.
Last year there was some talk here about advancing payment to the farmer for his crop held in storage, but nothing was done about it. It was not an oversight; the Minister of Trade and Commerce knew at that time that this situation was going to arise; for he said this, as reported in Hansard, 1940, page 2252:
Unless something is done to make available to the farmer more money than, owing to elevator capacity conditions, he can obtain from his first deliveries, there will be widespread suffering, and there would be widespread necessity for relief.
The minister is to be commended at least for his foresight. He knew that that condition was coming. So did the, rest of the cabinet know; they could not help but know it. Yet what was done? Always procrastination; always leaving until tomorrow what should be done to-day; no policy; no direction. Here was the situation, quite clearly known to at least one cabinet minister last year, but nothing was done. Apparently the whole thing fell down because there was no money.
Quite amusing things happen when one speaks of this question of money. I recall when the wheat committee of the cabinet was sitting here last year after the house closed, the government called in the experts to handle this wheat situation. Among the experts whom they called were bankers, and quite properly so. If you want grain raised you go to the farmers. If you want lumber you go to the lumbermen. If you want money you go to the bankers. They claim they are controlling money; they should be the ones to provide it. On this point I want to read an extract from the address of Mr. G. S. Mathieson, president of the grain exchange:
The problem of providing funds, where necessary, for the erection of storage buildings on the farm and to make loans against grain stored on the farm, would appear _ primarily to be a responsibility of the Canadian banks, whose business it is, under certain limitations, to lend money.
So the government did right in calling in the bankers. But what did the bankers tell them? They said, "Well now, listen; you fellows have got us all wrong. We did not come here to give you money; we came to give you only advice." So they were turned away and again the farmer was left to shift for himself.
We come now, Mr. Speaker, to the matter of next year's crop. I think we should be given
NOVEMBER 25, 1940	. d
The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
guidance 'by this government as to their policy in relation to the coming crop. This is necessary, it seems to me, if for nothing more than to attempt to ensure unity throughout the country. The prospects of the farmer are very poor indeed. The Minister of Agriculture's great love for th-e people is not going to get them food to eat next year, nor will it put clothes on the children's backs; and I am sure that the minister has no intention of doing either of those things.
We have suggested that the government take over the storage; in fact we have on the order paper a resolution which reads:
Whereas the system of wheat storage on the farms is quite inadequate and will not prove efficient in the years to come;
And whereas it is quite inequitable to ask the farmers to build or provide their own storage facilities:
Therefore be it resolved,-That, in the opinion of this house, the federal government itself be urged to make provision by the erection and/or purchase of storage facilities and accept delivery of wheat when tendered.
Now is the time when the government should be concerning themselves about storage for next year's crop. If they do not they are going to have the same difficulty they are finding this year, and there will not be any more satisfactory solution, because they will not be ready. What is the use of waiting until next year to start this enterprise of building up storage? Are we going to wait and pay the elevator companies another $15,000,000? Why not use that money to construct storage facilities? I can well remember the Minister of Agriculture making the remark a year or so ago that if the government were going into the wheat business and the wheat board were going to handle all the wheat, they would have to take over the storage facilities, and I think he was right. Then why does he not do something about the matter? There is no use in making these statements and then doing nothing about it.
The question of price has been raised. We have on the order paper another resolution dealing with the price of wheat. I want to put it on Hansard at this point in order to show what our attitude is. It reads:
Whereas the prices of farm machinery, all costs of living and farm wages have increased due to the war:
Therefore be it resolved,-that, in the opinion of this house, parliament should immediately take such steps as are necessary to ensure the farmers of Canada a fixed price of not less than one dollar per bushel for number one (1) northern wheat at their local elevator, on at least the first 2,000 bushels of the 1941 crop.
There is quite a variety of opinion on this question of price. I am glad to see that, as each session goes by, the government comes
to the conclusion that the resolutions which we have put on the order paper have been almost right as to price. At the 1938 session we had a resolution at that time asking for a price of 95 cents a bushel at the local elevator, and the Minister of Agriculture made a great oration-he is wonderful at that anyway-pointing out that farmers should not get 95 cents a bushel for their wheat because the cost of production was 30 to 40 cents. On page 2623 of Hansard for April 5, 1939, the Minister of Agriculture had this to say with regard to price:
It has been proven over and over again that twenty bushels to the acre of wheat can be produced at a cost of from 30 to 40 cents a bushel.
Then I asked him:
What is the basis of that estimate of from 30 to 40 cents a bushel as the cost ot production?
Mr. Gardiner: Estimates have been made by authorities in Saskatchewan university, and there are also the figures submitted by the Saskatchewan government to the Howell commission.
So the minister was quite convinced at that time that 30 to 40 cents was the right price. But he had to change his mind. On page 102 of Hansard for November 14, 1940, he is reported as saying, and I should like the house to note this particularly:
It is generally admitted that 70 cents advance at Fort William, which nets the farmer about 50 cents a bushel, does not cover his total costs of production and therefore does not maintain him as a contented producer.
That is, a return of fifty cents a bushel on the farm does not cover the cost of production, yet in 1939 the minister said that 30 to 40 cents was adequate.
Why then does the minister not do something about the matter? Surely he does not expect farmers to raise wheat at 50 cents a bushel at their local elevators when there is no profit in doing so. Manufacturers of war supplies do not work on that basis; members of parliament do not; no one else in the country does, yet he is asking the farmer to raise wheat at less than the cost of production. First it was 30 cents, then 50 cents; would it not be a grand thing if the Minister of Agriculture would make up his mind?
This question has been discussed on many occasions and the government have frankly admitted that they are at a loss to know how to settle it. They have travelled all over the country trying to get suggestions. But they never got an answer to their difficulty until they went to Alberta. When they were in Alberta the provincial cabinet met the committee and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) when he was
4	, ,	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
there with regard to this question, and gave him a written submission setting out how to handle the wheat problem. I have it here; it was reported in To-day and To-morrow in its issue of September 19 last. I read the last paragraph to show that one government at least has offered to help this government, but that offer was rejected;
Jn Persistently pressing for early action the Alberta government wishes to express once again its complete readiness to cooperate with the federal government in every possible way in dealing with the situation. Also, once more, the Alberta government reiterates its willingness to deal with the situation-
That is the wheat situation.
-in this province along effective lines if the federal government, for its part, will undertake not to interfere with such action and, where it is necessary to invoke federal powers, to extend full facilities and cooperation to the Alberta government.
That is to say, the Alberta government has said to this government:	We will handle
the wheat situation ourselves if you will just give us the necessary cooperation. It is not an impossible situation, although the Minister of Agriculture may think it is. As he has handled it, it would appear so.
Just consider the difference in attitude between 'the Alberta government and the bankers when they met with the wheat committee in Ottawa. The bankers said to the government: We will give you nothing but advice. But this government out in Alberta, that has been so greatly criticized and run down, especially by this federal government say:	We will take this wheat right off
your hands if you will give the necessary cooperation. One would think that at a time like this, with the government faced with this wheat problem, this offer of cooperation for maximum war effort by the Alberta government would have been welcomed. But what did the federal government answer? Nothing. The farmers are not getting any money; the government have no policy for next year's crop; what a pleasant outlook! People are asking, "What do you want us to do? Tell us and we will do it."
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) said the other day that in his province they are paying a dollar a bushel for ho. 5 wheat for chicken feed. Yet the people in Alberta cannot sell their wheat, or when they do they get less than fifty cents a bushel for No. 1. Obviously there is something wrong. The people in British Columbia have apples; we in Alberta and Saskatchewan have no apples. How willingly we would trade wheat for apples. Yet we 
cannot do it. This is war time; people are starving; in Alberta and Saskatchewan people are suffering.
If we cannot settle these interprovincial troubles, how can we expect to settle the world problem? Let us start at home, rectify these wrongs, set our own house in order, and then it will be time to look for something bigger to solve. This problem can be solved if the government will only look to the basic cause of all their difficulties, namely, the financial trouble. But that is the one thing they overlook. I do hope the government will take this question seriously and see that this condition does not exist next year. I am sure it can be disposed of if they just make up their minds to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming to this house I have tried to listen with an open mind to the arguments of our social credit friends. I have even gone so far as to read their literature, including the book written by their leader in this house, but this afternoon I have come to the conclusion that I have listened and read with a mind too open, simply drifting along. I am going to adopt the same attitude with regard to the anti-Gardiner speech to which we have just listened.
I think most of the people of Canada recognize the value to this country of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and will take the same position.
For two and a half weeks now we have been telling the world what we have been doing in connection with our war effort. I do not believe I would add to the discussion but for the fact that there never was a time in our history when there was so much to do and so little time in which to do it.
First, I wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne upon their fine speeches, because they set an example to the rest of us by keeping the discussion on a high plane. I believe that their example has been followed and that, for the most part, members on both sides of the house have tried to be constructive in what they have had to say.
I should like to refer particularly to the hon. gentleman who seconded the address (Mr. Jutras), and his appeal for understanding in dealing with the situation of the farmers in western Canada. I am interested, as all westerners are, in the success of western Canada. I have watched the growth of the west probably for longer than most members in this house; I have seen many of the sites now occupied bv towns

The Address-Mr. Mayhew
and cities, when they were bald-headed prairie.
I know the people; I know something of what they have to put up with in carrying on farming, and I know that their success means the success of the rest of Canada. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that the wheat problem can be solved, or that the situation of agriculture generally can be improved, by any bonusing proposition. If you bonus wheat and raise the price, you only make it more difficult to produce some of the other commodities that should be raised from the wheat.
I think we can best assist the farmer, and in doing so assist ourselves as well, by doing what any business man does; that is, by deciding how much we need for ourselves and to meet the requirements of our best customers. To-day Canada has only one customer left-Great Britain. Her requirements, together with our own consumption, are estimated at approximately 275,000,000 bushels. Therefore I think Canada should buy, at a good price, and store the 275,000,000 bushels necessary to look after herself and her best customer. We have at the present time an obligation to look after the people of Great Britain. But I think it is the obligation of the farmer to look after the remainder of the wheat. I have always found that the safest man to trust for assistance is yourself. Neither the government nor your neighbour will look after you as well as you can look after yourself. I was born and brought up on a farm, and I think it would be good business and good farming practice to keep your own grain in your own granaries under your own control. Then you would be greatly tempted to feed some of that surplus grain to your own stock and thus convert your wheat into butter, eggs, bacon and live stock, thereby greatly increasing our own consumption.
If I may refer for a moment to a local matter, I should like to express our appreciation of the visits of four members of the cabinet to our riding during the recess. The invasion was led by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). We never lacked confidence in him or in his ability, but that confidence was greatly increased after his short visit. Then we had a visit by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). That was really too much of a flying visit, but we have heard him speak and have seen him before, and our memories in that regard are still fresh. Then we had a visit from the newly appointed Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), who wins confidence and friends wherever he goes. I believe it was only his second visit to the Pacific coast, but it was
a timely and much appreciated visit. The fourth minister to visit us was our own Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), who comes and goes quite frequently.
I should like now to extend to another member of the cabinet, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) an invitation to visit our city. The people of Victoria feel that they owe the minister a great debt because of the way in which he has kept Canada a unit. He interprets our viewpoint to the people of Quebec and interprets to us the viewpoint of that province, and only through a visit by him can we really show our appreciation of his great efforts.
Recently the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) paid a visit to eastern Canada. We 'hope he will be kind enough to visit western Canada and the city of Victoria. I think he will be surprised at what his ministers have accomplished for him and for Canada in the way of protection on the western coast. While he is there we may point out some possible improvements, because there are always improvements that may be made; but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, we are proud of the many things that have been done.
I should like to refer briefly, if I may, to the speech made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). While my parliamentary experience may not be equal to his, possibly he will not object if I make reference to his observations because, after all, I do not believe there is much difference in the number of years we have served Canada. My observations, however, will not be critical; on the contrarjr I wish to compliment him on a statement which I suggest is to his credit and one with which I believe the people of Canada have been greatly pleased. He reached the high light in his address when he rededicated himself and his party to the support of the government's war effort. If there ever was a time when the people of Canada have been looking for those who were willing to forget party lines, to forget criticism and to offer constructive suggestions, surely that time is the present. My only regret is that he did not continue in his observations with an outline of his own programme for the prosecution of the war, so that we might have contrasted his suggestions with the effort which the government is now making. No doubt he will avail himself of an opportunity at some later time to present his suggestions.
May I refer to the speech, or possibly I should say the report of the Minister of Agriculture respecting his trip to the old country. We were greatly heartened when listening to what he had to say with regard to what is
The Address-Mr. Mayhew

happening in Great Britain, and we were encouraged by his description of how the people in England are standing up under the terrific strain they are now being forced to endure. We were particularly interested in his attitude. He did not go to England with a price tag on our commodities-our wheat, our bacon, our cheese or our butter. Had he gone there with price tags he would have failed to appreciate the sentiments of the people of Canada. He did, however, go with a determination to find out how much of certain commodities the people of Great Britain wanted from Canada, and he left it for them to say what they were willing to pay. If that money is not sufficient to pay the farmer a reasonable price for his products, then I suggest that the difference should be made up by the general taxpayers throughout the country.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has a heavy burden indeed. The time is not yet ripe to say whether he is making a real success of his undertaking, but I should say he has made a splendid start, and would seem to be on the road to success. I should like to compliment him upon one action he has taken, namely, that of making it possible for people to pay their income tax over a period of eight months. He has instituted an arrangement whereby one-third of the income tax may be paid in the first four months, and the remaining two-thirds in the last four. That is an arrangement which I hope may be repeated on future occasions.
The government and the people should remember that profits are not always liquid. They are liquid only in an industry or a business that is in a state of semi-decay. If a business is progressive it can pay only out of it profits. As the profits are made they are placed back in the business. I am sure the Minister of Finance does not want to harm the development of industry, nor is he willing to accept in lieu of cash the products of any business. He must therefore exercise great care so as to avoid destroying entirely the goose that is laying the golden egg.
I know that the minister is going to look for more money, and that he must have it. I believe there are ways by which he can get it. I would suggest to him that he adopt a more vigorous campaign in connection with the sale of war savings stamps. In the purchase of war savings stamps we have in essence a programme of superannuation. We now have a plan whereby one may buy a superannuation certificate, but the handling of that plan costs a great deal of money. I suggest that through the purchase of war savings stamps there would be no unnecessary expense. May I suggest to the minister that instead of having

the whole sum mature at the end of a seven-year period, he give the option of having the date of maturity set at the end of five, ten, fifteen or twenty years. Under such circumstances one might buy a superannuation certificate to suit his own requirements. I believe that a little encouragement, promotion and* persuasion would induce many employers to purchase the first stamp, and possibly the last one, in order to help their employees.
With the exception of the necessity of running errands for our constituents, hon. members have not had very much of a practical nature to do in connection with the war effort. Here is a job, however, which might be undertaken by them. I believe that in our respective districts we might organize so as to produce much more than is now being derived from the sale of war savings stamps, and at the same time we might promote the idea of superannuation funds for everybody.
I have a further suggestion to make, that the minister continue the home improvement plan. While that plan has not obliterated the slums from our cities, I think it has prevented other districts from becoming slums. It has given our people an opportunity to own their own homes. After all, our home life is the corner-stone of our country. There are also rumours that he may discontinue the national housing scheme, but I hope they are not true. I hope he will make an announcement at an early date that this scheme will be continued, either in its present form or in some modified way which will be acceptable to the people. In the belief that this scheme is to be discontinued the people of Canada, particularly of western Canada, have been rushing to get their homes built in order to come under the plan. This has created in many districts a shortage of labour which is wholly unnecessary.
I have one other suggestion to make to the Minister of Finance. He seems to have an abundance of auditors going through the country. An auditor is a fine man to check on what has been done, but it is generally too late. I suggest that the minister adopt a policy of having more inspectors going round to prevent things from happening, rather than of having the details put down on paper after they have happened. I do not offer these suggestions in a critical way; I offer them from the observations I have made in my travels.
I consider that the address delivered the other day by the Prime Minister was a masterpiece. While he was at times optimistic, I read into his remarks a definite warning to the people of Canada that theTe was a terrific struggle ahead. He pictured the territory in the enemy's hands, all the shore line from the

The Address-Mr. Mayhew
northern tip of Norway to Spain. He described what was back of that shore line, the resources of practically all of Europe with its generations of experience in engineering and manufacturing, all ready to attempt to wipe Great Britain off the map. Surely such a statement is not likely to lull one into a sense of false security; it was a definite warning to the people that they must bend themselves to greater effort.
I believe that the people of Canada should be told the truth at all times, no matter how black it may be. They should be told the truth without varnish. Only by being told the truth can we adjust our minds to the problem and our shoulders to the task and carry it through to completion. Canadians are not cowards. Canadians have faced difficult tasks in days gone by, and they are ready to face difficult tasks in the future. But they must know where they have to go.
During the recent election and during this session we have been told by our Prime Minister and other members of the government on more than one occasion that Canada's effort would be the utmost in human and material resources. I wonder whether we have reached that point? I compliment most sincerely the ministers of the different departments upon what they have accomplished. Recently I travelled from Victoria to Halifax; I visited many of the camps and the aeroplane fields;
I saw both naval yards, and I inspected some of our industrial plants. With all that the ministers have told us, they have not yet conveyed to the people of Canada the complete picture of what has been accomplished. I shall not attempt in my feeble way to do what they have not done. I feel that the accomplishments are beyond the ability of any one to picture, but we have still a road to travel before we have put the utmost of our human and material resources into the defence of Great Britain.
So long as there are idle people in our communities; so long as there are idle machines in any part of Canada; so long as there are shipbuilding ways which are wholly or partly idle, we in Canada cannot say that we have thrown our utmost into this struggle. It was the most natural thing for the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), when he was in a hurry to get what he wanted, to go to the centre of industry to ask them for what he needed. I do not think anyone can find any fault with that, nor do I think anyone can find fault with the length of time it has taken the minister to tell industry what he wanted. I am satisfied that when the picture is put before us more clearly than it has been up to the present time, we shall be most proud of him. But the back-bone of the
immediate need has been broken, and rather than have these activities centralized they should be spread through the whole country in order to give everyone an opportunity to express his patriotism in action.
As I speak, I think of the 75,000 tons of scrapiron now lying in the yards of British Columbia at a time when Beverley Baxter can describe in an article in a magazine how they came along and took the iron fence from in front of his place. Surely there ought to be some way of turning that scrap-iron, and the 50,000 tons which will be produced annually in years to come, into steel to help in the prosecution of this war.
Speaking in this house last year, I said that I thought Canada should build at least fifty merchant ships in order that we might be able to take the products of this country to any part of the world. That suggestion did not raise even a ruffle in the house, but I am glad that it raised a little ruffle outside. I understand that Great Britain to-day is buj -ing or having built in Canada eighteen such boats. We read that Lord Lothian when he landed in New York the other day said that Britain was drawing on all her resources and that her financial standing was becoming weak. But Canada, Mr. Speaker, has no debt owing to the United States; we are not in default. We can borrow money from the United States; we can lend it to Great Britain if we wish to, and we can produce the boats. The United States legislation does not apply to Canada.

speechtext:
I say that we in Canada should immediately take steps to build not only the eighteen boats Britain is asking us to build, but another thirty-two along with them, making the fifty originally mentioned in this house. Then we should be in quite a different position. To-day we are like a wheelbarrow without a wheel. We cannot transport our goods across the ocean. We grow our grain and make our munitions, and then we leave them on our doorstep and ask Britain to come and get them. That is not good enough. It is time that Canada stood on her own feet. Surely we have enough

The Address-Mr. Mayhew
resources -to do this. Only when we are doing our utmost can we truthfully say to our people that we have gone the limit.
This has been a comfortable war so far for us. Labour is better off, working longer hours and for better wages. Our merchants have never in years had as good a turn-over as they have had this year, and our manufacturers 'have never had a better year for keeping their plants going. It is the farmers and those who have lost their sons and daughters who have been doing most of the suffering. But our day will come, and it should come very shortly.
I speak now for the people of my own constituency, people who are predominantly British, people who belong to the oldest cities in Canada. Those who are Canadian-born may speak of the people in the homeland with a certain amount of sentiment, but when the people in my riding speak of the homeland they are thinking of their sons and their daughters and probably their fathers and mothers who -are in Britain now suffering under the daily bombardment, and it is hard for the people in my riding to stand idly by and not be able to express their feelings in action.
I want to say just a word or two about our troops. I think the only thing is to treat our boys as humanely as possible. The best that you can spend on help is not merely the wages that you pay a man. It is the small things that you do afterwards which bring you and the man together as human beings. These are the things that produce results. So I say, to put it on the lowest possible basis, we should, if only for the sake of a better morale in our Canadian forces, see to it, if it is at all possible, that our soldiers are given at least one trip home before they embark for overseas.
I see that my time is about up, and I shall take the few minutes left to refer briefly to the forthcoming conference of premiers of the provinces to consider the Sirois report.
I do not believe that these -men who hold the confidence of the people of Canada are going to come to Ottawa with the case prejudged, having decided that they are not going to do this and that they are not going to do that. I think that as men of experience in public life they will sit down and consider on what points they agree, and that upon the points on which they cannot agree they will try to straighten out their differences in order to give us something definite, because on that report hangs a long-term policy for Canada, and it is time that we had a policy that was longer than any policy that has been given to us yet for the development of this country. fMr. Mayhew.]
I should like to see sitting, at the same time as the conference or before, another committee of reliable citizens of Canada to study what we can do for the rehabilitation of the boys who come back from the war and for the rehabilitation of those who have not been to the war and are unable to find employment. We must first of all have a clear understanding of what we can do and what we cannot do, and I think it is time that serious consideration be given to this question and that definite steps be taken so that the people will know just what is being done to meet the situation which is bound to arise. I know what it is, Mr. Speaker, to work in the lumber camps of Ontario. I know what it is to drive logs down the river. I know what it is to work on the railways. I know what it is to be without a job and [DOT] without a nickel; and while, as I said before, and say again, the first one to depend on is yourself, I think it is time that we should now have a definite programme for the development of Canada.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
