The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the outbreak of the present war the problem of Canadian unity has been a subject of many discussions, but in my opinion it still remains a topic which warrants further consideration on our part at this time.
The mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Claxton), the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson),' and more particularly the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Picard), have made brief references to the part which Canadians of nonAnglo-Saxon origin play in our national life. I propose to discuss, further, other important phases of this subject which so far have hardly been mentioned.
There are two prevalent views on this subject of Canadian unity. There are those who feel that there is greater unity in Canada to-day than there has ever been before, and there are also those who view the whole situation with suspicion and doubt. I am inclined to agree, at least in part, with the former, that the present war has unified our people more than ever before. Nevertheless there are some prevalent viewpoints which

The Address-Mr. Hlynka
in my opinion deserve the immediate attention of this house, and the sooner the situation is remedied, the better it shall be for all concerned.
Sir Norman Angell, world-renowned analyst of national and international affairs, has recently discussed, in his two articles published in the Financial Post, some of the reasons why he thinks Hitler has been successful in overrunning several European countries. He maintains that Hitler has used the age-old weapon of "divide and conquer" in the most masterly and subtle way. In the first place, he used this weapon to get control of Germany. He then proceeded to unify his own forces at home, and at the same time set out to create disunity and distrust among the democratic countries of the world. Having done that, he concentrated upon dividing the people internally, in countries he set out to conquer, by cleverly scheming and creating class and racial disharmony. One has little choice but to agree with Sir Norman's analysis in the light of what has happened in Europe. Alas, the unscrupulous fifth-column tactics are too well known as an integral part of the blitzkrieg machine which is threatening to destroy the very existence of our democratic institutions in the world. Let us make sure, then, Mr. Speaker, that there is, no room in Canada for those who would seek to create disunity among our people by playing upon racial differences or racial superiority in our midst.
It is a well-recognized fact that there exists a greater unity to-day among all the peoples of the British commonwealth of nations than there has ever existed in the entire history of the British people. Since 1931, when by the statute of Westminster all the British dominions were granted equal sovereign rights, united only by their common allegiance to the crown, and each functioning as an independent unit, the bonds of unity have strengthened among all the dominions. They are now united on a voluntary basis. The British commonwealth of nations to-day is the greatest democratic unit in existence. This has been made possible only by the wise and tolerant British colonial policy towards its people of many racial origins and creeds. The British people to-day constitute, chiefly for this reason, one of the greatest powers the world has ever seen.
But our responsibility lies specifically here within Canada-we are assembled here for that purpose. The question before us is, how can we give maximum aid to Britain and at the same time be well prepared for our own home defence? At the moment I shall not discuss the material side of the question,
because that has well been done by others on previous occasions. My chief purpose to-night is to discuss the question of our Canadian unity.
I believe we are all of opinion that Canada must be united to the utmost if she is to be effective in her aid to Britain and if she is to be prepared for her own home defence. The people within the borders of Canada must assume equal responsibilities as well as share equal rights and privileges. We must have only one purpose in mind; that^ is victory. In answer to all agents of disunity, let me say that we must eradicate all possibilities of disharmony and check all those influences which tend to cause disunion and build racial barriers within Canada. Then, and only then, will Canada be looked upon as a powerful nation.
But to our regret, Mr. Speaker, we find that certain individuals who hold responsible positions in our public life make loose and ill-advised statements which may easily be misconstrued and made use of as the basis or cause for disunity.
In the first place, let me make a passing reference to a rather loose statement made by the Conservative leader in the British Columbia legislature. While speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne he said, as reported in the Edmonton Journal of November 1:
Planning for the period of readjustment which will follow the war and a vigorous stand against the "furtherance of foreign language or foreign creed in this country" were urged in the provincial legislature Thursday by R. L. Maitland, K.C., leader of the Conservative opposition.
And further it reads:
Mr. Maitland deplored the existence of foreign language schools in Canada. . . .
There may be several interpretations of what the hon. gentleman had in mind, but my chief objection is to the fact that utterances of this kind throw an unfair suspicion upon our loyal Canadian citizens who happen not to be of Anglo-Saxon extraction. This may and does create disunity at a time when unity is most imperative.
Secondly, I should like to refer to an item appearing in the Edmonton Bulletin, in its issue of November 4. I quote:
With the stress of war causing a widening of activities in the force, 500 new constables are being enrolled by the R.C.M.P. throughout the dominion.
Because of rigid requirements in the way of both mental and physical qualifications, few as yet have been accepted.
Applicants must be single of British racial origin.
3S0
The Address-Mr. Hlynka

Here again, the meaning of the words "of British racial origin" is vague. When interpreted broadly, it would appear to mean that any person born in any British dominion is eligible for enrolment, be he of Anglo-Saxon or any other racial extraction. But interpreted in a narrower sense, it would simply rule out the eligibility of all those not of Anglo-Saxon origin. Unfortunately, this narrower interpretation is being used by minor officials for the purpose of racial discrimination. I suggest that in future when the government is putting out circulars of this type, that a more specific choice of words be made.
Lastly, I should like to draw the attention of the house to a much more serious statement which appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of October 8. Mr. G. W. Parker, relief officer of Saskatoon, commenting on the administration of relief, is reported to have made this assertion. I quote in part:
There should be two scales of relief, one for central Europeans and one for " white people."
This, I submit, Mr. Speaker, is a vile form of racial discrimination. I challenge the authority upon which Mr. Parker bases his classification of people, in saying that central Europeans do not belong to the white race. I also question the mentality of those who would propose a higher scale of relief for one group of our citizens and a lower scale for another.
Probably the most notorious example of this same attitude of racial discrimination as well as higher and lower rations is exemplified in Hitlerian philosophy. We all know what that attitude of mind has brought upon us; let us, then, not have anything to do with it in Canada. No one who takes the attitude that this man does is fit to hold public office. In our country, where approximately half the population is of non-Anglo-Saxon extraction, ideas of this kind and at this time of national crisis should not be tolerated. It is about time some of our public men realized that they are nothing more than public servants hired to serve the people. I suggest that the defence of Canada regulations should also be made to apply to individuals who deliberately make malicious statements which cause dissension among our people.
I am happy, however, to be able to reply to the above and other would-be critics, on the authority of some of our eminent public men. Fortunately the great majority of our public men are much more broad-minded. It is gratifying to find that sincere efforts are being made by this government to bring about among all our people, of whatever racial 
origin they may be, a better understanding and singleness of purpose.
Some members on this side of the house have criticized the bureau of public information for being too partisan. I think that criticism is well founded. But so far as unity of our people of different racial origins is concerned, I believe that this bureau is rendering an invaluable service by publishing from time to time translations of articles appearing in the non-English press in Canada. I do not know of a better way of passing on to our Canadian public material which appears in Ukrainian, Czech, German and other publications. It helps to clear up a great deal of misunderstanding which may exist with regard to the stand these groups have taken in connection with the war. It is to be hoped that in future the press will take a greater advantage of this fine service.
I have not the time to quote many of these translations; let it suffice to give the house one short extract. But before doing so, let me quote the head-note by the director of public information, Mr. G. H. Lash, introducing one of these articles:
Note to editors: In view of the misunderstanding which seems to exist in some parts of Canada respecting the attitude of the foreignspeaking sections of our population towards Canada's war effort and our war aims, the following translation of an editorial which appeared ... in the German language newspaper Der Nordwesten is interesting. Nobody recognizes better than myself how precious newspaper space is these days, but if you could find room to reprint or to comment upon this editorial and others which I hope to send you from time to time from other foreign-language newspapers of Canada I think you would be making a fine contribution towards the development of national unity.
The following quotation from the above-mentioned newspaper was translated and reprinted in the circular of public information in the issue of October 10:
The war has created the spirit of unity among Canadians of every race and creed such as this country has not known. The full meaning of our Canadian citizenship is better understood, and if there be the few -who do not value its privileges, it must be apparent to them that this land has no place for them.
The people of Canada of whatever racial origin have one supreme duty-the winning of the war, and to that end there must be a complete unity in our land, and a determination to give and to sacrifice. And from the grave situation which has been thrust upon us by those who would destroy our way of life, we shall emerge a better people and a greater Canada.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a sample of material which is being translated and reprinted in these circulars. From that I would judge that there is a good-will on the part of all our

The Address-Mr. Hlynka
Canadian citizens, regardless of racial origin, towards a common understanding and national unity.
While discussing the subject of Canadian unity, I feel that I would not be doing justice to the topic if I did not refer to Doctor Watson Kirkconnell, who is undoubtely Canada's greatest authority on our population of non-Anglo-Saxon extraction. Doctor Kirkconnell has been for many years a keen student of all our racial groups. It is only to be regretted that this government has not, as far as I know, used Doctor Kirkconnell's exceptional talent in the interest of our national unity. I would recommend to hon. members to read, for example, Doctor Kirk-connell's recent booklet, entitled "The Canadian Ukrainians and the War". It is well worth reading.
Here is an interesting extract from the London Free Press reprinted in the Ottawa Citizen of October 31, regarding Doctor Kirk-connell's contribution.	To me it is an
encouraging bit of information.
According to Doctor Watson Kirkconnell of McMaster university, who is Canada's greatest authority on our foreign population, Herr Hitler lias done more than any other man to draw Canada together and to unite the dominion. Despite intensive propaganda which was carried on in Canada by Berlin, Moscow and Rome, Doctor Kirkconnell says that more than ninety-eight per cent of the peoples of alien birth are loyal to Canada to-day, and are enthusiastically lined up behind the British effort. ...	.
In most cases the nazis overran their home countries, while they realize that the freedom and liberty which they came to this country to seek will be lost if Hitler wins. Doctor Kirkconnell gave as one example the Ukrainians. He pointed out that in Saskatchewan they form ten per cent of the population, yet over ten per cent of the enlistments in that province are from peoples of Ukrainian stock. The war has brought English and French closer together, and it is optimistic to learn that it is making for national unity among those who are not of French or Anglo-Saxon origin.
In closing, may I sum up the whole problem of our national unity by quoting from one of Canada's greatest statesmen, who was a friend of all the Canadian people. He worked hard for Canadian unity and was a man who understood even the simplest soul in our land. I speak of Lord Tweedsmuir.
While addressing a large Ukrainian gathering of 1,500 people on September 21, 1936, at Fraserwood, Manitoba, Lord Tweedsmuir spoke in such a way that even to this day those who heard him hold sacred the ideas he expressed. On that happy occasion the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) was present. I crave the indulgence of hon. members while I read a part of that great statesman's short message. I would suggest that
they follow this masterpiece. Many hon. members find themselves at a loss at times, when they have to address a gathering of people of some other racial extraction. This is a wonderful example of an address to such a gathering, and is one of the most interesting short speeches I have ever read. These were the words uttered by Lord Tweedsmuir:
I thank you most warmly for the way you have received me to-day. I do not think that anywhere I have gone in Canada I have been welcomed with a more beautiful ceremony; your escort, your national ceremony of presenting me with bread and salt, and if I may be allowed to say so the beautiful and well chosen words of your address.
I realize that my welcome is due to the fact that I represent your king, and it will be my pleasure to convey to the king the cordial greetings of the Ukrainian people in Canada.
I am very happy to be among you to-day.
I am among people who have behind them a long historical tradition, for it was your race which for centuries held the south eastern gate of Europe against the attacks from the east.
I can well imagine that this country is home to you, for these wide prairies are very like the great plains of south eastern Europe from which you came. During my tour of the prairies I have come across many of your people, and I am glad to see that in a short time you have come to be a vital element in the Canadian nation. You played your part in the great war. To-day I find your sons in the permanent and non-permanent militia.
Wherever I go I hear high praise of your industry and hardihood and enterprise even under the most difficult conditions. You have become good Canadians.
Every Briton and especially every Scotsman must believe that the strongest nations are those that are made up of different racial elements. The Ukrainian element is a very valuable element to our new Canada. I wish to say one thing to you. You have accepted the duties and loyalties as you have acquired the privileges of Canadian citizens, but I want you also to remember your old Ukrainian traditions-your beautiful handicrafts, your folk songs and your folk legends. I do not believe that any people can be strong unless they remember and keep in touch with all their past. Your traditions are all valuable contributions toward our Canadian culture which cannot be a copy of any old thing-it must be a new thing created by the contribution of all the elements that make up a nation.
That was the outlook of a great man who understood the people. I think it would be worth while to compare utterances such as I quoted in the first part of my address with the sentiments to which I have just referred.
Let me say, then, that in this crucial and historic moment every Canadian, whatever may be his racial origin, must hold dear the principles for which the British flag stands, namely liberty, without which there is no true life; justice, so essential to all people, and fair play, which makes life worth
The Address-Mr. Tucker

living. In the name of all these things, Mr. Speaker, let us unite and work in harmony for the good of Canada and a brighter future for all our Canadian people, regardless of racial origin.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to extend my congratulations to the young member (Mr. Hlynka) who has just taken his seat. As a Canadian of British origin I should like to express my support and appreciation of what he has just said and what he represents to Canadian life to-day. I have been told by people who accompanied their majesties across Canada that the most moving episode of the whole trip was the welcome they received at Melville, where practically everyone was of other than French or English-speaking origin. I suppose those of Polish, Ukrainian and German origin predominated, and I am told that there the outpouring of affection for the head of our country and our commonwealth was such that it moved even the most staid and cynical newspaperman. Many people had come there, after a journey of perhaps a day, to look at their sovereign, and it was said that there was such an evident spirit of affection that among those humble people many had tears in their eyes that they should have the privilege of meeting their king and1 queen.
Then we hear of such utterances of racial hatred and discrimination as were quoted by the hon. member for Vegreville. We try to think those who are guilty of these things are endeavouring to be good citizens. The gentleman, Mr. Parker, mentioned by the hon. member is a returned soldier who served in the last war. I am certain he wants to be a good citizen and do his best for Canada, but I am at a loss to understand the psychology of such a man. Here are people who have left their own country, who glory in the freedom they find here, who intend to live and die in Canada, who expect to bring up their children to be good Canadian citizens, who to-day in Saskatchewan are enlist. ing for the defence of their country to a greater extent than might be expected from the portion of the population they represent.
In fact, of the first two young men from my constituency to give their lives in this war in the service of their country, in the sinking of the Fraser, one was of Ukrainian origin. Then, in almost the same issue of the newspaper that announced his death, we had the statement referring to these people of Ukrainian origin as not being "white". That Ukrainian mother laid her most precious possession upon the altar of freedom; then, after making that sacrifice she had to hear that statement made by a fellow-Canadian of British origin. It [Mr. Hlynka.)
was cruel. So with all my heart I support what the hon. member for Vegreville has said to-night; that sort of thing should have no place in Canadian public life.
As I have said, I have no doubt that this gentleman, Mr. Parker, meant well. He served his countiy in the last war. To him and to all other Canadians of English and French origin who want to serve their country, as I know every returned soldier does, I say that he Should consider whether he is really serving his country in giving utterance to such ideas. In the constituency of Rosthem, as I have said before, there is a large number of people of the Mennonite faith. They are partly of Swiss and German origin, but predominantly of Dutch extraction. There is a tendency on the part of a few returned soldiers to suggest that these people should be barred from the normal life of this country.
When people were being named to look after the national registration, a protest was made to Ottawa that too many Mennonites were being made registrars at a place called Aberdeen, where the people are entirely of that persuasion. I had the matter looked into, and this is what I found. I found that in that whole Mennonite district where the recommendations were made by Mennonite people they respected the claims of returned soldiers. Wherever there was a returned soldier in the district able or willing to do the work, he got the job. But there was one district in which there was no returned soldier who could be procured to get the work, and so a fine Mennonite citizen was named to do the work there. He was the only Mennonite in the whole district named to act as a registrar; his oldest son is serving in the Canadian active service force. I say: Who are these patriots who think they best serve their country by pointing the finger at a man who is appointed to take charge of this work, a man whose eldest son is in the fighting services? He was the only Mennonite in that district actually named to act as a registrar, and yet one or two thought they were doing right by attacking me because I believed that all people, regardless of racial origin, should be treated on the same basis.
I took the attitude that a mistake was made at the time of the last war when Canada said to these people that they should not have the vote, and thereby were not treated as citizens. As a result they naturally did not feel under the same obligation to serve their country. The attitude I have taken at this time is that every Canadian, every man, no matter what his racial origin may be, shall be regarded as a good Canadian and shall be expected to make his contribution to the country's great cause.

The Address-Mr. Tucker
The question respecting Mennonites serving in the armed forces of their country is one with which I probably should deal at this time. As we know, it is against their religion to bear arms. I do not believe there is one member in the house who would say that we should interfere with people's religion. In the regulations it has been stipulated that the training of Mennonites and Doukhobors shall be indefinitely postponed. But there was no suggestion that they should be deprived of the vote; they were to be treated as full-fledged citizens.
What do we find to-day? We find that within the last ten days representatives of the Mennonites of western Canada, the Mennonites of Ontario, the Quakers in Canada and the Tunkers came to Ottawa to interview the ministry of national war services to say to that department that while they do not believe in bearing arms, they are prepared to go into any branch of the service of their country where they could help to save life, where they could help the wounded, and for other services of that kind. It did not matter to them whether it was dangerous work or otherwise. All they ask is that they shall not be asked to bear arms; and -they have asked, too, that their operations should be under civilian auspices. So long, however, as they serve humanity, they do not care whether their work be dangerous or otherwise.
They appreciate the rights of citizenship in Canada. They wanted to show their appreciation, and they were not trying to get out of doing their full share. All this was done after the government had exempted them from military service. The people represented by this delegation do not want to be exempted from doing their share. Here we have a group of non-English-speaking and non-Frenchspeaking origin, a group which wishes to act as a group of good citizens. They are ready to serve their country, even to the extent of risking their lives. Is it not wise statesmanship, and good business, if nothing else, to let those people know and feel that they are accepted as full-fledged citizens?
I have in mind, for example, those people in western Canada who are of German origin. I claim-I am absolutely satisfied-that the overwhelming majority of those people are absolutely loyal to Canada and the British empire. But if people are going to suggest continually that they should be deprived of their rights, that they should be discriminated against and treated as if they are something less than citizens, what will the effect be?
Hitler teaches to the German people that they never will be accepted as full-fledged citizens in any country not under the German reich, and that the only way whereby in
America or elsewhere they may be treated as full-fledged citizens is by their backing of his government, so that Germany may rule every country. He points out that it is only by that method that they may become full-fledged citizens. Well, if by mistreatment and discrimination we bring about a condition whereby, even if they have lived in this country for one, two or three generations, the fact that they happen to have German names will preclude them from obtaining full citizenship, I suggest that we are playing right into the hands of Hitler, and substantiating his teachings and propaganda. So I say to my returned soldier friends and colleagues. Realize that if you attack a people who want to be loyal, a people who are loyal, just because they have German-sounding names or names of non-French or non-English origin, you are tending to make an enemy of those who want desperately to be friends. And today in this crisis of the world we need every friend we can get. You are not strengthening our cause by trying to treat as enemies those who want to be friends and loyal citizens.
These observations bring up another point with which I believe I should deal at this time. I am afraid I shall not be able to touch on all the matters with which I had intended to deal, but I shall proceed to discuss this one because it is along similar lines. It has to do with our fellow Canadians, our French-speaking Canadians. I have noticed a tendency on the part of many English-speaking Canadians to admit only grudgingly outside of Quebec the rights of French-speaking Canadians.
By the pact of confederation it was laid down that there should be two official languages in Canada-not only in Quebec, but throughout the country. This is a bilingual country, and I am satisfied that we will not get real unity if we, after making a deal, as we did at the time of confederation, try to whittle it down and to back out of it. Sometimes I have marvelled at the toleration and the willingness of French-speaking Canadians to forgive and forget the continual attempt on the part of some English-speaking Canadians to whittle down the rights the former obtained under the pact of confederation. I suggest it is of the very genius of the British people that, having first of all made a deal, they should live up to it one hundred per cent, and that above all they tolerate and respect the wishes and just rights of minorities-especially when those minorities, through fair days and foul, have shown themselves to be loyal, to their hearts' cores.
Why is Canada British to-day? That is a question which has been asked on the floor of this chamber. When the Marquis de Lafayette came over to assist in the fight for independence of the United States, and sent
The Address-Mr. Tucker

his delegate to see the French-Canadians who only recently had passed under British rule, he was told that they were well content to remain under British rule, and had no desire whatever to join the revolting colonies to the south. Had they been disloyal at that time and had they regarded lightly their allegiance to their sovereign, they had their chance then to show their lack of allegiance; but they did not take it.
Again in 1812 had they gone against the British crown, this country would have been lost to the British empire. We then come to the revolution of 1837. That was a fight for responsible government, and there was no more desire in lower Canada to get away from the British crown than there was in upper Canada. Then we come down to the days of the great war, when, in spite of provocation French Canada stood' behind the war effort of this country, and sent some of her best sons to give their blood for Canada on the soil of France; and there they lie to-day.
In this war there has been unity such as has gladdened the heart of every true Canadian. Bearing all that in mind, let us show these fellow citizens of ours who speak a Canadian language just as we do, that we do not want to take away from them some of their rights, that we respect them fully and that we are prepared to go half way to meet them in carrying out fairly the pact of confederation.
In this connection I should like to deal for a moment with the question of radio broadcasting. When a suggestion is made, many of us are apt to say that we agree with it, but when it comes down to actually agreeing to carry out the proposal, there is often a tendency to hang back. It is with that tendency that I wish to deal to-night. One of the things I should like to see accomplished is the setting up in Canada of one of the most powerful shortwave radio broadcasting stations in the world. Over one of the wave-lengths controlled by that station I should like to see broadcast the best programmes from Quebec so that they could be heard by our French-speaking fellow citizens in western Canada. They are entitled to hear programmes in their own language. These programmes would also be heard in occupied and unoccupied France.
Not long ago I had the privilege of listening to a speech delivered over the radio by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I was thrilled and proud to think that he was a fellow citizen of mine. But that speech was broadcast only once. We all know the dangers faced by the citizens of France when they try to listen to foreign broadcasts. Naturally the nazis knew that this speech was being broadcast, and it would have been particularly

dangerous for any French citizen to have listened to it. If we had had a powerful shortwave station, this speech could have been broadcast nine or ten times in order to be sure that every Frenchman on the continent of Europe could have an opportunity to hear this call to fight for freedom. What would be spent on such a shortwave station would be of far more value than ten times the amount spent upon arms.
Let us face the fact that Hitler has gained his victories largely by the use of propaganda. We should be able to send appeals from the French-Canadians on north American soil to Frenchmen in Europe. No one will ever know but what the appeal of the Minister of Justice to Marshal Petain may have had something to do with the breaking down of the scheme to get France under the control of Germany. If that is so, then that speech was worth almost a whole army corps. I ask the government to consider this, to realize the power we would have of heartening the French people, of calling on them to be of good cheer, of telling them that we know that France will yet rise again in all the glory of freedom, that it is not her destiny to languish forever under the nazi heel.
There was another speech delivered not long ago which I wish every Frenchman could have heard. This was delivered by that great Canadian statesman, the premier of Quebec. How his words would have thrilled the French people and heartened them against the dark days yet to come! He said:
To France, French-Canadians would say: " Mother, thou art not dead. You live in our blood and in our minds. And you live in the minds of those who understand you. We all know that the hordes of Hitler and Mussolini have not been able to tear out your soul and that you but await our victory, the victory of the British nations and their allies, to again take your place amongst the nations who are bearers of light."
Would it not have been a fine thing to have broadcast that speech several times each day for two or three days so that every Frenchman in France might have had an opportunity of hearing it and knowing that here in Canada were people who intended to stand by France until once more she was free?
Such a radio station would help our foreign exchange position. It is intended to send people to South America in order to encourage the people of those countries to come to Canada for a visit-to trade with Canada. For every man that such delegates will meet, a shortwave station would reach thousands. Over such a station it could be broadcast that although we are at war there are no difficulties about travelling in this country. In the past many of these people have spent their money upon travel in Europe, but we

The Address-Air. Tucker
should endeavour to encourage them to come to see Canada. We should be able to build up a tremendous tourist trade, and I have no doubt that the money made from such a trade would pay for the shortwave broadcasting station in one year.
There is the question of trade with the United States and the tourist traffic from that country. We know that last year Germany tried to destroy our tourist trade. W'e fought against this as best we could, but we should have been telling the people of the United States over a shortwave station all about the attempts that were being made to sabotage our war effort by destroying our tourist trade. I see my time is passing and I have used nearly all my allotment in dealing with this one subject. I think, however, its importance justifies my doing so.
For a moment I should like to refer to station CBK, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation transmitter for western Canada. This station broadcasts a total of 115 hours a week. The length of the bilingual programmes is three and one-sixth hours, while the French part of the bilingual programmes occupy only one-third of an hour, or twenty minutes. The time spent in broadcasting French programmes for the whole week is only three hours, out of the 115 hours, or 2-6 per cent. If there are English-speaking people who do not want to listen to more French than this, if more were put over, they can tune in on some other station like CKCK. They should not contend that there should not be more French broadcasts over CBK, because they do not have to listen if they do not want to. This would give our Frenchspeaking fellow citizens a chance to hear a little bit more, a fairer amount of broadcasting in their own language.
Here is something which is most important. The time spent daily in broadcasting news in English over CBK is 158 minutes, whereas the time spent in broadcasting the news in French is only five minutes. The English news is broadcast seven days in the week while the French news is broadcast only five days in the week. An increased use of the French language over this station should be made to meet the wish of our French-speaking fellow citizens. I think the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be asked to look into the situation. I do not think they are treating our French-speaking citizens in western Canada quite fairly when they give them only that proportion of the total time on CBK.
There is another matter. While a shortwave broadcasting station would be a good thing, there are in western Canada a good many people who cannot afford a radio 14873-25
of any kind whatsoever, and even less a shortwave receiving set. This means that if you are going to reach many of our people you have to put the programme over from the ordinary broadcasting station. I think the work that has been done in enlightening our English-speaking people on matters connected with the war and how we are carrying out our part in the war has been exceptionally good. But there are many people in western Canada who do not understand English very well. Yet they are good citizens, anxious to help in the war. They have been subjected, the people, for example, of German-speaking origin, to consistent nazi propaganda before the war.
The Deutsches Zeitung fuer Kanada, subsidized directly from Germany, was sent out from Winnipeg to mailing lists all over western Canada, and our people there, not being very well off and not being able to afford very much in the way of reading material, were subjected to this lying propaganda week after week, and yet they did not succumb to it. Here we are putting over to the English speaking people of the west the story of our war effort and the justice of our cause, but there seems to be the feeling in the minds of some of those in charge of the broadcasting corporation that if you put over a broadcast in German, somehow it is going to do some harm. Because of that, great chances to enlighten some of our people have been missed.
We had German refugees from Czechoslovakia, German refugees from Austria and from Germany itself who should have been put on the radio and permitted to tell their story in German to people of German origin in western Canada-the whole story of nazi oppression in Europe in all its horror. Would that not have been worth while? Would that not have been reaching people that it is important to reach? They are fellow-citizens and it is important that they should see the justice of the cause in which we are engaged. I submit that while we should, of course, carry on our programme of reaching our English-speaking citizens, we should take some steps to do a measure of justice to our French-speaking citizens, and then for the sake of promoting unity in Canada we should put over broadcasts in other than French or English to explain to those who are not French- or Englishspeaking citizens of Canada what is happening over in Europe.
There are people in the town of Rosthern who have not been very long in this country and who do not understand English very well. The only way in which they can

The Address-Mr. Tucker

hear German over the radio is if they manage to tune in on a German programme from London or Berlin. I venture to say that there are probably ten times as many people of German-speaking origin in Canada as there are in England, yet in England they do not think it is going to harm the British empire to put over the air speeches in German from the British broadcasting headquarters. How much more important for the unity of Canada that we should realize that it would be in the interests of Canadian unity to put over from time to time some speeches from good Canadians in German, Polish, Ukrainian and so on!
There is one matter which perhaps I did not make plain and which I should like to make very plain at this time with respect to what I have said about people like Mr. Parker and other returned soldiers. I am always ready to realize that they, like all of us at times since the war started, have been so worried about the very existence of our country and about the existence of the British empire in this time of peril, that, not understanding the true loyalty of our people who are not of English or French origin, they have been inclined to suspect them. I know that these gentlemen are acting with the best of intentions, and that is one of the reasons why I have spoken as I have to-night, to beg and beseech them not to play into the hands of Hitler, but to recognize these people as good Canadian citizens and to hold out the hand of friendship to them rather than throw suspicion on them.
There were many subjects with which I wished to deal to-night, but perhaps in this time of stress the question of Canadian unity is more important than almost any other. There is, however, one further matter with which being a pseudo-financial expert, I shall take a minute or two to deal.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) dealt with two things in particular, to which I should like to refer. I should like to read what he said:
I believe that the tax programme of the government has been and will continue to be such that some additional financing of a shortterm character, accompanied by some increase in total bank deposits, will not under the circumstances have inflationary results, and will, I believe, avoid undue stringency in the monetary field at a time when the working capital requirements of industry are increasing because of expanding business activity due to war orders.
That bears out what I and what many other Canadians have been contending for ever since the war started, that there should not be too stringent taxation or too stringent

borrowing until we get our economic machinery running at full blast, and then it can more easily carry the burden of taxation necessary to finance the war. I think it was for this reason also that the last war loan did not go over as well as it might have done. It was because we did not permit our whole economic machine to expand to full capacity before we began to crack down on it. It is not going to increase our strength as a nation to close up, for example, our automobile industry if we are not prepared to put all those people at work making munitions of war; in fact it is going to hurt our economic machine by throwing thousands out of work. The matter must be so handled that we build up our economic activity to its full height and then gradually, as needed, turn over our industrial machine to the task of making munitions of war.
I am glad to see that it is proposed to embark on a policy of some credit inflation in order to enable this nation better to bear the war burden.
There is another point in the address of the Minister of Finance with which I wish to deal briefly. I shall read what the Minister of Finance said about it because it is a matter of grave importance. He said:
In deciding to undertake some additional short-term financing, the government also had in mind the fact that the major portion of the new money which will have to be borrowed prior to next summer will be required for the activities of the foreign exchange control board. It has been decided that the board will finance the repatriation programme to a greater extent than it has in the past, and additional funds will be necessary for this purpose. You will recall that the process of repatriation involves the temporary accumulation of sterling balances by the foreign exchange control board, and these balances are later used to acquire Canadian securities held in the United Kingdom.
As I understand what is proposed there and what is actually happening to-day, it is that through the repatriation of Canadian securities money in the form of purchasing power in Canadian dollars is made available to Great Britain to purchase goods in Canada. Great Britain has caused the people of that country to turn over to the British government the Canadian securities they hold in order that Great Britain can turn round and sell these Canadian securities in Canada and with the proceeds pay in Canadian dollars for what she purchases in Canada.
So far as I understand it, the only purchases so far that we permit Britain to make in Canada are those which she is financially able to make through the exchange available to her by virtue of the goods she has shipped to Canada and the securities which have been repatriated in the manner I have

The Address-Mr. Tucker
described. If that is all that has been done, have we treated Great Britain in any different way from the way in which she has been treated by the United States, or the Argentine, or any other foreign country? While she has had the proceeds of her exports with which to buy in Canada, we have sold to her. While she has had the securities with which to procure Canadian dollars, we have sold to her.
We are now told by the Minister of Finance that, pending the disposal of her Canadian securities in Canada, the operation will be financed for the time being through this short-term credit programme. I am glad of that, that Great Britain is not going to be prevented by a lack of Canadian dollars from buying in Canada. But apparently all we are doing is lending, temporarily financing; we are not doing any more. That is quite a bit short, Mr. Speaker, of what was done by Great Britain for France before France's downfall. Great Britain put at the disposal of France all the pounds sterling that she needed to make any purchases which she required in the British isles. France did the same in francs in France with Great Britain, and they agreed that there would be a settlement after the war. This meant that money did not stand in the way of Britain helping France or France helping Britain. And I ask this, that consideration be given by our government to some similar policy. We must not be told that the limit of our assistance to Great Britain is what Great Britain is able to buy with her goods and her securities. Surely we are not going to stop at any such limited degree of assistance.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the British government, having taken over the securities, sends them here. They will have to be disposed of in Canada to realize Canadian dollars to the credit of the British government in order that they can make purchases in Canada. As a member of the banking and commerce committee I should like to know how these Canadian securities are being disposed of, or to be disposed of. In this time of crisis, are the needs of the British government such that they are being forced to sacrifice Canadian securities because they need the money? There is only a small group of Canadian financiers who have the money necessary to buy those securities. To what extent are we protecting or do we intend to protect the British investor or the British government by seeing to it that a small group of Canadian investors are not making a big profit at the expense of Great Britain?
I am not saying that this is or is not the case. But I do say this, that all too little use is being made of the private members of this H873-25i
parliament. When I consider the speeches made in this house, led off by the hon. member who moved the address in reply (Mr. Claxton), seconded by my young friend, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras); when I reflect upon the high-class speeches which they made on that occasion, their clearness of mind and their all-round ability; when I observe, as I get to know hon. members of the various parties, the ability represented in this chamber and their competence to serve their country in this time of crisis, I ask myself, is that ability being harnessed? We feel that what is happening is this. Experts-so called-are being called in to advise the members of the government. Sometimes they are experts and sometimes they are not. In that connection we have heard the definition of an expert as a man who does not know very much, far away from home. A policy having been decided upon, with the assistance of those experts, it is brought down to this house, and hon. members-well, I will not say what they have to do.

speechtext: Swallow it.

speechtext:
I submit that parliament
would be discharging its functions if, for example, in connection with this question of finance, the banking and commerce committee were asked to sit and the report of the Bank of Canada referred to it for examination, with all other matters having to do with the financing of this country's war effort and the financing of assistance to Great Britain -all these things laid before- that committee, with the right to call experts and to decide, in the light of the evidence given by those experts and the views of hon. members representing all parties in the house, as to the best way that the financial resources of this country could be harnessed. That, Mr. Speaker, would be true functioning of democratic government. The members of parliament would be given a chance to judge and advise the government as to whether those experts were really expert or whether they were, in- their opinion, fakes. I should like to see the banking and commerce committee given a chance to examine as to what is being done with the securities which are being taken from the British people in their hour of need and sold here in Canada. Does any single hon. member on the floor of this house know how these securities are being disposed of? Does any hon. member know whether the British investor and the British government are getting a completely square deal? We hope so, but do not know. Is my time up?

I suggest that the Bank
of Canada should make available all the Canadian money needed to pay a decent price for the securities in which the people of Great Britain have invested in. the past; that these securities, instead of being thrown on the market-I suppose they try to get the best price possible for them, but this is not a good time to dispose of securities of that kind-should be dealt with in this way. A credit should be granted by the Bank of Canada to the British government, representing a fair price for those securities, which would become the property of the bank. Somebody may say, "If you pay out Canadian dollars from the Bank of Canada in the sums necessary to buy those securities, you are going to expand the basis of your credit structure to that extent and inflation will follow." My answer to that is that I am satisfied, and I feel it cannot be contradicted-I should like to get the experts in front of the banking and commerce committee and see if they can controvert it-that as you put out more and more Canadian money to re-vest those securities in the people of Canada, to whom they should belong, at the end of the war, you could gradually increase your reserve requirements, if you saw that it was resulting in inflation.
To-day by law the banks are required to have on hand SI in Bank of Canada notes or Bank of Canada deposits for every $20 they owe their depositors. As a matter of practice the Bank of Canada require them to have on hand $1 for every $10 they owe their depositors; they ask them to have twice as much on hand as the law requires. There is nothing wrong with that. But if the Bank of Canada can require them to have on hand twice as much as the law requires, what is to prevent the Bank of Canada, if they saw any sign of inflation, saying to the banks: We require you to have on hand not $1 for every $10 but $1.10, or $1.15, or even $2 or more, for every $10.
In other words, they can absolutely control the situation. They can gradually increase the cash base for the commercial banking system of this country. They have a tremendous leeway. Until we get to one hundred per cent credit base, the Bank of Canada can put out well over a billion dollars. If that were done, and carefully watched by the Bank of Canada, as it could be watched, at the end of this war, instead of private investors in this country buying up Canadian securities

that were once the property of Britishers who had faith in the future of this dominion and invested in it, and perhaps getting those securities for less than they are worth, the Bank of Canada, representing the people of Canada, would own about a billion dollars' worth of Canadian securities on which it would earn interest and for which Britain had been paid a fair price.
Perhaps some hon. members may say that is impossible. When a great refunding transaction like that is going on, if we are to do our duty by the Canadian people we as members of parliament have a right to ask our financiers what is going on and ask them why this cannot be done. So in all earnestness I ask that the banking and commerce committee be set up to examine into the financial transactions that are taking place in this country. WTio has more right to look into those transactions than the members of that committee, representing the common people of Canada? AVe still have selfgovernment in Canada, thank God. We are not ruled by the financiers, we are not ruled by the manufacturers.
In any particular sphere this house is entitled to full information through its committees. So I suggest to t'he government that the banking and commerce committee be called together as soon as this house reconvenes, with full power to examine into that field of finance and the financial transactions that are taking place. Representing as it does the people of all parts of Canada, labouring people, farmers and so on, representing all parties in the country, if it was able in times past to arrive at good solutions, in this day of crisis, when every member of this parliament is anxious to do all he can for his country, it will get together in a non-partisan spirit and among the fifty members of that committee there may be at least one who will have an idea that is worth putting up to Mr. Towers and his expert advisers. At any rate it will give a chance to everyone on that committee to make suggestions as to the conduct of the financial policy of Canada. It is the right of this House of Commons to ask for that, and I ask for it to-night.
There are other matters I wanted to deal with, but I realize that my time is up. Before concluding, however, I should also like to ask that a committee be set up to examine the wheat problem. That problem should be referred to the agriculture committee which can have experts brought before it to make their suggestions and have them examined by hon. members from all sections of the house, and the committee can then report its conclusions to the government.

The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough)
Let me say that I would not want anyone to think that I am dissatisfied in any way with the successful manner in which the government have organized this country for its war effort. I am proud of the way in which our ministers of national defence, all three of them, have directed our war effort. I glory in the way in which our Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has organized the arming of our nation for war. But there again I make a suggestion. Various people have been put in important positions in which they control the whole industrial and economic life of this dominion. There should be a committee of this House of Commons to look into what is being done in that sphere and satisfy itself that it is being done properly. In other words, I ask that the members of this House of Commons be permitted to go to work to help the government win this war. We were elected to help run this country, not someone called in from Vancouver and someone else from Halifax. Some of them, I understand, could not get elected to this house no matter how they tried. They are all right-good men have been chosen-in their place as advisers, but this house has the right to see if they are as expert as they are supposed to be and to advise the government as to their work.
There are many other members of the government of whom I could say how much I think of their work, but I shall conclude with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself. I believe that his work in the realm of external affairs of this country will go down in history as the finest ever done by any prime minister. He has made an enormous contribution to the safety and security of British commonwealth of nations. To win this war it was all-important that we should have the help of the United States of America. In acting as interpreter and bridge between the United States of America and Great Britain, and helping to bring them together, our Prime Minister has done a work that this generation probably is not able to appreciate; but when history comes to appraise it, the Prime Minister will take a very high place and be greatly deserving of his country's undying gratitude.
The Ogdensburg agreement that he negotiated with the President of the United States was the culmination of a sustained effort. I happen to have seven children; I am proud of them; when I heard that the Prime Minister had made an agreement with the president of the great republic to the south that if Canada were attacked we could rely on the resources of the United States to help us in driving back the invader and protecting our homes, when I went to bed that night I
thanked God that that agreement had been brought into existence by the Prime Minister and the President, because I felt that my children were safer in our home than they otherwise would have been.
As I listened at this session to the declaration of the Prime Minister as to our war aims and the way in which Canada intends to meet the crisis, I say in all humility I thought it was the finest declaration of war aims and the noblest statement of the spirit in which our people should go forth to meet this present challenge to us and to civilization and freedom to which I had yet listened.

Mr. Speaker, this debate has brought out many constructive ideas, and I sincerely hope the government will act upon them. The hon. member who just took his seat (Mr. Tucker) made one or two very good suggestions. I think he rather spoiled his speech with his last few remarks, but the first part was excellent. As a member of the banking and commerce committee I agree that this committee should take up the question of the sale of securities when the house meets again after the recess.
The hon. gentleman also mentioned radio broadcasting. I have tried to obtain a copy of a speech which was made in the British House of Commons with regard to broadcasting. I have not been able to secure that speech, but I know its contents. It was stated that Hitler first used the radio to lower the morale of the people of the countries he wanted to invade. At the present time I understand that he has under his control over 170 Shortwave stations, including those of Norway, Sweden and Denmark, some of which broadcast in English twenty-four hours a day in an endeavour to break down the morale of the English people, but that will not be broken. Speaking of radio, I wonder whether something could not be done to prevent a certain German commentator from broadcasting to this country. Even some of our Canadian stations are carrying these broadcasts, and we do not know but what in those broadcasts there may be hidden code messages to his fifth columnists in this country or in the United States, because every word this'man says is first checked by the greatest double-crosser of all times, Hitler himself.
I have some questions which I should like to ask the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner), who lam sorry is not in the house at the moment. First, I should like to ask if any complaints have been received with regard to employers not taking back into their employ men who had to go to training camps; and, if so, what action has been taken.

Then I should like to protest to this government because of the manner in which they have drawn up the rules and regulations concerning the trainees. In England there was an act passed concerning conscription, and that matter was fully debated in the house. 3 honestly believe that the question of training our men should be debated here. As the previous speaker said, we do get some good ideas here in the house. Give the members a chance to discuss these matters, instead of putting them through by order in council. In the United States the whole procedure in regard to training camps is laid down in their act.
I should also like to ask the minister whether, in the event of the training period being extended to four months, the men called up in the first three classes are liable to be called up again. Finally, what action will be taken with regard to those men, something like 1,500, who were called up for training and given transportation but who did not show up?
I should also like to know whether any complaints have been received by the Department of National War Services concerning the seizure of chattels belonging to men who have been called up for training, I mean chattels purchased under lien or conditional sale agreements. I am informed that in Chatham a seizure was made by a finance company. That matter is covered in the United States regulations; a short-term moratorium is declared, so that the soldier undergoing training is not liable for suit, debt, mortgage foreclosure, repossession proceedings and so on. I realize that the United States man is called up for twelve months and that at present the Canadian boy is called up for only one month, but I really believe something should be done at once with regard to this matter.
Then I should like to refer to the public information bureau. Every week we receive reams of mimeographed sheets, though I knowr for a fact that not half this material is ever read. As a matter of fact I saw one newspaper man throw one of these envelopes into the waste-paper basket without even opening it. He said, " Why read that stuff? I had that information a week ago." I rather think some of this material is of a political nature, because on the first page of one article I see the words "free speech." We do not even have free speech in this house.

Yes; that means we have not free speech. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said he felt the awful seriousness of the war. If that is so, I wonder why he has not tried to keep up the morale of the soldiers who are training in this country, many of them without proper equipment, by giving free transportation on the railways. In any event they should be given free transportation on their own railway. They have been paying for that railway ever since they were knee high to a grasshopper; every time they bought a stick of candy they helped pay for it, and even though they are in training they are helping to pay for it to-day. There is no reason under the sun why those men should not have free transportation. Of course such transportation would have to be within limits; it might be only on authorized passes and perhaps only three or four times a year, but they should have it. I do not think one hon. member would be opposed to that, or is there one who might be? I do not think so. I think all hon. members are for the soldier, and I am glad they are.
I have before me clippings from papers and magazines concerning free transportation. I shall not read them all, because I know that most hon. members have received some of them. There is one, however, I should like to read, and it is as follows:
In response to an appeal that soldiers in active service ranks be given free transportation on railways the Hon. J. L. Ralston, Defence Minister, has replied that this is without precedent. Even Mr. Ralston must know that this is a most feeble excuse for refusing the enlisted men, whose pay does not permit such luxuries as travel on the people's railway.
In this statement he is not entirely correct, for in Britain leave for soldiers is accompanied by free transportation to their destination. If precedent must be followed, here is precedent.
We do not recall any precedent for Lieutenant Robert Davies and his engineering squad which removes time bombs at the danger of being blown to bits at any moment. Nor is there an established precedent for a mad rush to air raid shelters when enemy planes come overhead with their cargoes of death.
I have here an advertisement paid for by the Liberal government in Ontario, and at the bottom I find these words:
Special request to motorists.^ When driving along highways these increasingly cold days and nights, give our soldier boys a ride.
Red tape can be cut. All that is necessary is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) give the word. The soldiers throughout the country are waiting for that word,

The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough)
and I sincerely hope that they get it before Christmas. I mentioned this matter in the house on June 28 and again on July 22. This is November 25; I wonder how much longer the men will have to wait.
Then, I believe we should do something in regard to insurance for the enlisted men. Perhaps we should have a committee of the whole house, or a select committee which would have the duty of dealing with the matter. Possibly the committee on banking and commerce could do it. One suggestion put forth is that five per cent be taken out of dependents' allowances and assigned pay, then the government put in the same amount, and that an insurance company or a group of insurance companies be given the duty of handling the insurance. After Great Britain has won the war and the soldiers return, they would have nest-eggs with which to begin life again. They would have something in the bank with which to start up business.
I am pleased to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has accepted a suggestion from this part of the house-in fact, he has accepted a number of them. I refer to the one whereby the income tax may be paid on the instalment plan. This suggestion was made during the last session, and I know it will be a great help to the taxpayer. In fact at the present time throughout Canada people are opening savings deposit accounts so that they may be in a position to pay their income taxes when due.
The Minister of Finance was good enough to accept that suggestion. I sincerely hope he will accept others which may be passed on to him not only at this session but during the recess. One suggestion I would make at this time is that tax-free bonds be issued bearing an interest rate of not more than one and a quarter per cent. In that way I believe we would collect large sums of money.
In moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) suggested that the estimates to improve the tourist trade should be increased from 8500,000 to $1,000,000 this year. I agree with him, but would suggest that we set up a committee to deal with the matter, and that the committee have the services of the director of tourist traffic, Mr. D. Leo Dolan, a most capable man, and one who will see that every dollar spent will bring back $100 or $150 in United States funds.
I find that $311,695 was spent last year by the bureau. The sum is now raised to a million dollars, and the increase may seem rather heavy. We must remember, however,
that we need United States dollars, and we know that the people in that country want to visit Canada. We can get United States dollars and we can get United States tourists; all we have to do is go after them. They want to be friendly with us, and we want to be friendly with them. Yes, we want to be friendly with them even in a business way.
Our business with other nations should be carried on in a businesslike manner. Especially is that true of the Department of Agriculture. At the head of that department, however, we have one who is not a business man. Therefore our transactions with other countries have been to their benefit, and not to that of Canada. In fact the trade agreements made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) have set the farmer back, instead of sending him forward. In fact the plight of the farmer and the price he receives for his products remind me of a verse which was handed to me on the occasion of my starting in business about thirty years ago. The two lines of the verse are as follows:
Count that day lost whose low descending sun See prices shot to flinders and business done for fun.
The farmer in Canada has long passed the point where he sees the funny side of it. He wants to know where he goes from here. I am asking the Minister of Agriculture what the farmer is to do; I doubt if the minister knows.
The following newspaper clipping I should like to place on Hansard:
Seattle, Nov. 3.-A telegram received here from Paul H. Appleby, United States undersecretary of agriculture, advised apple growers in the Wenatchee region of Washington state that the department of agriculture has sent two representatives to Ottawa to consult on steps to safeguard any injury to the U.S. market for domestic fruit.
I sincerely hope the deputation was received in a friendly manner, that no concessions were given away and that Canada got just as much as she gave.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) has said that Canada spent $24,000,000 in the United States on foreign fruits and vegetables. We would not spend that much if our trade agreement had been better drawn. I have described the Ontario farmer as the forgotten man, and I believe I am right. He has been forgotten ever since this government took office. But the Department of Agriculture has not been forgotten, so far as estimates are concerned. In 1935 estimates for that department stood at $7,121210.24, and in that sum was included $500,000 for the operation of the Natural Products Marketing Act. This year they have been cut down from the

816,000,000 of last year to 813,254,323.09. But this year the salaries alone of that department amount to almost $7,000,000. That is not helping the farmer of Ontario, of the west or of the east one bit. The farmer has not a chance. The Minister of Agriculture has said that this government is doing more for the farmers of Canada than any other government ever did. I quite agree with him. This government is doing more for the farmer, more to put him in the hole, more to make him mortgage his farm, more to put him in the red. The farmer to-day merely exists; he does not live. One farmer said that he had a full pocket-book. In that pocket-book he had a copy of his mortgage and the stubs of notes that he owed at the bank, but no money.
Last session one hon. member said that the west did all the talking; apparently the squeaky wheel got the most grease and he thought he would rise in his place and talk to see if he could not get a little grease. Personally I feel that the west and the east get the grease, but Ontario pays for it. As I said before, the Ontario farmer is the forgotten man. His markets have been taken away from 'him and foreign farm products are being dumped on his doorstep. Hothouse businesses have been put out of business because they have been given no protection. The hog growers have got it in the neck, and they are still getting it. In the last month the price of shorts, middlings and bran have jumped as much as $4 a ton. I believe this is due to the miller just handing it right back to the farmer. The farmer raises the wheat, the miller processes it and the farmer pays for it. As I say, the farmer has no chance at all. In most sections of Ontario the potatoes have been quite poor this year because of heavy rains and a cold fall. In the Port Hope-Peterborough section tomatoes were two weeks late in ripening and then heavy frosts killed off sixty per cent of the crop.
An hon. member to my left referred to the distilling of spirits from wheat. The United States has been doing this for a few years and Canada will eventually have to do the same. Every day England is requiring more high-octane spirits for aeroplanes and Canada should be the country that supplies it. We are adding to our air force every day and we do not know when the supply of oil from south and central America will be cut off. We should be considering new means of obtaining motor spirits. It has been said that it would cost fifty cents a gallon to manufacture these spirits, but I understand that the government is paying more than fifty cents a gallon for high-octane gasoline.
[Mr. G. K. Fraser. 1
This year in our district we were unable to obtain a decent cob of table corn because the com borer had got it all. One would have thought that the Minister of Agriculture with the many millions that he has to spend would have tried to check the ravages of this borer, but I did not see any checking in our part of the country. In fact, the situation is such now that the farmers have given up hope. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) has suggested that this house should sit as a committee of the whole to discuss the wheat question. We should discuss the problems of the Ontario farmer at the same time.

An hon. member over here says " disgusted." Yes, the Ontario farmer is disgusted. The Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) made a statement which, as I said before, proves that he is no business man. You, Mr. Speaker, and every hon. member know that the manufacturers and workmen of Canada are ready and willing to produce and will produce if given a chance. I know this statement has been brought up before, but I think it should be again brought to the attention of the minister. He said:
Factory managers who contend they cannot produce to capacity without interfering with the training of men may have to be told by someone that they as factory managers are not good enough for war time.
Suppose the housekeeper of this House of Commons went to the charwomen when they were cleaning up and handed one of them a brush having only half the necessary bristles and asked her to do as good a job as another woman who had a brush with all the bristles; there likely would be a kick. Factory managers have resented that statement of the minister very much. The factories will produce if they are given the necessary man-power. They are crippled by their need of skilled labour. Some years ago this government was warned that labour should be trained. We are short to-day even of unskilled labour. Our manufacturers are losing men all the time to the different arms of the service. They are glad to see them go, but the fact is that many managers, storekeepers and other employers are working eighteen hours a day, and some of them almost twenty-four hours trying to keep things going. I saw one storekeeper delivering goods at six o'clock in the morning because he could not get a messenger. All I say to the Minister of National War Services is that he will have to play ball. The manufacturers and workers are ready to play ball,

The Address-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough)
but they must have a man in the pitching box who knows how to pitch. These manufacturers cannot be bulldozed.
I feel, and I believe everyone in Canada feels that small war contracts should be checked just as closely as the large ones. Hundreds of feet of fire hose were sent to the airfield at Brantford and not one coupling would fit the hydrants. Ninety-eight fire axes were sent to another training camp. I do not know whether that camp was near an Indian reservation because it is possible the person who sent them thought they could be used as tomahawks. But a mistake was made and apparently the shipment was not thoroughly checked. I do not blame the Minister of National War Services for this because this is a matter having to do with the Department of Munitions and Supply. How many more blunders have been made you, Mr. Speaker, do not know and I do not know, but what I say is, check first. The hose and axes could have waited a few days which would have permitted a thorough check-up by an expert to see that everything was all right. If a mistake was made, even if only $3,000 a day, that would amount to over $1,000,000 a year. Money does not grow on trees, as the leader of the social credit party seems to think.
On June 17 of this year I asked, this question in the house:
Has the government stopped the export of iron, steel and scrapiron?
Mr. Howe: We have appointed a steel controller who has complete charge of the import and export of any iron or steel product, and he is now in control of the situation.
I have here a copy of P.C. 2742, dated June 24, 1940, the order in council appointing the steel controller. In other words, he was appointed one week after the minister said he was appointed. I do not think I would go slow in a matter of this kind. If they have to appoint a steel controller, they should jump to it.
I would also suggest to hon. members that they read the debates of the British House of Commons of October 10, 1940, at page 479, with respect to the shipping of oil. I have the volume here.
I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister announce that we are going to have a representative in Brazil and one in the Argentine. I was also pleased to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) say that he was going down to south America and was going to visit both the west and the east coast. I sincerely hope that when we are choosing representatives of Canada for Brazil
and the Argentine extreme care will be taken in picking the right men because the south Americans are a very proud people, and they have a great deal to be proud of. They had universities many years before there was one in any part of Canada or the United States, and one has to be extremely careful with regard to their customs and traditions. I would suggest that we send to south America someone who has been in that country before and knows the customs of the people.
Our director of tourist traffic, Mr. D. Leo Dolan, is at present chairman of the PanAmerican Highway Congress Association, having been appointed in San Francisco two years ago. The Pan-American union I believe would be pleased if Canada would join up with them. The people of central and south America are friendly, and for the benefit of hon. members I would suggest that they all subscribe to the monthly bulletin of the Pan-American union. They can get it in English, Spanish or Portuguese, although I imagine not many in the house speak Portuguese. I know that hon. members who subscribe to the bulletin will be more than repaid.
On the west coast of south America two men could do all the work that would be required because Spanish is spoken in all those countries, but they would have to be men used to flying because that is how they would have to travel from place to place, although they have in south America about three thousand miles of paved road.
Mention has been made in this house on more than one occasion of leadership with regard to women's activities. I understand that the Minister of National War Services has appointed a man to take charge of that work. I think that is all wrong, and the women will very much resent it. An outstanding woman who is known to be a leader should have been selected. In the city of Peterborough the women's war service auxiliary corps is over two hundred strong, and takes drills and lectures once a week. In the same city we have also a women's service committee doing good work.
In closing, I should like to say that we Canadians should have faith that right is might and that right will be victorious. Let us be thankful, all of us who are privileged to live as citizens of a free country where liberty and justice continue in a world tom by suffering. Let us pray that peace, prosperity and friendship among all the peoples of our war-weary earth may soon materialize and live forever. Let us continue to love our country, respeot its democratic institutions and honour its flag. Let us thank God for Canada.
