Mr. Speaker, the thoughts of everyone in this house and in Canada are concerned with our war effort, and also with the efforts that will have to be made at the close of the war to reestablish not only those now engaged in military operations but also those engaged in the manufacture of munitions and the implements of war. It is even difficult in a debate of this kind to interject any other matter because our thoughts are with the British people and the heroic fight they are putting up. Our minds turn to the women and children of the old land who day and night are bravely enduring bombardment. Our minds can hardly visualize those scenes. We in this country are fortunate when we picture what can take place in this machine-age war. Perhaps we do not fully realize how fortunate we are, for we can only dimly picture the destruction that is taking place in the old country.
Our hats go off at this time to Greece for the gallant effort she is making in defending her independence and halting unprovoked aggression of her borders by another country. Her heroic stand is an encouragement not only to us but to other countries that pride themselves on their nationhood, not to allow themselves to be subjected to ruthless aggression by foreign invaders.
Our thoughts go out, too, to our gallant Canadian soldiers who have 'taken their place in the line with such outstanding credit to themselves and to Canada. They have taken their places on the sea, in the air, and on the land, with valour unsurpassed. We must constantly keep before us, as people on the home front, the ever-increasing problem of knowing what we can do towards making their efforts more effective.
We have already heard statements from the various ministers of the crown pertaining to particular phases of Canada's war effort. They have shown a record of achievement and accomplishment which is phenomenal. This country, normally a calm, peaceful nation, has been changed from its ordinary peace-time pursuits into a gigantic war machine, capable of great expansion in the course of a few months. What has been accomplished in this regard stands as a creditable contribution on the part of the Canadian people of well-directed effort to the common cause.
With full recognition and appreciation of what this nation has done and can do towards assisting the mother country in her war effort, I believe many if not all Canadians will agree with me 'that the part this country has played in developing friendly relationships with the great republic of the United States may prove to be one of her most important contributions towards the defence and maintenance of

democracy in the old land and throughout the world. We look at this accomplishment with gratification and pleasure. The credit for bringing about the understanding and goodwill which exists between our country and the United States must go to the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King), who throughout his life has paid particular attention to that one necessary object of human endeavour, namely the creation of good-will among men and between nations.
Much as one would like to discuss further the country's war effort, there are of course other items of interest to discuss. Various hon. members who have taken part in this debate have discussed the war activities of the departments much more intelligently than, I feel, I could do at this time. I propose therefore to discuss one or two other matters. The address in reply to the speech from the throne provides that opportunity; it is a part of our parliamentary procedure designed for that purpose. Its importance, however, in influencing government policy may not be so great to-day as it was in days gone by. I can believe that when we did not have the radio, the daily press, the telephone and telegraph services, the gathering together of 245 members of parliament from all over Canada, bringing to this assembly their different points of view, proved of particular value in expressing to the government of the day the interests of the people throughout the country, and that the government would probably pay heed to such views in developing its policies. Nevertheless, that function of parliament, though possibly somewhat less important at the present time, is fundamentally unchanged. Contributions are made by the various hon. members to the formulation of governmental policy.
I have this feeling, and it is somewhat in line with a suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), that the debate we carry on upon the address in reply to the speech from the throne may be a little too formal. More might be gained by a debate in committee, where each question as it was brought up could be answered and cleared up at once. That is not possible in a debate of this kind. Opportunity is provided, of course, for committee debate when the estimates of the various departments are under consideration. Nevertheless, it seems to me that there is much to be gained through discussions in committee, and particularly, if the course were followed of referring more items to special committees or to standing committees. I do not refer necessarily to military items; I refer as well to items which

The Address-Mr. Weir
are of general interest to the country and to which members of the house could make their contributions. I suggest this for another reason, having regard to departmental activities. It would have the effect, if civil servants were called before those committees, of bringing the civil service more in contact with members of the House of Commons. By this means they would, come more closely in contact with the people of this country, and I believe that that would be all to the good.
Referring again to the speech from the throne, we from western Canada are particularly pleased to note that the government is prepared to proceed with implementing the report of the commission on dominion-provincial relations. This, next to the successful prosecution of Canada's war effort, will be the most important item considered by this parliament. I trust that when the delegates are called together they will approach and consider this report as Canadians, recognizing that the men who made the inquiry and prepared the report were representative citizens, who were not interested in any particular section, but who gave their best efforts towards developing a policy in the interests of Canada as a whole. It would seem only reasonable, therefore, to conclude that their point of view was rational and impartial, having regard to the circumstances of all parts of the country. If the representatives of the provincial governments who are called together to consider this report will consider it in the same manner, we can hopefully look forward to something worth-while being accomplished as a result of these deliberations.
There is an opportunity of making this report the basis of a new pact of confederation. What comes from it will probably be the determining factor in cementing the far-flung sections of Canada into a closer harmony and a greater unity of purpose. The policy of the government in deciding to call together the representatives of the provinces is a proper step to take. Let us hope that these representatives will proceed earnestly and sincerely with their deliberations, and that those features of the report upon which there is agreement will be implemented without undue delay.
I wish now to talk of another matter, of more particular interest to western Canada. Coming as I do from western Canada it is to be expected that I should say a word or two with respect to the wheat situation, including some references to the general agricultural situation as I see it. In so doing, may I say to the farm people of other parts of Canada that we in the west are not unmindful of the circumstances of
not only the farmers but also other primary producers in other parts of the country. We are not unmindful of the situation as it affects the fishermen of the maritime provinces or the tobacco growers of certain sections or the fruit growers in other parts of Canada. These all have their problems; likewise we have a problem in western Canada. The chief difference is that our problem happens to loom a little larger in the general economy of the country.	As
far as the individual is concerned, perhaps the effect on the one is no greater than it is on the other.
I have noticed that in discussions in this house so far regarding the present situation in western Canada the approach to the problem has been much more realistic and more reasonable. There may be some who may feel that we from Manitoba should not be as much concerned in this matter as those in other parts of the west, for the reason that our production is largely diversified. Even with the low price of wheat last year, only one-third of the gross-return from agriculture in the province of Manitoba came from wheat. Nevertheless, to those who are growing wheat the problem is equally as important as it is to farmers in other parts of the country.
Wheat did not carry our province last year. It will not carry it this year at fifty cents a bushel net to the farmer, and at that price it never will.
In what I have to say this evening regarding the marketing of wheat I do not propose to offer a solution. I may offer some suggestions, as others have, in the hope that they may be of assistance to the government in formulating a policy for the future.
There is no doubt that so far as the country's war efforts are concerned at this time, our wheat industry appears to be one of the first casualties. We are facing not only low price but increased production and fewer markets. Nevertheless, in spite of those difficulties confronting us at present, I am not unduly pessimistic over the wheat situation. Like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and also like my friend the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), I think this thing will work itself out. What is essential is a little reason and care in attempting to see that the problem is properly handled.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) in his statement the other day placed on the record a great deal of valuable information which will help to bring about a proper understanding of the wheat situation, particularly with regard to
14873-26*

The Address-Mr. Weir
the manner in which wheat was marketed during the past year. I was particularly pleased-and this is a point I wish to emphasize-that he mentioned that a policy for the coming year could be expected to be announced early in February when this house reassembles. I hope that will be so. There has been criticism of the government because of the delay last year in announcing a wheat policy. There were good reasons for delaying the announcement of policy last year. The same reasons, however, do not exist at this time.
Last year there were many uncertainties to be considered. For example, France and also the low countries were still possible purchasers of Canadian wheat. These countries are now pretty certain not to purchase Canadian wheat. Moreover we did not know by any means the size of the crop we would have or the amount of storage required. These factors are now known, or will be known by the end of this crop year. One thing that is certain from the evidence we have at present is that our storage capacity will be completely filled by the end of the crop year. That being so, it is essential for the government to take into consideration at an early date the matter of providing additional storage to house next year's crop if it is going to be marketed at all.
I want now to say a word regarding compulsory reduction of wheat acreage. Those who think we can materially reduce wheat acreage, I am afraid fail to recognize all that is involved. We can reduce our wheat acreage but, in so doing, we must of necessity turn to something else. It is not as easy as it would appear. Nature plays too great a part. As indication of the uncertainty that existed even last year with respect to the size of the wheat crop, I think it is safe to say that had we experienced another week or ten days of the kind of weather that we had during the last two weeks of July and the first week of August, we might easily have had 150,000,000 bushels less wheat, with practically a failure in coarse grains. .
Let me put it another way. Had we had last year a reduction of five bushels to the acre in yield of wheat, there would have been 135,000,000 bushels less produced, which would have largely done away with our storage problem. Had there been no increase in acreage, we would have had 35,000,000 bushels less wheat. If the yield in Alberta, for example, had been the same as it was a year ago, we would have had 34,000,000 bushels less. Or had Alberta had the same crop as she did last year, we would have had
40,000,000 bushels less. I am not picking out Alberta except to illustrate the point that

we cannot hope to control this matter of production. We are glad that Alberta was fortunate in having a very good crop this year-.
I wish to couple what I have to say with respect to wheat with something in respect of coarse grains. I want to link up in part the live stock industry in this country and indicate the extent to which western Canada is engaged in mixed farming. There are many who think that we should further expand the development of mixed farming in western Canada. I hope that before I close I may at least indicate that we are pretty well on the way as far as mixed farming is concerned.
I should like to go back to point out one or two things that I see in the picture as far as the coarse grain situation is concerned. I do this because of the live stock population we have in Canada and more particularly because of the agreements which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has entered into with the British government to supply that country with bacon, cheese and other dairy products. I know we want to see these agreements carried out. That being so, then we require a high production of feed grains in order to maintain our live stock.
Just by way of illustration I should like to Show the situation at the present time with regard to coarse grains. The estimated production of oats, barley and rye for 1940 is 501,000,000 bushels, while the estimated consumption for the same year is 473,000,000 bushels, leaving a surplus of 28,000,000 bushels. I point out, just to indicate what might happen in this respect-, that a reduction of only two bushels to the acre on the coarse grain acreage of western Canada would give us an actual shortage of 8,000,000 bushels in these grains to carry the live stock population of this country this year. From 1939 to 1940 our hog population increased by 37 per cent. The sows to farrow this fall have increased by 27 per cent compared with last year. Cattle production is up one per cent and sheep production two per cent. To-day hog production stands higher than ever before in Canada; this year the figure is 5,882,000 compared with 4,294,000 last year. Here again I would point out to my eastern friends that this year the hog population of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta is estimated at
2,640,000,	while the hog population of Ontario and Quebec stands at 2,935,000. Therefore it will be seen that as far as hogs are concerned western Canada is pretty well into that business.
Figures with regard to the hog population show that this year Ontario increased hog production by 29 per cent while Manitoba increased hog production by 60 per cent; Saskatchewan, by 68 per cent, and Alberta,

The Address-Mr. Weir
by 38 per cent. These figures again indicate the extent to which we in the west are already engaged in mixed farming, as well as the possibility of expanding that branch of agriculture. I could go on and say a word or two with regard to the feed situation as computed on a unit basis of live stock, compared with the unit basis of feed requirements, but I shall defer that until another time.
I think we should face this cereal production situation in Canada from a practical point of view. It is no longer a western problem only. It is a problem for all Canada, a problem for the municipalities as well as for the provincial governments. We should approach it on that basis. In that connection I think the government might well take more closely into their negotiations the producers and those primarily interested in this problem in formulating future policy, not only for wheat but as well for all other branches of agriculture.
With regard to wheat, I feel the government can now say that it knows the actual situation. It knows that at the beginning of the next crop year the storage facilities of this country will be completely occupied. The farmer knows that the government cannot be expected to continue to take a 500,000,000 bushel wheat crop year after year. Knowing these things, then, I think the government should be prepared fo call to a conference the people actually producing grain along with those concerned with handling wheat, and ask them to assist in formulating a policy which they will be prepared to follow.
Just at this point may I say that I believe the farmers of western Canada are prepared to follow any reasonable lead the government will give them. They are waiting for that lead, and when it is given I believe the response will be remarkable. I suggest, therefore, that in dealing with this matter for next year, and also for future years, the government should take into consideration the advisability of referring this matter to a committee of this house to which those interested could be called. Such a committee might sit even during the recess and before it the representatives of various organizations concerned with agriculture, from eastern as well as western Canada, might appear and advance their suggestions. Following that an attempt could be made to formulate a policy to which all would adhere for the marketing of next year's crop.
A moment ago I mentioned the question of storage. I do not think there is any doubt that the government will have to assist in providing additional storage in order that next year's crop may be marketed. I think in the marketing of last year's crop we have
gained some experience that will be of value to us in formulating a policy for next year. The quota system has worked with reasonable satisfaction, and I think should be continued. Perhaps certain restrictions should be introduced to deal with the man who has a large acreage. The government might at the beginning limit deliveries under the quota to five bushels to the acre for those with up to 300 acres, and then reduce the quota for the man with more than that acreage. I think farm storage should be continued. It seems only reasonable that if the farmers are to be required to store their grain at home and attempt to finance on it, they should be entitled to a storage earning equal to that of the elevator companies.
The question of credit on this farm stored grain is one of the important matters that must be considered. I am hopeful that if the grain cannot be all marketed and paid for, the government will be able to work out some arrangement under which either the banks or the elevator companies will assist in providing loans on grain that may not be delivered. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) suggested the summer fallowing of one-third of the acreage of western Canada and that the government should pay the farmer $5 an acre for the land summer fallowed. The cost of such a policy would be $60,000,000 or $70,000,000. I do not believe that summer fallowing on a large scale such as is suggested, is the solution to this problem. Summer fallowing, as it is done in western Canada, has many hazards and drawbacks. Certainly it does not improve the soil; as a matter of fact it may increase the yield, and it may actually encourage another period of soil drifting, which we have been trying to avoid.
So far as Manitoba is concerned, other methods than that of summer fallowing can be followed. The growing of corn now has become pretty general in the southern part of Manitoba, and can be extended. Other row crops might be introduced.
With regard to the suggestion that bonuses might be paid for summer fallowing in order to cut down wheat production, I would much prefer to see any bonus paid for grass seed, thus assisting the farmers to get a greater portion of this land back into grass.
This leads me to say a word or two with respect to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I hope this year the government will be able to see its way clear to increase the amount of money available for this work. I think this is one branch of agricultural policy that can do a great deal toward stabilizing western agriculture.
I would particularly urge the development of community pastures, and providing adequate

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended
taking part in the debate, but my reason for departing from that well-intentioned purpose is that I wish to refer to a few features of the government's war preparedness to which little reference has been made by hon. members on either side of the house who have spoken.
I wish first to refer to the war-time prices and trade board which was so wisely and so promptly appointed by the government at the very outset of the war. In that connection I would congratulate the government upon its wisdom, vigilance and foresight. This measure has offered a most effective resistance to what I might describe as internal aggression in the form of the profiteer and the hoarder. This is the element which during the last war was permitted to run an unbridled and relentless course across this dominion, a course which not only had an ill effect upon the prosecution of the war but left in its trail a period of depression and deflation from which this country had not fully recovered at the onset of the present war.
I believe that this measure not only expedited and enhanced the war effort of this dominion, but showed wise planning on the part of the government for the aftermath of the war. Some people may argue that any consideration given to the aftermath of this war is premature, but with that argument I cannot agree. While I believe that the thoughts and efforts of this nation should be concentrated upon the successful prosecution of this war, it shows wisdom on the part of this government when they give serious consideration to the day when this downpour of red rain will have ceased, when this tragedy of carnage is ended, when the men who to-day are employed in the manufacture of implements of war and destruction will have reverted to their ordinary pursuits in civil life and when trade and industry shall have toppled from the dizzy and precipitous heights of war time to the more stable economic levels of peace. This forethought
at the very beginning of this war has been beneficial to the producer, to the consumer, to the wage-earner, indeed to every citizen. It has added considerably to that unity of sentiment which is so necessary in a total war effort.
While our people are tolerant of the claims that are made upon them; while they are ready to bear the expenses of this war; while our men are overseas, armed against the forces of the tyrannical aggressors, there is no individual, no corporation, no element in this dominion growing fat on the sacrifices and the needs of this nation. Military contributions alone are not sufficient if we are to resist successfully the onslaughts of the dictators.
I congratulate the government upon their vigilance and activity in dealing with the subversive fifth column. Canada, being rich in resources and so sparsely populated, provides a perfect ground for exploitation by fifth columnists. I exhort the government to continue to exercise this vigilance against this enemy in whatever form it may show its head.
I do not intend to go into the details of our military preparations which have been made so expeditiously and so adequately. I have tried to gather information along this line from the most authentic and authoritative sources, and I am glad to say that the factual recitations of the different ministers correspond absolutely with the information I have gleaned. I do not think anyone in this dominion can say that Canada is not contributing adequately, especially when he reads the pronouncements of the great statesmen of England and of other men who have to deal directly with this war effort, of men who have jurisdiction over the forces that are standing between tyranny and democracy. All these men express not only surprise but admiration, and render plaudits at the expeditious manner in which this contribution has been made. Surely this should be sufficient to make everyone confident that this government and this country are doing their bit, contributing not only the full commitments, but in many instances being far ahead of schedule.
I should like to refer to one other matter which may be regarded as being to some extent localized, or it may savour somewhat of criticism. If it was my intention to criticize, I do not know just where I should direct my criticism. I refer to what I regard as the maldistribution of our military projects. I understand that the selection of military sites is left to our war experts and that such selections are made with due con-
The Address-Mr. McGarry

sideration to the economic and strategic importance of the site chosen. Unfortunately certain sections of the dominion feel that they have been more or less penalized, and such is the case with the constituency which I represent.
The citizenship of my constituency is descended from French and Scotch forbears, with just enough Irish to make the racial mixture sparkle. In my constituency are to be found men who are as loyal as any in this great dominion. We have people just as ardent in furthering our war effort as any others, just as tolerant of the taxation burden. It may be because we are not economically and strategically located, but the fact is that we have had but a small part of the industrial projects having to do with our war contribution. I want to bring this matter to the attention of the responsible departments.
The people of my constituency are usually employed in fishing and farming, but last year the fisheries were a failure. To aggravate that economic condition, two mines, one a gypsum mine employing 100 men and the other a coal mine employing 200 men, were closed down for some reason or another. This left our people in a rather serious economic condition. If it were not for their pride and tolerance, I believe we would have to have in certain sections of my county what could be characterized as a relief measure.
At Port Hawkesbury the town owns a ten-acre field upon which aeroplanes have landed in emergencies. Adjoining that wide-open space are acres and acres of level land. It overlooks the strait of Canso, which should warrant its strategic importance. The town of Hawkesbury is willing to give this field to the government gratis. I feel that this is one proposal which should be brought to the attention of the experts in charge of the selection of sites, and if they should decide that it would not be suitable for a landing field, why not put up a large barracks there to house from 9,000 to 10,000 soldiers? It would make a splendid training ground for the troops, and even if the government did not want to train troops there, it would be a splendid place for the soldiers to play football and run foot races, which would be much better for them than being around the cities in beer parlours and such like. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister concerned and I ask the government of Canada to look into it and see if something cannot be done to allow our good people to participate in at least a fractional way in some of this war work.

As I said before, our people are tolerant, and I think the civilian population of Canada as a whole is tolerant. I believe that they know what the results of war will be. I believe that they regard war as I do and as every sensible man does, that they look upon it as the greatest crucible in the world into which is cast all the organized institutions of civilization and all the established institutions of national politics. They realize that no nation will be the same after this war, that the changes which will take place in the belligerent countries will obtain identically in the neutral countries. They do not know what the end of this war will be. They do not blame Britain or Canada for going into this war. There was nothing else for Britain to do. If she had offered no resistance to the fiendish and infamous programme of the dictatorial tyrants; if she had stood idly by and allowed them to run their fiendish course, the honour of Britain would have been betrayed and the trust of our dominions in her would have been put to shame. If Hitler and his hordes proved triumphant, our day of sorrow would soon follow and we would have nobody to assist us and very few to lament our fate.
So I say that our people to-day are tolerant and. their hearts are in this cause. They are looking upon this conflict not as one of flesh against flesh but as one between two ideologies. On the one hand we have democracy, which accords to our people the prerogatives of freedom of the press, freedom of thought, freedom of action, freedom of assembly and the right to live decently. On the other we have dictatorship, which denies these prerogatives to the people.. The purpose of the dictators is to trample down civilization and to destroy everything that is spiritual in man. That is the crisis we are up against. That is the crisis which the people realize that we are up against, and they are meeting it with the proper attitude. They are looking upon it as the greatest tragedy of carnage that ever obtained in this world., and the very ghost of that tragedy hovers over our own homes. Is it any wonder, then, that we Canadians who have enjoyed the prerogatives of democracy are calling up every reserve of strength and courage, of faith and fervour, in order to combat the tyrannical aggression of these satanic hordes who have gone mad with the lust for world domination? We who are Christians know that the Creator of all

Mounted Police-Qualifications
things is still in His realm and that He will see to it that eventually, although possibly not in our way, all will be well with the world.
In closing, I make reference to one matter which the previous speaker (Mr. Weir) mentioned, namely, free transportation for our soldiers. I am in favour of free transportation for our soldiers on long leave, such as Christmas leave, or, say one leave a year. When a soldier leaves his home he sacrifices his job, his civil liberties and the comforts of home. He goes out for what purpose? To see that we shall not be molested but that we shall remain free. We have men who are engaged on the railroads, who remain at home; they are not sacrificing their homes or their jobs or any of the liberties they have always enjoyed, but they are entitled to free railway passes not only for themselves but for their wives. This government has to contribute financial support to the railways, and I would say to the government, let the railways pay for their keep, and let us transport our soldiers home on long leave free of charge.
On motion of Mr. Abbott the debate was adjourned.
